title: The Unfinished Church
subtitle: Calling, Vision, and the Future God Is Still Building
blurb: The church is not a monument to defend or a method to chase. It is a building still rising, founded on a promise older than any of us and aimed at a city we have not yet seen. This book is about what it means to belong to something God is building and we are not finishing.

chapters.title: A Building Still Rising
chapters.summary: The church is unfinished by design, not by failure, and the promise that it will be built belongs to Christ, not to us. To see it rightly we have to stop measuring it against either its imagined past or its anxious future.
chapters.body:
There is a sentence in Matthew that we have domesticated almost beyond recognition. Jesus is standing at Caesarea Philippi, in the shadow of a rock face carved with the niches of dead gods, and he says to a fisherman who has just confessed him: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18). We quote it on cornerstones. We engrave it over doors. We have made it sound like a guarantee of permanence, as if the point were that the building would stand forever and never need another nail.

But that is not what the sentence says. It says he is building. Present tense reaching into future. A thing underway.

It matters where he said it, too. Caesarea Philippi was not a quiet place to teach. It sat at the base of a cliff honeycombed with shrines, a place the locals called the gate of the underworld, where the old religions of the region had piled up over centuries. Pan was worshiped there. Caesar was worshiped there. Standing in front of all that dead and dying religion, with the niches of the gods cut into the stone behind him, Jesus picks that exact spot to say he is going to build something the grave cannot stop. He did not pick a temple. He did not pick Jerusalem. He picked a graveyard of gods and announced a building.

I want to start there because I think most of our trouble starts there, with a misreading we never noticed we made. We hear "I will build my church" and our hearts file it under finished work, completed monument, a thing handed down for us to guard. And then we spend our ministries guarding it, and we cannot understand why guarding feels so much like dying.

I have spent fifteen years inside the institution of the church, most of them here at First Baptist in Fenton, and I have watched pastors and members alike treat the church as a finished structure that needs protecting. We protect the carpet. We defend the order of service. We argue about the color of the walls in the fellowship hall as if the kingdom hung on it. I sat in a meeting once where grown believers, people who loved Jesus, people who had buried spouses and raised children in that room, spent the better part of an hour on whether the new chairs should match the old chairs. I am not mocking them. I understand it better now than I did then. When you believe the building is finished and your job is to keep it, then every small thing becomes a battle over the keeping. We talk about the church the way a family talks about a house their grandparents built, with reverence, with grief, with the quiet assumption that the best work was done before we got here and our job is mostly maintenance. We are curators. We dust the relics. We keep the lights on. And we wonder why the young people who grew up in the back pews look at all that dusting and decide they would rather be somewhere alive.

That is not what we were handed.

The earliest picture the New Testament gives us for the church is not a fortress and not a museum. It is a construction site. Peter, the same man who heard the promise at Caesarea Philippi, writes years later that we are "living stones," being "built up a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:5). Look at the grammar. The verb is passive and it is ongoing. We are being built. We do not lay ourselves. Somebody else is doing the laying, and the work is not done. Paul says the same thing to the Ephesians. The household of God is "built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone," and in him "the building fitly framed together groweth unto an holy temple in the Lord" (Ephesians 2:20-21). Groweth. A temple that is still going up. The Greek word there is the word you would use for a body or a plant, something organic and increasing, not a stone block that gets quarried once and sits.

And notice what kind of stone Peter calls us. Living stones. That is a strange phrase if you stop on it. A stone is the deadest thing in a building, the thing that does not move, the thing you can count on to stay put. But Peter says living, because the wall is not finished and the stones in it are still being shaped. Anybody who has ever done masonry knows you do not lay a stone and walk away. You set it, you check it, you tap it down, you scrape the mortar, you come back and check the line again. A wall going up is a wall being fussed over. We are stones, and we are still being fussed over, by hands that have not stopped.

If you have ever lived next to a building under construction, you know the feeling of it. Scaffolding everywhere. Mud where the garden is supposed to be. Wires hanging out of walls that will one day hold paintings. Plywood over the windows. A dumpster in the driveway. A construction site is not a beautiful thing to look at, and anybody who walks past and judges the architecture by the present state of the rebar has misunderstood what they are seeing. The mess is not the failure of the building. The mess is the building, caught in the middle. You do not get the cathedral without the scaffolding first.

I think most of our despair about the church comes from forgetting this one thing. We look at the divisions, the scandals, the empty pews, the embarrassing things Christians say online, the slow leak of the young out the back door, and we conclude the project is failing. And let me be honest with you, because I am not going to write a book that pretends the church is fine. There is real failure in the church. I have contributed to it. I could tell you about decisions I made out of fear and called them faith, conflicts I handled out of pride and called them conviction. There was a man in this church I let walk out the door because I was too proud to make the first phone call, and I told myself I was protecting the church when I was protecting my own ego, and he is gone now and I do not know where he worships and that is on me. The failure is real and naming it is part of loving the thing. But there is a difference between a building that is collapsing and a building that is unfinished, and to the untrained eye they can look the same. Both have exposed beams. Both have gaps where the walls should be. Both look like something is wrong. One of them is dying. The other one is being born, and the only way to tell them apart is to know whose project it is.

And look at the rest of the sentence, the part we hurry past to get to the part we like. The gates of hell shall not prevail against it. We hear that and we picture the church as a fort with hell's army battering the door, and we cast ourselves as the desperate defenders inside, bracing the gate with our shoulders. But gates do not attack. Gates do not march. Gates are what you build when you are afraid of what is coming, and what you do to a gate, if you are on the offensive, is break it down. The picture Jesus draws is not a frightened church holding a wall against the assault of hell. It is hell on the defensive, hell with its gates shut, and the church coming up the hill against it. That is a strange thing to say about a hundred-some scared followers and a fisherman who would deny him within the year. But it tells you which direction the whole thing is supposed to move. We were not built to crouch behind the gate. We were built to go up against the other one.

I have to keep relearning that, because by temperament and by training I am a defender. I read the news about the church and my hands go up to brace the door. Somebody mocks the faith, somebody passes a law I do not like, some pastor falls and it makes the headlines, and the old instinct fires, protect the building, hold the line, batten it down. And every time, the sentence at Caesarea Philippi turns me around by the collar. Not your gate to defend. His to break. You are not the last man at the wall of a dying fort. You are a laborer on a building that is still going up against a hell that is still, two thousand years later, losing ground it cannot hold.

That is the question that decides everything. Whose project is it?

If the church is our project, then its future depends on our competence, our strategy, our ability to read the culture and adjust before the culture leaves us behind. And if that is true, then we have every reason to be afraid, because the evidence of the last hundred years is not encouraging. We have tried program after program. We have chased relevance and then chased rigor and then chased relevance again. We have driven to conference after conference, each one promising the next method that would finally work, and we have come home and tried the method, and the building has not risen the way the brochure said it would. If the church is our project, we should be terrified, and a lot of pastors I know are exactly that, terrified, lying awake at two in the morning doing math on the giving statements. I have done that math. I have sat at the kitchen table after everyone was asleep with the offering numbers in front of me and the roof estimate beside them, and felt the whole weight of it settle onto my chest, as if the survival of the body of Christ in this town came down to whether I could close a gap of a few thousand dollars by the end of the quarter. That is what it feels like to believe it is your project. It feels like a man holding up a ceiling with his arms, knowing his arms will tire.

But it is not our project.

"I will build my church." The pronoun is the whole sermon. He is the builder. We are the stones, and we are also the laborers, and somehow at the same time we are the material being shaped by the work, which is a strange thing to be, all three at once, but that is what we are. Augustine understood this. He was writing as the Roman world fell apart around him, and he made it the spine of his great book, The City of God. He watched Rome get sacked in the year 410, and the whole empire panicked, and people blamed the Christians for offending the old gods, and Augustine refused to grieve the fall of Rome as the end of anything that finally mattered. Because the city he belonged to was not built by Roman hands and would not fall when Roman walls fell. There is a city, he said, being built across the whole length of history, and its architect is God, and its completion is certain because its builder does not abandon what he starts. Augustine wrote that book over more than a decade while the lights of his civilization went out one by one. He died in the year 430 with an army of Vandals literally outside the walls of his own city of Hippo. And the last thing he was working on was a defense of the unfinished, unfailing city of God. Picture that, an old bishop, the harbor already cut off, the enemy at the gate, writing not a will and not a surrender but a book about a building that could not fall. That is not denial. He could see the Vandals as well as anyone. It is that he could see something further off than the Vandals.

That is the posture I want for us. Not the curator's reverence for a finished past. Not the strategist's anxiety about an uncertain future. Something older than both and steadier than both. Call it the bricklayer's confidence. The confidence that the architect knows what the building will be, even on the day when all you can see is mud and scaffolding and your own small course of bricks, laid a little crooked, in the rain. The bricklayer does not need to see the cathedral to do his work. He needs to trust that there is an architect, and that the plan is sound, and that the course he lays today will hold the course somebody lays tomorrow. He is not responsible for the dome. He is responsible for his row.

There is a freedom in this that I genuinely did not expect when I first understood it. When I believed the church was mine to finish, every problem in it was a verdict on me. Every family that left was my failure. Every drop in attendance was a referendum on my worth. Every conflict was a wall I had to hold up with my own back, and I was exhausted, and I was bitter, and I was the kind of pastor who controls everything because he is convinced that if he lets go, the whole thing comes down on top of him. I micromanaged volunteers who were better at their jobs than I was. I rewrote other people's prayers in my head while they were praying them. I have repented of that more than once. I will probably repent of it again before I am done. The man who thinks he is holding up the temple has confused himself with the cornerstone, and there is only one cornerstone, and it is not me.

It is not you, either. I mean that as relief, not as an insult. You can set it down. The weight was never yours to carry, and the fact that you have been carrying it as though it were is a big part of why you are so tired.

Let me put a name to the feeling, because abstractions do not keep anybody up at night, and this does. A church I know lost its biggest giving family in a single autumn, a couple who carried a real share of the budget, and they left over something small, a disagreement about a hire, the kind of thing that should not split a man from a body he had loved for twenty years. The pastor told me he sat in his office the Monday after they walked and did the arithmetic, and the arithmetic said the church could not survive the loss, and he felt the whole structure come down on him in that room as if he personally were the only thing between the congregation and the grave. He started measuring his worth in that gap. He started preaching a little harder, a little more desperately, the way a man holds on tighter when he is afraid. And the harder he gripped, the more the gripping showed, and the more it showed, the more people felt it, and a frightened pulpit makes a frightened pew. It took him the better part of a year to understand that the building was not coming down on him because the building was not his. The couple's leaving was a real loss and a real grief, but it was not a verdict, and it was not a collapse, and it was not the gates of hell prevailing. It was one stone moving out of a wall that the builder was still building, and the builder did not flinch, even though the pastor did.

I have been that pastor. I have done that arithmetic at that desk. The math is real and the fear is real, but the conclusion is a lie, and the lie is always the same lie. It says the project is yours and the outcome is on you. It is not.

There is a young family in our church, and I think about them when I am tempted to despair. They came in a hard year, a year we lost more than we gained, and they had every reason to look at the thin attendance and the worn carpet and the older crowd and keep driving to the bigger church across town with the better children's program. They stayed. I asked the husband once why. He shrugged and said it felt like a real place. Not a polished place. A real one. He did not know he was preaching to me. He was telling me that the unfinished thing, the honest, half-built, scaffolded thing, was exactly what drew him in, while I had been losing sleep over the very rough edges that made him stay.

So this is a book about hope. But I want to be careful right at the start about what kind of hope, because there are two cheap versions on offer everywhere, and both of them will let you down on a hard Tuesday. One says the church's best days are behind it and our job now is to defend the ruins of a Christian past, to hold the line, to keep what is left from washing away. That is a hope that is really nostalgia. It is hope facing backward, and we will spend a whole chapter on why it is a kind of unbelief. The other one says the church's best days are still ahead if only we find the right strategy, the right brand, the right technology, the right next thing. That is a hope that is really pragmatism, a hope that depends entirely on us, and we will spend a whole chapter on that one too. I want to refuse both of them. The hope I am after faces forward, like the pragmatist's, but it depends on God, like the nostalgic's God once did. It is the hope of a building still rising under the hands of a builder who has never once failed to finish what he started.

Somebody will push back here, and the push-back is fair, so let me answer it. If the church is God's project and he cannot fail, then why does anything I do matter? Why not put my feet up and let the architect work? But that gets the building backward. A builder who cannot fail does not make the laborers unnecessary. He makes them unafraid. The reason you can lay your crooked course in the rain and keep laying it is precisely that the outcome does not hang on your skill. You are freed to work hard without the work crushing you, because the success of the whole was never riding on your row. The cathedrals of Europe took centuries to build. The man who carved the gargoyle high on the north tower died long before the doors ever opened. He carved it well anyway, in the dark, where no one would ever stand close enough to see his work, because he trusted there would be a cathedral. That is not passivity. That is faith with a chisel in its hand.

The church is unfinished. I want you to hear that as the good news it is. It is not the bad news. It is the gospel of an ongoing God who said, at the foot of a rock full of dead gods, that he would build something the grave itself could not stop, and who has been building it ever since, through every generation, including the generations that were sure the whole thing was collapsing. The plague years, when the church buried its own dead and the dead of strangers and kept on. The fall of Rome. The corruption of the medieval church and the fire of the Reformation that followed it. The wars. The decline. Every one of those generations had people who were certain the church was finished, in the bad sense of the word, and every one of those generations was wrong, because the builder was still building. Do you understand what good company that puts us in? Every age that thought it was watching the end was actually only watching its own small section of the scaffolding come down and another go up. The funeral they kept planning never came.

And here is the part that should steady your hands. You will not see it finished. Almost certainly you will die in the middle of the work, the way nearly everyone who ever loved the church has died in the middle of the work, with the scaffolding still up and the wiring still hanging out. That used to feel to me like a tragedy, like coming to the end of a book with the last chapters torn out. It does not feel that way to me anymore. It feels like permission. I do not have to finish it. I was never asked to. I was asked to lay my courses well and hand the trowel to whoever comes after me, the way it was handed to me by people who are in the ground now and never saw what their faithfulness became. The woman who taught me the catechism is gone. She is not coming back to inspect her work. And her work is sitting here writing this. That is how the building rises. Not in one lifetime. In a relay of laborers who trust the architect enough to die mid-course.

He is still building it now. He is building it through people like you, who feel like rubble more days than stone. He has not changed his mind. He has not packed up his tools and walked off the site. The scaffolding is up, and the mud is everywhere, and the wiring is hanging out of the walls, and that is exactly what an unfinished building under the hands of a faithful builder looks like in the middle of the work.

He said he would build it. He did not say he was done.
chapters.verdict: He said he would build it. He did not say he was done.
reflect: Where in your life do you treat the church as a thing to preserve rather than a thing being built?
What would change if you believed the future of the church were a promise rather than a problem?
What unfinished work has God given you that you keep trying to finish on your own?

chapters.title: Between the Garden and the City
chapters.summary: Scripture begins in a garden and ends in a city, and the church lives in the long middle, called not merely to recover Eden but to participate in something Eden never was. Understanding our place on this arc reorders both our nostalgia and our ambition.
chapters.body:
The Bible opens in a garden and closes in a city, and almost nobody notices the distance between those two facts.

I did not notice it for years. I had read Genesis. I had read Revelation. I knew there was a garden at the front and something glorious at the back, and if you had asked me what the goal of the whole thing was, I would have said, without thinking too hard about it, that we were trying to get back to the garden. Back to before the fall. Back to innocence. That is the instinct most of us carry, and the church has fed it for a long time. We sing about the garden. We talk about getting back to Eden, getting back to how it was meant to be, recovering what was lost. There is an old hymn that has us walking in the garden alone, and it is a sweet song, and I am not coming for it. But notice the direction. Back. Always back. As if the whole point of grace were to undo, to return us to the start, to hit some cosmic reset.

And there is truth buried in that instinct, so I do not want to be too hard on it. Something was lost in the garden. Something does need recovering. The fall was real and its damage runs through every one of us. But if you actually read the last two chapters of Revelation, slowly, the way you would read a will that left you something, you notice that God does not put humanity back in the garden. He does not run the film backward. He does not reset us to factory settings. The end of the story is not Genesis chapter two restored to mint condition. It is something Genesis chapter two never was and was never going to be.

John sees "the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven" (Revelation 21:2). A city. With walls and gates and streets, with the nations walking by its light, with the kings of the earth bringing their glory into it (Revelation 21:24). Stop and feel the difference. The garden had two people in it. The city has multitudes that no one can count. The garden was raw potential, unworked ground, innocence that had never been tested. The city is cultivated, gathered, finished, fulfilled. A garden is what you are given. A city is what gets made, over generations, by people who lay stone on stone and dig wells and raise walls and bury their dead and teach their children the names of the streets. The garden was a gift. The city is a gift that has history in it, that has labor and love and even grief baked into its foundations. There is still a river there, and the tree of life is still there (Revelation 22:1-2), so the garden has not been abandoned. It has been taken up into something larger and carried forward. The end contains the beginning and then goes far past it. We do not end where we started. We end somewhere we have never been.

This matters enormously for how we think about the church, because the church lives in the middle of those two facts. We are after the garden and before the city. We are the people of the long between, and almost everything that confuses us about our situation comes from not knowing where on the road we are standing.

Notice too what the city does not have, because the absences preach as loud as the presence. There is no temple in it. John looks for one and cannot find it, and he tells us why, that the Lord God and the Lamb are the temple of it (Revelation 21:22). In the garden, God walked with man in the cool of the day, but there was distance built into it, a place to hide when you had sinned, and after the fall there were cherubim with a flaming sword keeping the way. In the temple that came later, there was a veil, a thick curtain that said this far and no farther. The whole architecture of the long middle is the architecture of separation, of a holy God and an unclean people kept apart for the people's own safety. And the city has none of it. No veil. No sword. No hiding in the trees. The dwelling of God is with men, the voice says, and he will dwell with them (Revelation 21:3). That is not a return to the garden. The garden had a gate that swung shut behind us. The city has gates that never close (Revelation 21:25), because there is no longer any night to lock them against and no longer any enemy to lock them from. We are not headed back to the supervised innocence of two people in a garden who could still fall. We are headed to a settled, unlosable, face-to-face nearness that the garden only hinted at and never held.

N.T. Wright has spent a good part of his life trying to wake the church up to this, especially in his book Surprised by Hope, where he argues that the Christian future is not the disembodied escape we have so often preached but the renewal of all things, heaven and earth joined together, a new creation that fulfills creation instead of throwing it away. He points out, and he is right, that our hymns and our funerals are full of leaving. Going up. Flying away. The soul departing for a better shore beyond the river. And the actual hope of the New Testament runs the opposite direction. God coming down. The city descending. Bodies raised. The earth made right. We have been singing the wrong direction at our own funerals. The hope is not evacuation off a sinking ship. It is restoration that surpasses the original ship, a world made not merely as good as new but better than new, because it will be a world that has been through death and come out the other side and can never die again.

I stood at a graveside last winter, cold ground, a small group of us, burying a woman from our church who had loved the Lord through forty hard years and a husband who drank and a son who left. And I caught myself, standing there in my coat, about to say the comfortable thing, the going-home thing, the she-is-up-there-now thing. And it is not that those things are simply false. But I made myself say the truer thing instead. That what we were doing, laying her body in the ground, was not the end of her body. That the same God who would not leave the garden behind will not leave her bones behind either. That we were planting her, the way Paul says, like a seed (1 Corinthians 15:42-44), and that a seed in the ground is not the opposite of a harvest. It is the beginning of one. The family did not need me to fly her away. They needed me to tell them the ground was not the last word. That is a different sermon than the one I almost gave, and it is the one the city teaches you to preach.

Somebody will object, and it is a serious objection, so I do not want to wave it off. Does this not make the present world too important? If we are building toward a city that God himself brings down out of heaven, finished, then are we not just decorating a house that is going to be demolished and rebuilt anyway? Why pour your life into a marriage, a congregation, a town, if the real thing comes down from above at the end regardless of what we do? I have felt the pull of that objection in my own chest on tired days, the suspicion that none of it finally matters because God will sort it out in the end with or without me. But read the city again. The kings of the earth bring their glory into it. Their glory. Something made down here, in history, by human hands and human faithfulness, is carried up into the city and is not burned but kept. The picture is not demolition. It is harvest. The farmer does not plant because the barn already has grain in it. He plants because the planting and the barn are connected, because what goes into the ground in the spring is what fills the barn in the fall. Wright argues this carefully, that the resurrection of the body tells us God does not scrap the material world, he raises it, and what is true of our bodies is true of our works. The good you build does not get thrown away. It gets raised. That changes everything about a Tuesday.

I find this clarifying for what the church is actually for, because it means we are not maintenance workers on a decaying world, hanging on until the rescue helicopter comes. We are early laborers on a project God fully intends to complete. The garden was given to us, free, at the start. The city is being built, and one day it will be handed down, finished. And between the gift and the finishing stretches the whole length of human history, including these particular years that we happen to have been handed to live in, and the church is the community that knows where the story is going and lives now in the light of where it ends.

A great deal of the church's confusion in this generation comes from losing our place on that road. When we forget the city ahead, we cling to a garden behind. We turn the church into a recovery project. Recover the 1950s. Recover Christendom. Recover the culture we used to have, the deference, the full pews, the sense that everybody more or less agreed with us. And so we become reactionary and grieving and suspicious, and we spend our best energy holding ground instead of building forward. We become the people who, told to march toward a city we have never seen, keep turning around to weep over a garden we can never reach and were never going back to in the first place.

The Israelites did this in the wilderness, and I think about them constantly because they are us. Brought out of Egypt and pointed toward a promised land they had never laid eyes on, they spent a remarkable amount of energy romanticizing Egypt. The fish they used to eat. The cucumbers. The melons, the leeks, the onions, the garlic (Numbers 11:5). Egypt. Where they had been slaves. Where Pharaoh had ordered their babies thrown in the river. The memory edited out the whips and kept the fish. That is what nostalgia does, and it does it to us as surely as it did it to them. It is not memory. It is memory with the suffering carefully removed, and it is one of the most powerful forces working against the church's calling, because it tells us the best thing God could possibly do for us is take us backward.

But the wilderness generation had a second temptation, and we have it too, and it is the opposite one, and I want you to see both ditches because the road runs between them. Some of them did not want to go back. Some of them wanted to seize the land by their own strength, on their own timeline, before the promise was ready. When the spies came back with their report, one faction wept and wanted Egypt, and another faction grabbed their weapons and charged up into the hill country without God going with them, and they got slaughtered (Numbers 14:44-45). Read that scene carefully, because it is easy to feel sympathy for the second group. At least they wanted to go forward. At least they were not weeping for cucumbers. But Moses tells them plainly, do not go up, for the LORD is not among you, and they go up anyway, and the ark of the covenant stays behind in the camp while they charge. That is the whole tragedy in one image. The presence of God remains in the tent, and the people storm the hill without it, and they are cut down. Nostalgia and pragmatism. The two ditches on either side of the road. One wants to go back to a past that never quite existed. The other wants to take the future by force, today, on its own steam. And both of them, underneath, are refusing the same thing. Both are refusing the slow, faithful, forward walk of a people who are being led by God toward a place they have not yet seen and cannot reach on their own.

I have watched both ditches in one congregation at one time, which is its own kind of education. We went through a season of decline in this church, a string of years where the funerals outnumbered the baptisms and the average age in the room kept climbing, and the two factions formed almost without anyone deciding to form them. There were the rememberers, the dear ones who wanted the church the way it had been, the hymns the way they had been, the building the way it had been, who heard every change as a small betrayal of the people now in the cemetery out back. And there were the fixers, mostly younger, who wanted to tear it all up and start over, new everything, new music, new name maybe, certain that the right overhaul by next spring would fill the parking lot. And I stood between them in the board meetings feeling the pull of both, because the rememberers loved something real and the fixers wanted something real, and both of them, underneath, were certain the future of the church depended on whether they won the argument. Neither of them was looking at the city. One was looking at Egypt. One was looking at the hill country they meant to storm. And the slow, unglamorous work of just walking forward together, burying the dead with honor and baptizing the new with joy and refusing to make either group the enemy, was the work neither faction had patience for, because it does not feel like winning. It just feels like walking.

The church is meant to walk that walk, right down the middle, between the weeping and the charging. Eugene Peterson called the Christian life a long obedience in the same direction. He borrowed the phrase from Nietzsche, of all people, which I have always found funny and a little perfect, and the direction matters every bit as much as the obedience. We are not walking in a circle back to Eden. We are walking a straight line, however much it feels like it winds, toward a city.

There is a thread running from Abraham straight through to that city, and once you see it you cannot stop seeing it. The writer of Hebrews says Abraham went out not knowing where he was going, and that he lived in tents in the land of promise like a stranger, because, the text says, "he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God" (Hebrews 11:10). Read that. The first man God called was already looking for the city at the end. He never saw it. He died in a tent. He owned, at the end of his long life, exactly one piece of the promised land, a cave he bought to bury his wife in. By every visible measure his faith failed to arrive. And Hebrews calls him the father of all of us, precisely because he kept walking toward a city he would not reach, and counted himself a stranger and a pilgrim the whole way (Hebrews 11:13). That is the company we are in. Not people who arrived. People who walked, in tents, toward foundations they trusted God was laying somewhere out ahead of them. The faith of the Bible is mostly the faith of people who died in the middle of the build.

So what does this mean on an actual Tuesday, in an actual church, with an actual budget shortfall? It means the work you do in the church right now is not the preservation of a fading thing. It is construction toward a coming thing. When you teach a seven-year-old the catechism she does not understand yet, when you sit with a widow in the afternoon because nobody else will, when you forgive the man who wronged you and have to forgive him again the next week, when you keep a congregation alive in a hard town that the young keep leaving, you are not slowing a decline. You are laying courses of brick in a wall whose blueprint is the New Jerusalem. Let me make that concrete, because I need it concrete as much as you do. There is a woman in our church who has taught the four-year-olds for thirty-one years. Thirty-one years of felt boards and goldfish crackers and little hands and the same flannelgraph Noah. She will never write a book. No conference will fly her in. And there are grown men in this congregation, fathers now, who know the name of Jesus because of a song she taught them when they could barely talk. She is not babysitting. She is laying brick. The blueprint of that work runs all the way out to a city she has not seen, and not one Sunday of it is wasted. Paul ends his great resurrection chapter, the longest sustained argument about the future anywhere in his letters, with exactly this logic. Because the dead are raised, because the future is secure and the city is coming, therefore, he says, "be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 15:58). The labor is not in vain because the city is real. He does not say work hard because it might pay off. He says work hard because it cannot fail to, because the end is already secured by the resurrection, and your courses of brick are going somewhere.

I will confess to you that I am a man more tempted by the second ditch than the first. I do not pine for the garden much. I am not really a nostalgia man. My temptation is to storm the city. To see it finished in my lifetime. To make it happen by strategy and effort and the sheer force of my own will, to be the pastor who built the thing. And that is its own kind of unbelief, and it took me longer to see it than the other one because it looks so much like faithfulness. It looks like zeal. But it treats the future as a thing I build rather than a thing God gives, and it always, always ends the way that charge up the hill country ended, in exhaustion and defeat, because I keep trying to seize by force what can only be received as a promise. I have charged the hill with the ark sitting back in the tent. I have launched the program and prayed about it afterward. I know which ditch is mine, and I have the bruises to prove it.

So here is the discipline of the middle, and it is harder than either ditch, which is why so few people stay on the road. We refuse to go back, and we refuse to charge ahead alone. We walk. We lay the courses we are given to lay. We trust the architect for a building we will not live to see finished. And we keep our eyes up, on the city, because the people who know where the road ends walk it differently than the people who are lost. The people who are lost get frantic, or they sit down and quit, or they turn around and head for Egypt. The people who know where the road ends just keep walking. There is a steadiness to them. You can feel it when you are around them. You have met them. The old saint in your church who is not impressed by the latest crisis and not impressed by the latest fad either, who has buried friends and survived three building disputes and four pastors and still shows up Wednesday night, still tithes, still prays for the missionaries by name. They are not in a hurry and they are not despairing, because they have read the end and the end is a city, and they are headed for it, one ordinary obedient day at a time. I want to be that when I grow up. I am not yet. But I know which direction it is in.

Jürgen Moltmann wrote a whole book on this, his Theology of Hope, written out of the rubble of postwar Germany by a man who had been a prisoner of war and had watched his own country reduced to ash, and his argument was that Christian hope is not a quiet add-on to faith but the engine of the whole thing. A church that has lost its forward hope, he said, does not become neutral. It becomes a defender of the status quo, a chaplain to whatever is, because if there is no city coming then the best you can do is shore up what you have. The hope of the city is what keeps the church from settling, from making peace with the way things are, from becoming a museum of a past glory. People who are headed somewhere do not redecorate the waiting room and call it home. They keep their coats on. They keep watching the door.

We are not going back to the garden. We are going on to the city.
chapters.verdict: We are not going back to the garden. We are going on to the city.
reflect: Do you imagine the goal of faith as a return to innocence or as arrival at something new?
What does it mean that the Bible ends in a city rather than a garden?
How does knowing where the story is going change how you live in the middle of it?

chapters.title: The Fire That Started It
chapters.summary: Pentecost is the church's beginning and its blueprint, the moment the Spirit launched a community that was never meant to be self-sustaining. The church runs on a fire it did not light and cannot replace with strategy.
chapters.body:
The church did not begin with a strategy. It began with a fire.

I want you to read the opening of Acts again and notice how little of it is human planning, because we tend to read it through eyes trained by a hundred leadership books and we import all kinds of strategy that simply is not on the page. A hundred and twenty people in an upper room. And the instruction they have been given is not to act, not to organize, not to launch, not to cast vision or build a team. The instruction is to wait. To wait "for the promise of the Father" (Acts 1:4). That is it. Wait.

Think about who is waiting. They have no building. They have no budget. Their leadership roster includes a man who very recently denied even knowing Jesus, three times, in a single night, with cursing. It includes a group that scattered and ran the moment the soldiers came. By any reasonable assessment, this is not a movement poised to outlast the Roman Empire. This is a frightened remnant hiding in a borrowed room. And then, on the day of Pentecost, "there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind," and "cloven tongues like as of fire" sat on each of them, "and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost" (Acts 2:2-4).

Everything the church has ever been, it became in that moment. Not because the disciples finally got their act together. Not because they workshopped a strategy in the upper room and emerged with a plan. Because God came down.

It is worth saying that the timing was not random either. Pentecost was already a feast, the feast of weeks, fifty days after Passover, and Jerusalem was packed with pilgrims from every direction, the very crowd that hears Peter preach and the very reason three thousand can be added in a day. God did not light the fire in a private room and leave it private. He lit it on the one morning the city was full of strangers who spoke a dozen languages, and the first thing the fire did was make itself understood in every one of those languages at once. That is not a strategy the disciples cooked up. They were as surprised as anyone. They did not pick the day. They did not gather the crowd. They were handed both.

And do not miss what the fire reverses. Long before, at Babel, humanity had gathered to build a tower with its top in the heavens, to make itself a name, to climb up to God by its own engineering, and God scattered them and confused their languages so they could not understand one another (Genesis 11:1-9). That is the picture of every human attempt to reach heaven from below by sheer competence and ambition. It ends in a half-built tower and a crowd that cannot talk to each other. Pentecost is Babel run backward. This time heaven comes down instead of man climbing up, and instead of confusing the languages God transcends them, so that a Galilean fisherman opens his mouth and a Parthian and a Mede and an Egyptian each hear the wonderful works of God in the tongue of his own cradle. The tower was a human project to manufacture access to God, and it collapsed into babble. The church is a divine gift of access to man, and it produced understanding. We are still tempted, every one of us, to build the tower. To make a name. To climb up by our own competence. And the fire still falls the other direction, every time, from heaven down, never from earth up.

I keep returning to this, and I make myself return to it, because I think the modern church has quietly stopped believing it. We would never say so. We would affirm the doctrine of the Holy Spirit if you asked us. But watch what we actually depend on. We have become extraordinarily good at the parts of Acts that do not require the Spirit at all. We can organize. We can market. We can build systems and platforms and brands and funnels. There is a conference for every conceivable competence and a podcast for every conference. And I am not against competence. Acts itself is full of organization. Deacons get appointed when the widows are being neglected (Acts 6). Money gets collected and distributed. Councils get convened to settle hard questions (Acts 15). The early church was not allergic to structure. But underneath all of its structure ran a fire that no committee produced, and when we forget the fire, all our competence quietly turns into machinery running on momentum, a flywheel that is spinning down, and the terrible thing is that a flywheel spinning down still spins, for a while, so you do not notice anything is wrong.

There is a moment in the gospels that I think names our exact danger, and it is the church at Laodicea in Revelation, though John writes it down later. The risen Christ says to that church, you say you are rich, increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and you do not know that you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked (Revelation 3:17). What strikes me is that Laodicea did not know. It is not a church that had taken stock of its condition and despaired. It is a church that felt fine. The reports looked good. The treasury was full. The self-assessment was glowing. And the only one in the room who could see the truth was the one standing outside the door knocking to be let back in (Revelation 3:20), which is its own terrible picture, the Lord of the church on the porch of his own house asking for entry while the people inside congratulate themselves on how well it is all going. That is the flywheel made into a letter. A church can lose the fire and keep every appearance of warmth, and the loss is invisible from the inside, which is precisely what makes it deadly. You do not get a warning light. The machinery hums right along. The only way to know is to ask whether the one who lit the fire is still in the room, or out on the porch, knocking.

Lesslie Newbigin saw this with painful clarity. He spent decades as a missionary in India, gave the strength of his life to it, and then came home to England in the 1970s and found a church there that had forgotten it was a missionary church at all. A church that simply assumed the culture, that ran on the borrowed momentum of a Christendom that had already, in fact, departed, though nobody had announced it. He started writing about the West as a mission field, which scandalized people, because we were supposed to be the ones who sent missionaries out to the dark places, not the ones who needed them sent to us. But Newbigin understood that a church living on cultural momentum rather than the present power of the Spirit is a church burning through fuel it stopped replacing a long time ago. Eventually the tank runs dry. And on that day you find out whether there was ever a fire at all, or only a flywheel that had been coasting.

I have pastored long enough to feel this in my own ministry, and I am going to tell on myself here because the book is no good if I do not. There are seasons when the machinery just runs, and you mistake the running for life. The services happen. The bulletin gets printed. The programs fill up. The reports look fine, the budget more or less balances, nobody is complaining loudly. And then one perfectly ordinary week you realize that you have not prayed. Not really prayed. Not the kind of prayer that admits you cannot do this, the desperate asking that gets down on the floor of the office and says God if you do not show up here, there is nothing. You have not prayed like that in longer than you want to admit. You have been running staff meetings and answering emails and preparing sermons the way a competent man prepares sermons, and you have been coasting on competence, and the fire is somewhere behind you, and you cannot quite remember when you left it. I will tell you when I noticed it last. I had preached what I thought was a good sermon, tight, well-built, a couple of lines I was a little proud of, and a man shook my hand at the door and said, that was nice, pastor, and went out to his car, and I stood there and realized that nice was exactly right. It had been nice. It had moved no one, least of all me. It was a sermon I could have written without God in the room, and I had. That is the flywheel. Nobody complains about the flywheel. It runs smooth. That is the danger of it.

The disciples could not have manufactured Pentecost. That is the point I cannot get past and do not want to get past. They did not work themselves up into it with the right music and the right lighting. They did not generate the wind by holding their breath together. The text is careful, almost stubborn, about making the whole thing arrive from outside them. From heaven. Given. The church is, at its very root, a receiving community before it is ever a doing community. We receive the Spirit. We do not produce him, and we cannot, and every generation of the church faces the same temptation to forget this and start running on what it can produce by itself, right up until the day the produced thing fails and we are reminded, usually painfully, that we were never the source of anything.

Jonathan Edwards understood the rhythm of this better than almost anyone, because he lived through it. He was a pastor in New England in the 1730s and 40s, and he watched the revivals come, watched whole towns turn to God in a matter of weeks, more people awakened in his little town of Northampton in six months than he had seen in years. And then he watched the fire recede, and the coldness return, and the town go back to its arguments and its business. He did not conclude from the receding that the fire had been fake. That is the mistake the cynics made. He concluded instead that the church lives by outpourings it cannot schedule, that revival is something God sovereignly gives and not something men engineer, and that the right posture is therefore not control but readiness. To pray. To wait. To seek. And to receive when God pours out, and not to despair when he does not. Edwards was a man of staggering intellect, a philosopher who could have done anything, and yet he built his whole understanding of the church on the conviction that it runs on a power it does not own and cannot command. And here is what cuts me about Edwards. The same town that he watched come alive eventually voted him out of his own pulpit. He preached a farewell sermon to people he had seen weep under conviction, and they let him go. He did not respond by deciding the awakening had been a sham. He went and preached to the Indians at Stockbridge and kept believing in a fire he could not schedule. That is a man who knew the difference between the fire and his own hands.

Here is an objection that deserves a straight answer, because I have heard it from good and serious people. If the church runs on a fire we cannot light, then is not all our work pointless? Why build the website, why train the deacons, why study for the sermon, why fix the leaking roof, if the only thing that matters is a wind we cannot summon? It sounds spiritual to say so, and it has wrecked more than one church to believe it. But it gets the relationship between the fire and the work exactly backward. Think of a fireplace. You cannot make the fire out of nothing, that is true. But you can lay the wood. You can build the structure that the fire, when it comes, will catch and spread through and warm a house by. A man who refuses to lay any wood because he cannot make the flame is not trusting God. He is just cold. And a man who lays the wood and then sits there demanding the fire obey his schedule has confused the kindling with the spark. The work is the laying of the wood. The faithful pastor, the trained deacon, the studied sermon, the sound roof over the heads of the people, these are the dry wood stacked and ready, so that when the wind from heaven comes through, there is something for it to catch. I have seen churches with all fire and no wood, all heat and no structure, and they flare and burn out in a season. I have seen churches with all wood and no fire, every system in place and the room stone cold. The whole art of it is to keep stacking the wood while you pray down the flame, and to refuse to despise either one.

This is humbling for those of us who like to be useful, and I am one of those. I am a builder by temperament. I want to do something, fix something, launch something, see a result by Friday. And the gospel keeps telling me, patiently, the same thing over and over, that the single most important thing about the church is something I cannot do, did not start, and cannot sustain by my own effort no matter how hard I work. The Spirit, Jesus told Nicodemus, "bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth" (John 3:8). You cannot command the wind. You cannot order it to blow on Sunday at 11. You can only raise the sail and be ready.

But watch what that does not mean, because people get this exactly wrong in the other direction. It does not mean passivity. It does not mean we sit and do nothing because it is all up to God. The disciples waited, yes, but look at how they waited. They waited together, in one place. They waited in prayer, constant prayer. They waited in obedience, doing the one thing they had been told to do. They even did some organizing while they waited, choosing a replacement for Judas. When the fire fell, they were positioned to catch it. There is a false spirituality that hides behind the sovereignty of the Spirit as an excuse to do nothing. Well, if it is all God, I will just sit here and wait for lightning. That is not the posture of Acts 1. The posture of Acts 1 is the sail raised in the dead-still air, the boat already pointed in the right direction, the whole crew at their stations, watching the horizon for a wind they cannot summon but fully mean to be ready for the second it comes. The sailor who refuses to raise the sail because he cannot make the wind blow is not being humble. He is being lazy and calling it trust. And the sailor who thinks his raised sail is what produces the wind is a fool of a different kind. The truth is in the middle, and the middle is uncomfortable, which is why so few of us live there.

There is a paradox in Paul that I lived inside for years before I understood it. He tells the Colossians that he labors, striving with all his energy, and then in the very same breath he says it is the energy "which worketh in me mightily" (Colossians 1:29). Whose energy is it? His, or God working in him? Both. At full strength, both at once. He is not half working and half trusting, splitting the difference, doing 50 percent and asking God for the rest. He is working with everything he has, and the everything he has is itself a power being supplied to him from somewhere he did not generate. That is the secret of the whole thing, and it took me a long time to stop dividing it. I used to think dependence meant doing less, that if it was God's work then my part must shrink. But Paul's dependence made him work harder, not softer, because a man drawing on a power not his own is not afraid of running out. The exhaustion I have known in ministry has almost always come from the other arrangement, from working in my own strength and calling on God only when mine failed, treating him as the reserve tank instead of the engine. The reserve-tank Christian works until he breaks and prays out of desperation. The engine Christian works just as hard and is somehow not consumed, because the strength is being supplied at the rate it is being spent.

So what does it actually look like, in a real church, to depend on a fire you cannot light? It looks like prayer that genuinely asks God to do what you cannot do, instead of prayer that is really just a religious way of reviewing your plans. It looks like preaching that aims past technique, past the clever turn and the moving illustration, at the conviction that only the Spirit can give, and that is content to fail by every visible measure if the Spirit does not come, and refuses to manufacture a counterfeit of his work with emotional manipulation. I have done the counterfeit, by the way. I have known how to dim the lights and drop my voice and play the song that gets the tears going, and I have watched people respond, and I have walked away knowing I made that happen, that it was me and not him, and that the thing I made will not last past the parking lot. It looks like planning that holds its plans loosely, with open hands, ready to be overruled by a wind from heaven that blows the whole plan sideways. And it looks like a church that measures itself not by the smoothness of its machinery but by its hunger for the presence of God, because that hunger is itself the first sign that the fire has not gone out. The cold church does not even know it is cold. The hungry church, the one that aches for more of God, is already nearer the fire than it feels.

I think of a Wednesday night prayer meeting we held in a hard stretch, and I almost did not hold it, because I knew who would come. Seven people, mostly older, the same seven who always came, in a room built for two hundred, the chairs cold and the lights too bright for so few. By every metric I had been trained to value, it was a failure of a gathering. No momentum. No buzz. Nothing to put in a report. And an older man named in that little circle prayed a prayer I have never forgotten, not eloquent, not polished, just a farmer's son asking God plainly to come and do what none of us could do, to save his grandson who had walked away, to wake the church up, to send the wind. And I sat there embarrassed at first by the smallness of it, and then ashamed of my embarrassment, because I realized those seven cold-chaired people, asking God for what only God can give, were nearer the engine of the whole church than I had been in months of my smooth and competent labor. The fire is not in the size of the room. It never was. It is in whether anyone in the room is actually asking. Those seven were asking. I had stopped, and dressed up the stopping as strategy.

Pentecost was not the church's launch event, a one-time ignition that we now coast on, the way a company tells the story of its founding. It was the revelation of how the church always runs. On the present power of a present God. Given and not earned. Received and not produced. The same Spirit who fell in that upper room is the Spirit your church needs this morning, this exact morning, not a memory of him and not a doctrine about him but him. And the temptation in every single generation is to swap him out, quietly, for our own competence, our own momentum, our own machinery, and then to keep the lights on for years after the fire has gone out, not even noticing how cold the room has become, because the flywheel is still turning and the reports still look fine.

So ask the only question that finally matters about your church and about your own soul. Not whether the machinery is running, because it can run cold for years. Not whether the reports look good, because Laodicea's reports looked wonderful. Ask whether anyone is still hungry. Ask whether you are. Because the fire does not begin with a strategy and it does not begin with a budget. It begins, every single time, in a borrowed room full of people who have nothing and know it, waiting on a promise, asking God to come down. That was the first morning. It is still the only way.

The church began with a fire we did not light, and it will not run on fuel we manufacture.
chapters.verdict: The church began with a fire we did not light, and it will not run on fuel we manufacture.
reflect: Are you depending on the Spirit's power or on your own competence to sustain the work God has given you?
What in your church life is running on borrowed momentum rather than present fire?
When did you last ask God to do what only God can do?

chapters.title: When the Empire Adopted Us
chapters.summary: The conversion of the empire and the long age of Christendom gave the church power and respectability at the cost of forgetting how to live as a minority witness. Its passing is loss and gift at once, and the church must learn again what it was before the empire adopted it.
chapters.body:
In the year 312, a Roman general saw something in the sky before a battle and changed the shape of the church for the next seventeen centuries.

You know the story, or a version of it. Constantine, marching on Rome, claimed to see a sign, a cross of light, and the words in this sign conquer. He won the battle at the Milvian Bridge, credited the God of the Christians, and within about a decade the faith that the empire had been feeding to lions in the arena was the faith the emperor himself protected and promoted. By the year 380, under the emperor Theodosius, Christianity was not merely legal. It was the official religion of the Roman state. The catacombs emptied out. The persecuted became the established. And the church, which had spent three hundred years learning, in blood, how to be a minority, gathered in homes, suspect, powerless, occasionally hunted down and killed, suddenly had to learn how to be a majority, with property and prestige and money and the sword of the state never far away.

Sit with the speed of that for a second, because we read it as a paragraph and they lived it as a whiplash. There were Christians alive in the year 320 who could remember the Great Persecution under Diocletian, which had only ended a few years before, when churches were burned and Scriptures were confiscated and believers were tortured to make them hand over the sacred books. Some of those same people lived to see the emperor build basilicas and seat bishops at his table. One generation hides in the catacombs. The next generation gets invited to the palace. Nobody had a manual for that. How could they? Nothing in their experience or their Scriptures had prepared them to be the favored religion of the most powerful man on earth. They had a field manual for being hunted. They had to improvise everything about being preferred.

It is worth saying that not everyone went quietly when the change came, and the ones who resisted are worth remembering, because they understood what was at stake before most of the church did. Out in the deserts of Egypt, while the bishops were learning to dine with emperors, men and women walked away from the newly comfortable church and went to live alone in the sand. We call them the desert fathers and mothers. People have read their flight as a kind of extremism, and some of it was. But underneath a good deal of it was a stubborn instinct that the faith had cost something when it was illegal, and now that it cost nothing, something essential was draining out of it, and they meant to go find the cost again on purpose, since the world would no longer supply it. They sensed, the moment the persecution stopped, that comfort was its own kind of danger, maybe a subtler one than the lions. They were not entirely right and they were not entirely wrong. But the fact that the church's most serious people fled to the desert at the very moment the church won its great worldly victory should tell you something about what that victory quietly cost.

Historians call the long age that followed Christendom. It is a useful word and we are going to use it a lot in this book, so let me say plainly what it means. Christendom is the arrangement in which the church and the surrounding culture were assumed to be one and the same thing. Where to be born in a Christian country was, by default, to be counted a Christian. Where the church set the calendar and the holidays, blessed the king and his wars, occupied the center of public life, and where unbelief, not belief, was the strange and difficult position to hold. For most of us who were raised in the church in the West, Christendom is the only church we have ever personally known, and so, without ever deciding to, we have mistaken its particular habits for the gospel itself. We assume that of course the church is at the center. Of course the culture more or less shares our values. Of course the prayer opens the town meeting and the cross hangs in the public square. We think this is Christianity. It is Christendom, which is a very different and much more recent thing.

Let me put it close to home, because the abstraction does not bite until it gets local. When I was a boy, the stores were closed on Sunday. Not because everyone in town was converted. Because the whole culture was arranged around a Christian assumption, and the assumption was so total that nobody noticed it was an assumption. Little League did not schedule games during the worship hour. The public school choir sang carols in December and nobody wrote a letter about it. A man running for county office let it be known that he was a churchgoer, whether or not he had ever met God, because it helped him with voters, the way it helped him to be seen as a good family man. None of that was the gospel. Every bit of it was Christendom, the cultural scaffolding that made being a Christian the path of least resistance. And I grew up assuming it was just how the world was, the natural order, the way water assumes the river it is in. I did not know I was swimming in something that could drain.

And that arrangement is ending. It has been ending for a long time, slowly, but in the last few decades the ending has sped up, and you can feel it in any congregation in the country, you can feel it in the parking lot before the service even starts. The culture no longer assumes the faith. The church no longer occupies the center of anything. The young no longer drift in by default the way their grandparents did, because the social machinery that used to drift them in has been switched off. Christianity in the West is becoming, again, a minority position. Sometimes tolerated, sometimes mocked, increasingly just strange, the way a vegetarian was strange at a Midwestern dinner table forty years ago, not hated exactly, just odd. And I have come to believe that a great deal of the church's anxiety right now is really grief over this, the grief of a community losing a status it held for so long that it forgot the status had ever been granted, forgot it was a loan and not a possession.

I sat with a man in my office not long ago, retired, faithful his whole life, and he was grieving, genuinely grieving, and what he said was, this is not the country I grew up in, and the church is dying, pastor, the church is dying. And I understood him, and I loved him, and I had to gently take those two sentences apart, because he had welded them together and the weld was the whole problem. The country he grew up in was changing, yes, that part was true. But the second sentence did not follow from the first. He had so deeply identified the faith with the culture that surrounded it in his boyhood that when the culture moved, it felt to him exactly like the faith was being lowered into the ground. I asked him whether his grandson, who had recently come to a living faith out of nowhere, out of a campus ministry his grandfather had never heard of, whether that boy was evidence of a dying church. He stopped. He had not connected the two. The culture of his youth was indeed passing. And in the same season, in a way that owed nothing to that culture, the Spirit had laid hold of his grandson. Both things were true at once, and he had only been able to see the first.

Now I want to say something that is going to sound like betrayal to some of you and like deep relief to others, and I want both kinds of readers to stay with me through it. The passing of Christendom is not the death of the church. It may turn out to be one of the better things to happen to the church in a thousand years.

Let me tell you why I believe that, because I am not saying it to be provocative. Christendom gave the church power, and power is a dangerous gift to give to sinners. The very same arrangement that filled the cathedrals also produced the crusades, where the cross was carried into slaughter. It produced the inquisitions, where the church tortured people for the good of their souls. It produced the slow, terrible fusion of cross and sword and crown, until ordinary people could no longer tell where the gospel ended and the empire began, where Christ stopped and Caesar started. When the church sits at the center of power, it stops needing to persuade and it starts being able to coerce, and coercion is so much easier than persuasion, and so much cheaper, and so much more deadly to the soul of the one doing the coercing. It stops being a witness and starts being an establishment. Look at how the church grew in the first place, before it had any power at all. The early church converted the empire from below, from underneath, by the strange and unaccountable power of love, by martyrs who sang while they died, by a community that took in abandoned babies the pagans had left out on the hillsides to die, that nursed the plague-stricken when everyone else fled the city. When the great epidemics swept the Roman cities and the wealthy ran for the countryside and left the sick to die alone, it was the Christians who stayed and carried water to strangers and buried the dead and caught the disease doing it. People noticed. You could not buy that kind of witness. You could only live it, or die of it. The established church, too often, maintained itself from above, by law and pressure and the simple assumption that everyone was already in, so why bother loving anyone into it.

Kierkegaard saw this in nineteenth-century Denmark and it made him furious, and his fury is worth listening to. A whole nation of baptized people. Official Christians. Everyone a Christian, by birth, by registration, by the fact of being Danish. And in that situation, he said, being a Christian cost you absolutely nothing, and therefore it meant absolutely nothing. When everyone is a Christian, no one is. The faith that the early church had died for had become, under Christendom, a thing you were simply born into, like your nationality or your eye color, requiring nothing, costing nothing, changing nothing. And Kierkegaard thought this had hollowed out the whole thing, emptied it of everything that made it actually the gospel. He was not gentle about it. He thought Christendom had to die in order for Christianity to have any chance of living again. He spent his last energy attacking a comfortable state church that he believed was the most dangerous enemy the faith had, precisely because it looked like a friend.

Augustine, again, saw the heart of it from inside the wreckage of his own age. When Rome fell in 410 and the pagans blamed the Christians for abandoning the old gods who had supposedly kept the city safe, Augustine refused to defend Rome as though Rome were the thing that mattered. He drew his famous line between two cities, the city of man and the city of God, built by two loves, the one by love of self even to contempt of God, the other by love of God even to contempt of self. And the point he kept making, page after page, was that these two cities are mingled together in this age, intertwined, impossible to fully separate until the end, which means the church is always tempted to mistake the city of man for the city of God when the two happen to be wearing the same clothes. Christendom was exactly that mistaking, four centuries after Augustine warned against it and a thousand years after, the two cities wearing the same robes for so long that we forgot they were two. The end of Christendom is, among other things, the two cities taking their robes back off. It hurts. But it lets you see again which city you actually belong to, which is a thing the comfortable centuries made very hard to see.

I do not romanticize persecution. It is easy for a comfortable Western pastor to wax poetic about the purifying fire of opposition from the safety of a heated office. I am not eager to lose what the church has had. I am not standing in a cell in another country. I drive a paid-off car to a building with a working furnace, and I do not get to lecture the suffering church about the blessings of suffering. There is real loss in this, and we will sit with the loss. But I cannot help noticing a pattern in church history that runs the opposite direction from our fears. The church tends to grow most vital not at the center of power but at the edge of it, not in the seasons of comfort but in the seasons of cost. And here is something we forget. The entire New Testament was written from the edge. By a persecuted minority. With no political power, no cultural assumption working in their favor, no establishment to lean back against. The letters of Paul assume a church that is strange to its neighbors, that has to explain itself constantly, that wins people one at a time by the visible difference of its life, not by the weight of the culture pushing them in the door. That is the church we are becoming again. And the remarkable thing, the genuinely hopeful thing, is that we have, sitting right there in our New Testament, a complete field manual for exactly this situation, written by people who never knew Christendom and frankly would not have recognized it if they saw it. They would not have understood a church at the center of power. It would have looked to them like a contradiction in terms.

The real danger in this moment, the thing I most want to warn against, is that we will spend our limited energy trying to recover the empire's version of the church instead of the church underneath it. We will fight to get the center back. The laws. The prayers in the schools. The cultural deference, the assumption of belonging, the Christian nation. We will mistake the recovery of influence for the recovery of faith, and pour ourselves into the first while neglecting the second. And I understand the impulse, I feel it in my own chest, especially when I watch things I love get pushed to the margins and mocked. I have caught myself reading the news and feeling the old establishment grief rise up, the sense that we are being evicted from a house that was ours. But here is the question I have had to ask myself in those moments. Was it ever ours? Or did we just live in it long enough to think we held the deed? A church that organizes itself primarily around regaining lost power has fundamentally misunderstood its own founder. The one who was offered all the kingdoms of the world, every bit of the power we are scrambling to recover, and who turned it down flat (Matthew 4:8-10). The one who told Pilate to his face, "my kingdom is not of this world" (John 18:36). The one who built his church not on a throne but on a cross, not by seizing the center but by being driven outside the city walls to die. The author of Hebrews makes a point of it, that Jesus suffered outside the gate (Hebrews 13:12), and then tells us to go to him there, outside the camp, bearing his reproach. The center was never where he was. We are not being exiled from his church when we lose the center. We are being sent back to where he has been the whole time.

Bonhoeffer learned all of this in the hardest possible school, and it cost him everything. He watched the German church, the established and respectable church of a supposedly Christian nation, fold itself almost entirely into the Nazi state in the 1930s. That was Christendom's final and most monstrous logic playing all the way out, the cross fused to the swastika, pastors giving the salute, the establishment doing what establishments do, which is bless the powerful. And out of that catastrophe Bonhoeffer came to believe, with his whole life on the line, that the church must actually be the church. Distinct. Costly. A community that follows Christ even against the nation, even against the culture, even against the very empire that had adopted it and now demanded its loyalty. He paid for that conviction with his life. They hanged him in April of 1945, days before the camp was liberated, the war all but over, the regime already collapsing, and they killed him anyway because a costly church is exactly the thing an empire cannot abide. But he left the church a vision of itself stripped of all establishment, the church as a costly minority that belongs to Christ before it belongs to any nation, any flag, any party, any culture.

Let me be concrete about what the difference looks like on the ground, because this can float off into theory and I do not want it to. A church organized around recovering the center spends its energy on the levers of the center. It wants the right people elected, the right symbols protected, the right laws restored, and it measures its health by how much deference it can still command in the public square. A church organized around the gospel underneath the empire spends its energy somewhere else entirely. It feeds the people the food bank misses. It takes in the hardest children in the county welfare system, the ones nobody else will house, the way the early Christians took in the babies left out on the hillsides. It tells the truth at cost to itself. It loves the neighbor who mocks it. It wins one skeptic at a kitchen table over two years of patient friendship rather than trying to win a culture by force in a season. The first church can be powerful and empty at the same time, and history is full of examples of exactly that. The second church can be small and poor and have almost no standing at all, and be the most alive thing in the county. I have to ask myself honestly which church I am actually building with my weeks, because my anxieties pull me toward the first and my Lord points me toward the second, and the schedule does not lie about which one is winning.

That is the recovery actually on offer to us in this moment. Not the recovery of the empire's church, which I am increasingly convinced we should let go of without a fight. But the recovery of the church beneath the empire. The gathered, peculiar, persuading, serving, costly community that existed before Constantine ever saw his sign in the sky and will go on existing long after the last so-called Christian nation has forgotten it was ever Christian.

So I refuse the grief that treats the loss of cultural power as if it were the loss of the faith itself. We are not losing the church. The church was never the cathedral at the center of the medieval town. It was never the prayer that opens the legislative session, or the cross on the courthouse wall, or the comfortable assumption that the neighbors share our creed. The church was always the body of Christ. The living stones. The people of the fire. And every one of those things survives the end of Christendom completely intact. What dies, what is dying right now in front of us, is the arrangement. The comfortable fusion that let us mistake a culture for a faith and a borrowed status for a divine calling.

Let it die.
