Grieve it if you need to, and I do, some gray afternoons, when I drive past a church building near here that is now a brewery, the sanctuary windows still there above the taps, or the old downtown chapel that got carved into apartments with the steeple left on for charm. Grieve it honestly. There were real prayers prayed in those rooms, real babies baptized, real hands held at real deathbeds, and it is right to feel something when the room becomes a bar. But do not confuse the funeral of Christendom with the funeral of the church. One of them is an empire's borrowed clothing, finally wearing out. The other is a building God is still raising, course by course, and no empire ever held the deed to it, and no empire's collapse can stop the builder's hand.

I find, the more I sit with it, that I am less afraid of the margin than I used to be, and more afraid of what the center did to us while we held it. A church at the center can coast for generations on borrowed assent and never know it has stopped persuading anyone of anything. A church at the margin cannot coast at all. It has to mean it. Everyone in the room on a given Sunday is there on purpose, against the grain, at some cost, because the culture is no longer carrying them in. That is a smaller church. It may be a poorer one. But it is awake in a way the establishment church was allowed to forget how to be. The first Christians built a movement that outlasted Rome itself with none of the advantages we are mourning the loss of, and they did it from a position weaker than ours will ever be. We have the same Lord they had, the same Spirit, the same field manual written for exactly this. We are not being abandoned. We are being handed back the conditions under which the thing was born.

We are not losing the church. We are losing the empire's version of it.
chapters.verdict: We are not losing the church. We are losing the empire's version of it.

Where are you grieving the loss of influence as if it were the loss of faith?

chapters.title: The Sin of Nostalgia
chapters.summary: Longing for a golden age of the church is not faithfulness but a refusal to trust God with the present, and it edits the past into a fiction. The church is called forward, and nostalgia is a way of facing backward while pretending to be devout.
chapters.body:
Every church I have ever served has had a golden age, and it is always just barely out of reach.

For some of them it was the 1950s, when the pews were full and the culture agreed with us and the parking lot could not hold all the cars. For others it was a particular pastor, the one before the one before me, the one everybody still talks about. For others it was a building program, or a revival, or a single charged year that everyone who was there remembers as the time when God was really among us, after which everything was somehow a little less. The details change from church to church, but the structure is always identical, and once you learn to see it you cannot unsee it. There was a time when the church was what it was supposed to be. We have fallen from it. And our task now is to grieve the fall and, if we possibly can, to get back.

Let me show you how it sounds, because it almost never announces itself. It comes out sideways, in a comment after a meeting, in the parking lot, when the cars are starting up. A man in his seventies stops you by your car door. He is not angry. He is wistful, which is harder to answer than anger. "You should have seen this place when Pastor Harmon was here," he says. "We had three hundred in Sunday school. The choir loft was full. We had to put chairs in the aisles at Easter." And then he looks at the half-empty lot, and he looks at you, and he does not finish the sentence, but the sentence finishes itself in the silence. And what could you possibly say? You were not here. You cannot defend a present against a past you never saw. So you nod, and you say something soft, and you drive home with that unfinished sentence sitting in the passenger seat the whole way.

I have had a hundred versions of that conversation. The deacon who keeps the old attendance ledgers in a drawer and brings the numbers up at the annual meeting, not to plan but to mourn. The widow who tells you, gently, that the music used to feed her and now it does not, and you understand that she is not really talking about music. The longtime member who looks at a sanctuary that holds four hundred and seats ninety and feels the emptiness as a personal accusation. None of these are bad people. Most of them are the most faithful people in the building. That is part of what makes nostalgia so hard to deal with. It lives in the most committed hearts, not the least.

Here is what unsettled me when I first started noticing this. I have heard this exact lament in churches that are, by any honest measure, healthier than they have ever been in their history. More people genuinely converted. More real discipleship happening. Less dead nominal attendance. And still, the golden age. Still the sense that we have lost something. I remember a congregation, not far from here, that had cut its Sunday count almost in half over twenty years and, in the same twenty years, had baptized more adult converts off the street than in the previous fifty. People coming in from nothing. People with no church background at all, no grandmother who dragged them, sitting in those pews because something real had happened to them. By every measure that matters to heaven, that church was more alive than it had ever been. And the old guard grieved. They grieved the count. They could not see the fire for the empty seats. And that is when it finally clicked for me. The golden age is not a fact about the past at all. It is a feeling about the present, projected backward, dressed up in old photographs.

I have come to believe that nostalgia is one of the most spiritually destructive forces loose in the church, and at the same time one of the least examined, and the reason it goes unexamined is that it does not look like a sin. It does not feel like a sin. It looks like love. It looks like reverence for what God has done in the past. It wears the costume of devotion, and it speaks in a warm and trembling voice about the old days, and who would dare call that sin? You cannot rebuke a man for loving the church he gave forty years to. You cannot stand in a pulpit and tell a room full of saints that their fond memories are a problem. So nobody does. The thing goes unnamed, and unnamed things grow. But underneath the costume, nostalgia is a quiet accusation against the God of the present. It is a way of saying that the best of him is behind us. That he was more himself back then than he is now. That the building he is raising today is a cheaper, lesser thing than the building he raised before, and that we are stuck living in the disappointing later chapters of a story whose good parts are already over.

Say that out loud and it sounds like blasphemy, because it is. But nobody says it out loud. We only feel it, and we let the feeling steer the church.

The Bible is remarkably unsentimental about this, and I find that bracing. When the second temple was being rebuilt in Jerusalem after the exile, after seventy years of the people longing to go home, the old men who had been children when Solomon's temple still stood looked at the new foundation and they wept. Not with joy. With grief. Because the new one was smaller, poorer, less glorious than the one they remembered (Ezra 3:12). Picture the day. They have come back from Babylon. They have crossed a desert. They have rebuilt their houses and replanted their fields, and now, finally, the foundation of the house of God is laid, and a great crowd gathers, and some of them shout for joy so loud you can hear it for miles. And mixed into the shouting is a sound of weeping, the old men, who can see in their minds a building these younger ones never saw, and who cannot make the new foundation match the old glory, and so they cry. And the text says you could not tell the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping. They blended together into one sound. That is the church right there, on most Sundays. Joy and grief in the same room, in the same song, indistinguishable from the parking lot.

And God's word to those weeping old men, through the prophet Haggai, is not the comfort you would expect. It is a rebuke. "Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing? Yet now be strong... for I am with you" (Haggai 2:3-4). And then the line that should stop us cold: "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former" (Haggai 2:9). Read that again. The old men were weeping over a building that God himself said would surpass the one they were mourning. Their nostalgia had them in tears at the precise moment they should have been on their feet hoping. They were grieving at a groundbreaking.

I want you to feel how strange that is. God does not pat them on the back. He does not say, there, there, I know the old place was beautiful, let us have a moment for what we lost. He says, in effect, your eyes are lying to you. You are measuring with the wrong ruler. The thing you are crying over is going to be greater than the thing you are crying for, and you cannot see it because you will not stop looking backward long enough to look up. That is what nostalgia does to a person. It positions you to weep over the better thing, because the better thing does not match the remembered thing, and the remembered thing has become the only measure you trust.

And the remembered thing is almost always a fiction. This is the part I learned by pastoring people through their own golden ages, by sitting with them long enough to hear the whole story and not just the highlight reel. The memory has been edited. The 1950s church that people pine for was full, yes, but it was full in large part because the culture made church attendance a basic social requirement, a thing you did to be respectable, to be hireable, to be marriageable. The boss went, so you went. The neighbors went, so you went. Your name being on a church roll was a kind of social credit. And so a great deal of that famous fullness was nominal. It was the Christendom attendance we talked about earlier, the pews packed with people who had never once been converted and were there because their boss was there, or because their mother would have died of shame if they were not.

I have learned to ask one gentle question when somebody starts telling me about the glory days. I ask them to tell me the whole story. Not the highlight. The whole thing. And it is remarkable what surfaces. The packed church of 1958 had a split in 1961 that people still will not talk about, families that left and never came back, a feud over the new building that ran along bloodlines for two generations. The beloved former pastor, the one whose name still gets spoken like a benediction, had a temper, or a drinking problem, or a way of running roughshod over the deacons that everyone tolerated because he filled the pews. We forget the worst things about people once they are gone. We canonize them. The remembered revival conveniently leaves out the burnout that followed it, the people who flamed hot for a season and then disappeared, the marriages that the emotional pitch of that year actually strained rather than healed. Nostalgia is memory with the suffering surgically removed, and the operation produces a past that never actually existed, a perfect past, against which the real and difficult present can never possibly compete. You cannot win against a fiction. The present is real, and reality always has mud on it, and the fiction never does, because we washed the mud off in the remembering.

The Israelites in the wilderness remembered Egypt as a land flowing with fish and cucumbers (Numbers 11:5). They left out that Egypt was the house of bondage, the place of whips and dead babies. Read the menu they recited, standing there in the desert with God's own bread falling out of the sky every morning. We remember the fish, they said. The cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, the garlic. Listen to that list. It is a grocery list. It is a man romanticizing the cafeteria of his prison. Not one word about the lash. Not one word about the foremen, or the quotas, or the order to drown their sons in the Nile. The edit is always the same in every generation. Keep the comfort. Delete the bondage. And the spiritual result is always the same too. It makes you want to go back to the very place God shed blood to bring you out of. That is the terrible end of it. Nostalgia does not just make you sad. It makes you homesick for slavery.

I think this is exactly why Scripture so consistently commands one particular kind of remembering and so consistently warns against another kind, and we miss it because we lump all looking-back together. We assume the Bible is simply for memory, since it tells us to remember so often. But it is not. It is for one kind of memory and against another, and the line between them is the whole thing. Israel was commanded, over and over, to remember the exodus. Remember that you were slaves in Egypt. Remember the night God brought you out. Build the festivals around it, tell it to your children, keep it alive. But notice how they were to remember it. As deliverance. As evidence of God's faithfulness. As fuel for trusting him going forward, into the unknown land. That is memory in the service of hope. It looks backward in order to give you courage to look forward. Nostalgia is memory in the service of despair. It is the same physical act, looking backward, but it runs in opposite directions and produces opposite people. One kind of remembering sends you forward with courage. The other kind sits you down in the dust to weep for a country you were rescued from. You can usually tell which one a person is doing by what it makes them do next. Holy remembering makes you braver about tomorrow. Nostalgia makes you bitter about today.

Walter Brueggemann thought about this as deeply as anyone in the last century, and his work on what he called the prophetic imagination has shaped how I read the whole Old Testament. He argued that the prophet's central task is to break the grip of a frozen past and a foreclosed future, to crack open the present so that the people can imagine God doing a genuinely new thing instead of just repeating or restoring the old one. He drew this straight out of Isaiah, where God says to the exiles, of all people, "Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing" (Isaiah 43:18-19). Sit with who is hearing that. People in exile. People who had lost the temple, the land, the monarchy, the priesthood, everything that had made them who they were. People with every conceivable reason to romanticize the past, because the past was objectively better than their present captivity. Their golden age was not a fiction. They really had lost something glorious. And to those exact people, the ones with the most legitimate grievance, God says, stop looking back. Do not even consider the things of old. I am about to do something you have never seen.

That is the part that arrests me. He does not say it to people whose memories are false. He says it to people whose memories are true, whose loss is real, and he still says stop looking back. There is a kindness in that severity that we miss if we only hear the sharpness. God is not telling the exiles their grief is foolish. He is telling them their grief, if they let it become the whole posture of their lives, will blind them to the very rescue he is bringing. The most dangerous nostalgia is not the kind built on a fiction. It is the kind built on a real and beautiful loss, because that kind feels so justified that you will defend it to the death, and you will sit in it, facing backward, while deliverance walks up the road behind you and you never turn around to see it. The prophetic word, again and again, turns out to be a word against nostalgia, because nostalgia is the single greatest obstacle to hope. You cannot keep watch for the new thing on the horizon while your face is turned around weeping over the old one behind you. You will miss it coming. It will come up the road in front of you while you are facing the wrong way, and you will not even see it, because you were looking at Egypt.

Now I can hear the objection, because I have raised it myself. Is it wrong to be grateful for the past? Is it a sin to love the church my grandparents built, to treasure the saints who taught me, to be thankful for the seasons when God was near? No. A thousand times no, and if I have made it sound that way I have failed. Gratitude for the past is the soil hope grows in. The exodus people were commanded to remember precisely so they could hope. The difference is not whether you love the past. The difference is what the love does. Gratitude says, look what God did, therefore I can trust him with tomorrow. Nostalgia says, look what God did, therefore today is a disappointment and tomorrow is a threat. One kind of love opens your hand toward the future. The other curls it into a fist around the past. You can love what was without resenting what is. The patriarchs are honored all through the Bible. But honoring the fathers and idolizing a vanished golden age are two different acts of the heart, and they pull in opposite directions.

Now here is the part that implicates me, and I would not be honest if I left it out, because I am not standing above this thing diagnosing other people. I have golden ages of my own. There was a season early in my ministry when everything felt charged with the presence of God. Prayer was easy. The work was joy. I was sure of my calling with a clean, uncomplicated certainty. I would walk into the church building on a weekday afternoon and feel something I can only call nearness, a sense that the work was holy and I was at the center of it. And there have been long gray stretches since then when I have wanted that season back, when I have held the present up against that remembered fire and found the present cold and wanting and ordinary. I have stood at the same window, in the same building, on a gray afternoon, feeling nothing, and grieved the man I used to be and the God I used to feel.

And I have had to learn, slowly, against my own emotional grain, that this is unbelief. Plain and simple. It assumes God was more present then than he is now. It assumes that the dryness I feel is his absence rather than his hiddenness, his withdrawal rather than a deeper and less flattering work he is doing in me that I cannot feel while it happens. The God of my golden age is the exact same God of this gray Tuesday, and to pine for the one while quietly resenting the other is to refuse the God who is actually, presently, here in the room with me, just not in the way I prefer. The early ease may have been a gift to a young man who could not yet have borne anything harder. The later dryness may be the gift God gives to a man he is finally trusting with something. I do not know. What I know is that he is no less here in the dry season, and that my feeling otherwise is a lie my heart tells me with great sincerity, in the warm and trembling voice of reverence.

The church does not move forward by recovering its golden age. I want to say this as plainly as I can, because so much of our energy is spent on the recovery project. There is no golden age to recover. There is only a remembered fiction that keeps us facing the wrong direction, weeping into the past while the future goes unwatched. The church moves forward by trusting that the God who built the former house is building the latter house, and that the latter will be greater. Not because we are better than our forebears, we are not, but because the building is rising, course by course, generation by generation, toward a glory that will one day make every former glory look like what it always was, a foundation, the necessary first layer, beautiful in its place but never meant to be the whole.

Think about what that does to the man at my car door. I cannot give him 1958 back, and I should not want to. But I can stand beside him and tell him the truth, which is that the foundation he helped lay was never meant to be the building. He poured a footing. It was good work, holy work, and the house rising on it now will be greater than the footing, not because we are greater than he was, but because a footing is supposed to be exceeded by the house. The day they finish the cathedral, nobody stands in the nave weeping for the foundation. They stand in the thing the foundation made possible. His grief is the grief of a man who confused the footing with the finished work, and the cure for it is not to pretend the present is glorious. It is to lift his eyes off the empty seats and onto the builder who has not stopped building. And here is the strange mercy in it. The very faithfulness that makes him grieve is the faithfulness God still wants to use. The man who weeps at the empty seats is not the church's problem. He is, if his eyes can be turned, the church's hope, because he is the one who still cares enough to weep, and a man who can weep over a church can also, by grace, be turned to work for one. The tears do not have to be wasted on the past. They can be poured into the foundation of the latter house, which is exactly what God asked of the weeping old men at the second temple. He did not tell them to stop feeling. He told them where to point the feeling.

Be strong, the prophet says to the weeping old men at the groundbreaking. The latter glory will exceed the former. Now stop grieving the foundation, get up off the ground, and help raise the house.

Nostalgia is unbelief wearing the costume of reverence.
chapters.verdict: Nostalgia is unbelief wearing the costume of reverence.

What suffering does your nostalgia conveniently edit out?

chapters.title: The Sin of Pragmatism
chapters.summary: The opposite error to nostalgia is the frantic pursuit of the next method that will save the church, a faith in technique that quietly replaces faith in God. The church cannot be engineered into the future; it can only be entrusted to the one who builds it.
chapters.body:
If nostalgia faces backward, pragmatism faces forward, and the strange thing I want to convince you of is that they are the same sin wearing opposite costumes.

I have spent a lot of years inside the conference economy of the evangelical church, and I want to describe it honestly because I have both profited from it and been quietly deformed by it, and I cannot warn you off a thing I am pretending I never touched. Every year there is a new method. A new model of doing church that promises to reach the people the old model lost. A new book with a one-word title and a subtitle full of promises. A new framework, a new set of practices that some fast-growing church somewhere has discovered and packaged and is now selling, at a reasonable per-seat rate, to the anxious pastors of declining churches. I have watched them come and go like fashions. The seeker model. The attractional model, build it big and smooth and they will come. The missional model, send them all out. The organic model, tear it all down and meet in houses. The multisite model, one preacher on a hundred screens. And then the model after that, and the one after that. Each one arrives wearing the promise that it is finally the thing that works, the answer, and each one gets adopted by thousands of churches who are, underneath the excitement, quietly terrified that without it they are going to die.

Let me take you inside one of those weekends, because the abstraction does not capture how it actually gets to you. You drive three hours, you and an associate and a couple of the more energetic elders, and you check into a hotel by the airport, and in the morning you file into an arena with eight thousand other people who do what you do. The lights go down. The band is better than your band. The first speaker is a pastor of a church that grew from forty to four thousand in nine years, and he is funny and humble and he tells the story of how it happened, and somewhere around the second point you feel it start, the thing the whole weekend is engineered to produce. Hope. Real hope, mixed with a sharp edge of shame, because his church grew and yours did not, and he is clearly not smarter than you, so the difference must be the method. You buy the book in the lobby. You buy the workbook. You fill three pages of notes and you drive home talking the whole way, and you roll it out that fall, and some of it even helps, for a while. And then it fades, the way they all fade, and the next year there is a new arena and a new pastor and a new book, and you go again, because the alternative to going is sitting still in your fear, and almost anything feels better than that.

I am not describing a stranger. I am describing my own car on the interstate, my own three pages of notes, my own lobby receipts. I have the books on my shelf still, a whole row of them, one-word titles in confident type, each one bought in a season when I was afraid, each one promising the answer, each one now mostly forgotten. I do not throw them out. I keep them as a kind of monument to my own anxiety, a reminder of all the years I went looking for a technique to do what only trust could do.

I am not going to stand here and tell you that all of this is worthless, because that would be a lie and it would also be lazy. There is real wisdom in studying what God seems to be blessing, in learning from healthy churches, in being willing to change a method that has stopped serving the mission. The early church changed methods constantly. They went from the temple courts to private homes. From Jerusalem out to the whole Gentile world. They adapted to every new city and culture they walked into, Paul becoming all things to all men that he might by all means save some. Adaptation is not the sin. Studying is not the sin. The sin is the belief underneath the studying, the belief that almost nobody states out loud but nearly everybody assumes, that the right method will save us. That if we can just locate the correct technique, run the right play, find the model that fits our context, then the future of the church will be safely in our hands.

It is not in our hands. That is the whole point of this book, said from a different angle, and pragmatism is the precise and respectable way that the church denies it while looking busy and responsible the entire time. That is what makes it so much harder to see than nostalgia. Nostalgia at least looks backward, and you can catch a man looking backward. Pragmatism looks forward, and it is hard to tell forward-facing unbelief from forward-facing faith, because they stand the same direction and they work the same hours. The pragmatist is not lazy. He is the hardest worker in the building. He is at the office at six. He has read everything. And that is exactly why nobody calls it what it is.

There is a story in the Old Testament that has bothered me for years, and I think it is the key to this whole chapter. David, near the end of his long reign, decides to take a census of Israel. He wants to count the fighting men, to measure the military strength of the nation he has built (2 Samuel 24:1-10). On the face of it this seems completely harmless. Responsible, even. It is the kind of thing a competent administrator does, the kind of thing a good chief executive would do, know your numbers. Even his battle-hardened general Joab, who was not exactly a tender conscience, tried to talk him out of it, which should tell us something. But David insisted, and the count went forward, and it took the better part of a year to walk the whole land and tally the men. And it provokes the anger of God. And David himself, afterward, before any consequence has even landed, is struck through with conviction. His heart smites him. And the whole episode ends in a plague that kills seventy thousand people.

For years I could not understand it. Why is counting a sin? We count things all the time. God himself counts, the Bible is full of numbers, whole books of them. Then I understood. David was measuring the kingdom's strength as if the kingdom's strength lay in its numbers. As if the future of Israel depended on how many swords it could field, rather than on the God who had brought it out of nothing, who had taken a shepherd boy with a sling and made him a king. This is the same David who once stood in front of a giant with five smooth stones and said the battle is the LORD's, the LORD saveth not with sword and spear. That David did not need a census. He knew where the strength was. But forty years of success can move a man's trust without his noticing, slide it off of God and onto the inventory of his own resources, until the old shepherd who beat a giant with a sling now needs a spreadsheet to feel safe. The census was unbelief expressed as arithmetic. It quietly moved David's trust off of God and onto the metrics. It was a spreadsheet that had become an idol.

The church does this constantly, and we have made it sophisticated. We count. We measure attendance, giving, baptisms, salvations, engagement, reach, conversions, retention, the whole dashboard. There is software for it now, lovely software, with graphs that update in real time. And let me say it again so I am not misheard, there is nothing wrong with counting itself. Acts counts. Three thousand were added at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and Luke bothered to write the number down, and he wrote it down because it was a marvel of God's doing, not a metric of the apostles' technique. The sin is never in the counting. The sin is in where the counting moves our trust. When the numbers quietly become the thing we are actually depending on. When our sense of the church's future rises and falls, week to week, with the attendance graph. When we start adopting methods chiefly because they move the numbers and abandoning faithful work because it does not. I have caught myself doing exactly this, checking the giving report on a Monday morning and letting the figure set the temperature of my whole soul for the week, high if it was up, sick if it was down, my peace pegged to a column of numbers like a man whose joy lives or dies with the closing bell of the market. That is when we have made David's mistake. We have located the kingdom's strength in something we can measure, manage, and take credit for, which is to say, in ourselves.

Tim Keller wrote helpfully about all of this, and what I appreciated in him was that he refused the easy version of either side. He warned hard against turning ministry methods into idols, against the kind of pragmatism I am describing. But he also refused to let anyone use that warning as an excuse for laziness or thoughtlessness. He held a difficult balance, and held it for decades. Be genuinely wise about how you do ministry. Study your actual city, not a city from a book. Think carefully, plan well, do not be a fool about it. And never, ever confuse your wisdom with the power that actually changes a human being. Because the conversion of a single soul is a work of God that no method on earth has ever produced. You can fill an auditorium with technique. We have proven that many times over. You can engineer a crowd. We are very good at engineering crowds. You cannot make one dead heart alive with all the strategy in the world. "Paul planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Corinthians 3:6). Planting is a method. Watering is a method. Both matter, both are commanded, both should be done with care and skill. But the increase is not on the menu of things we control. The increase is given, or it is not, by God, and our most sophisticated dashboard cannot conjure a single ounce of it.

I think of a man I will call Dale, though that was not his name. He came to faith in our church, late, in his fifties, a hard man who had buried a marriage and most of his relationships in alcohol. Nothing we did reached Dale for two years. He sat in the back. He came and went. We had no program for Dale. He did not fit any model. And then one Tuesday he showed up at my office having read the gospel of John on a whim because he could not sleep, and something had broken open in him in the dark that no strategy of ours had touched. I did not plant Dale and I did not water Dale, or if I did I cannot tell you which Sunday it took. God gave that increase in a rented apartment at three in the morning with a Gideon Bible somebody had left in a drawer years before. Now multiply Dale by every real conversion you have ever witnessed and ask yourself honestly how many of them ran on schedule, fit the funnel, came when and how the plan said they would. None of mine did. The ones I engineered did not last. The ones God gave I could not have engineered if my life depended on it.

Church history says the same thing on a larger scale, and it is worth a hard look, because the pragmatist assumes that the great movements of God came from great strategy, and the record says otherwise almost every time. The First Great Awakening that swept the American colonies in the 1730s and 40s was not the product of a campaign. Edwards in Northampton did not run a program. He preached the old doctrines plainly, and prayed, and then something fell that no man scheduled, and whole towns turned in a matter of weeks. Edwards spent the rest of his life trying to describe what had happened, not to reproduce it, because he understood it could not be reproduced on demand. The Welsh revival of 1904 began largely through ordinary praying people and a handful of unknown men, and it ran for a season like a fire through dry grass, and then it receded, and nobody has been able to switch it back on since with any technique at all. The pattern is stubborn. The increase comes, when it comes, from outside our control, and our methods at their very best only prepare the ground for a rain we cannot summon. The pragmatist looks at a movement of God and reverse-engineers a method out of it, and then sells the method, and the method never produces the movement, because the movement was never the product of a method in the first place. It was a gift. You can study the conditions under which God has given gifts. You cannot manufacture the gift. To forget that is to make Edwards's revivals into a marketing case study, which is exactly what we have done, and exactly why it has not worked.

Let me bring it down to a room. Picture a deacons' meeting in a church that is shrinking, because I have sat in a hundred of them. The numbers are down. The youngest family just left for the big church across town with the better youth program. There is fear in the room, the specific gray fear of men who love a place and can feel it slipping. And the meeting almost always goes the same way. Somebody says we need to do something, and the something is always a method, a new program, a new push, a new push to get the young families, a marketing idea, a building improvement, a name change. Everyone leans toward it, because doing something feels like faith and sitting still feels like death. And the thing almost never raised, the thing I have learned I have to be the one to raise, and have too often failed to raise, is the question, when did we last get on our faces in this room and ask God to do what no program can do? Have we prayed about this congregation with the desperation we are now pouring into strategy? Usually we have not. We have moved straight from fear to technique, skipping the one step that matters, because technique gives us something to control and prayer gives us only something to trust, and a frightened man wants control. I have led those meetings the wrong way more times than I want to count. The right way is slower and quieter and it does not produce a plan by nine o'clock, and it is the only way that has ever actually worked.

I have come to think that pragmatism is, at the root of it, a failure of patience. That is what it really is, underneath the strategy and the conferences. The future feels uncertain. The decline feels real and personal. The anxiety is honestly unbearable, especially at two in the morning, especially when the giving is down and the building needs a roof and the roof does not care about your theology of patience. And into that unbearable anxiety, a method offers the one thing the frightened soul wants more than almost anything else, which is control. If I just do this, then that will follow. It converts the agonizing, white-knuckle trust of faith into the manageable equation of technique, and that is an enormous relief, right up until it fails. And it always eventually disappoints, because the church was never an equation in the first place. Jesus told a parable about exactly this, about a man who scatters seed and then goes to bed. "The earth bringeth forth fruit of herself," Jesus said, while the farmer "should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how" (Mark 4:27-28). The growth happens in a hiddenness the farmer cannot see into and cannot speed up. He knoweth not how. That is in the text. The man who grows the crop does not understand the mechanism of the growing. His job is to plant faithfully, and then to wait, and to sleep. The anxious farmer who digs up the seed every single morning to check whether it has sprouted yet kills the very thing his anxiety was trying so hard to save.

I have been that farmer. I want you to know I am not describing other pastors. In certain seasons of real fear about my church's future, I have chased methods the way a sick and frightened man chases cures, certain that the next one would be the one, ordering the books, driving to the conference, coming home and rolling it out, and growing a little more frantic and a little less faithful with each disappointment. There was a stretch where I changed the order of service three times in a year, and renamed the small groups twice, and launched a new initiative every season, and I told myself this was leadership. It was not leadership. It was a man digging up the seed every morning, dressed in the language of vision. My congregation was tired. They could feel the anxiety underneath the energy, the way a child can feel a parent's fear no matter how steady the voice. People do not follow a frightened man for long, even a busy one, because fear is the one thing you cannot hide for more than a season.

Let me answer the obvious objection head on, because a lazy man could read this chapter and feel justified. If it is all God's increase, why plant at all? Why not stop working, stop planning, stop counting, and just pray and wait? Because the same Bible that says God gives the increase also says Paul planted and Apollos watered, and commends them for it. The farmer in the parable sleeps, but first he scatters the seed. He does not refuse to farm. He farms and then he rests, because he has done the part that is his and entrusted the part that is God's. The cure for anxious overwork is not lazy underwork. Both of them are unbelief. One says it all depends on me so I cannot stop. The other says it all depends on God so I will not start. The faithful man works hard at what he can do and refuses to grip what only God can do, and the peace lives exactly in that distinction, in knowing where your hands end and God's begin.

Brueggemann had a phrase for the alternative to all of this. He spoke of the prophetic imagination as the capacity to live out of God's promised future, rather than out of the present's foreclosed despair or the technician's managed control. And I have come to see that the pragmatist and the nostalgic, the two we have spent these two chapters on, actually share a single underlying unbelief. They both think the future is fundamentally a problem of human management. The nostalgic tries to manage it by recovering the past. The pragmatist tries to manage it by engineering the future. But both have their hands on the controls, both think the outcome depends on getting the management right. Sit them down at the same table and they would argue about everything and agree about the one thing that matters, that it is up to us, that the church will be saved or lost by the quality of our decisions. The prophet refuses both stances. The prophet plants in faith, and then watches the horizon for an increase that only God can give, and is not destroyed when it tarries. He has put the outcome in hands stronger than his own, and so he can plant without panic and rest without guilt.

So hear me clearly, because this is easy to misuse in either direction. I am not against method. I am against the idol that method becomes the moment it quietly replaces trust. Use the best wisdom you can find. Study hard. Plan well. Adapt when you must. Count, if you have to, just keep your hand from gripping the numbers. Go to the conference, even, and bring home what is useful, and throw away the shame they sold you alongside it, because the shame was never from God. And then lay every bit of it down at the feet of the only one who gives the increase. And sleep. And rise. And not know how. And trust the God who makes the earth bring forth fruit of herself while the exhausted, anxious, faithful farmer finally rests.

I think the deepest thing pragmatism steals from us is sleep, and I mean that almost literally. The man who believes the future of the church rests on finding the right method cannot rest, because the search is never finished, there is always another book, another conference, another church doing better than his. But the farmer in the parable sleeps. That is the detail Jesus chose to include, of all the details he could have left out. The seed grows while the man is asleep. The kingdom advances in the hours when the most competent strategist in the world is doing nothing at all, because the kingdom was never his to advance. There is a rest available to the faithful that is not available to the frantic, and the only door into it is the surrender of the one thing pragmatism most wants to keep, which is the illusion that the outcome depends on us. Give that up, and you can finally close your eyes. The seed will grow tonight. It does not need you awake.

You cannot strategize your way into a future that only God can give.
chapters.verdict: You cannot strategize your way into a future that only God can give.
reflect: What method or model have you secretly hoped would save your church?
Where has anxiety about the future driven you to act faster than you have trusted?
What would faithful patience look like in the part of the church's work you find most discouraging?

chapters.title: Living Stones, Not Finished Statues
chapters.summary: The church is built of people still being shaped, not perfected monuments, and its unfinished members are not a problem to be solved but the very material God is using. Grace means belonging before becoming, and the church is a workshop, not a showroom.
chapters.body:
Peter, who watched the temple from the outside as a fisherman and from the inside as an apostle, reached for a building image when he tried to say what the church is, and the image he chose tells you everything. "Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house" (1 Peter 2:5). Living stones. Sit with how strange that phrase is. A stone is the deadest thing in the world. It is the thing we reach for when we want a picture of something permanent, finished, immovable. A tombstone. A milestone. A stone wall. And Peter takes the deadest noun in the language and hangs the most alive adjective in front of it. Living stones. Stones that grow. Stones that are still being cut.

We do not build with living stones. Nobody does. You quarry a stone, you cut it once, you dress it to fit, and then it is done, and you set it in the wall, and it stays exactly the shape you cut it for the next four hundred years. That is the whole point of stone. It does not change. And Peter looks at the church, looks at this band of fishermen and tax collectors and reformed zealots and freed slaves and Roman soldiers and prostitutes, and he says, that is not what you are. You are stone that is still alive. Still being shaped. Set in the wall and somehow still under the chisel at the same time, which is a thing that exists nowhere in the world of actual masonry, and which is exactly what the church is.

I think we forget this almost immediately, and the forgetting causes more pain in the church than nearly anything else. Because what we secretly want, what I have wanted, is a church of finished statues. We want to walk into the building and find people who have arrived. Christians who have it together. Marriages that work. Tempers that are tamed. Tongues that are bridled. We want a showroom, where everything on display is the finished product, polished and lit and placed just so, and we get angry, genuinely angry, when the church turns out to be a workshop instead, full of half-cut stone and dust and the noise of the chisel and figures that are nowhere near done. We came expecting a museum and we got a construction site, and we file it under disappointment.

Let me tell on myself here. I have stood in the back of my own sanctuary on a Sunday morning and felt, God forgive me, embarrassed by my own congregation. There is the man who corners visitors and talks too long and too loud. There is the woman whose theology is a mess and who says something cringeworthy in the prayer meeting almost every week. There is the family whose teenagers are clearly in open rebellion and everyone can see it. There is the recovering addict who relapsed again and is back, again, looking like he has been dragged through gravel, because he has. And some ugly, fastidious thing in me has wished, in those moments, for a tidier church. A more presentable church. A showroom. And every time I have wished it, I have had to repent of it, because what I was really wishing for was a church with no grace in it, a church that had stopped admitting sinners, which is to say a church that had stopped being the church and become a country club with a cross on the sign.

A church of finished statues would not be a glory. It would be a graveyard. Walk through any old cemetery with good statuary and you will see exactly the church we say we want. Perfect figures. Beautifully finished. Not one of them out of place, not one of them embarrassing, not one of them talking too loud in the foyer. And not one of them alive. The finished stone is the dead stone. The reason the church is full of unfinished, half-cut, embarrassing, in-process people is that the church is full of living people, and living things are never finished, they are always becoming, and the day a man stops being cut on is the day he is no longer under the hand of the sculptor but only laid out for the viewing.

This is, I have come to believe, the single hardest thing about belonging to a real church, and it is also the entire point of it. You have to belong to people who are not done. You have to sit in a pew next to a man whose politics make your skin crawl, and call him brother, because the blood of Christ says he is, whatever your skin says. You have to forgive the woman who gossiped about you, and not just once, because she is not finished and neither are you, and the cutting is slow. You have to extend to the relapsed addict the same welcome you would want extended to you on the worst Sunday of your own secret life. None of this is comfortable. All of it is the workshop. And the discomfort is not a sign that something has gone wrong. The discomfort is the dust. You cannot have a working shop without dust, and you cannot have a church full of living stones without the friction of people being cut down to fit, right next to you, while you yourself are being cut.

Bonhoeffer saw this with a clarity that has rebuked me for years. In his little book Life Together, written out of an underground seminary in Nazi Germany, where the cost of Christian community was not theoretical, he says something that ought to be read aloud in every church before every membership meeting. He says that the man who loves his dream of community more than the community itself becomes a destroyer of community, even though his intentions may be ever so honest and earnest and sacrificial. Read that again slowly. The dream of the perfect church is the enemy of the actual church. The person who arrives with a vision of how Christian fellowship ought to be, polished and harmonious and edifying, and who then measures the real, dusty, half-finished people in front of him against that dream, will end up despising them, leaving them, or trying to force them into the shape of his dream. And Bonhoeffer says God hates that visionary dreaming, because it makes a demand of God and of the brothers that neither has agreed to meet. The actual brother, the irritating, unfinished, real one sitting next to you, is the gift. The dream of the better brother who would be easier to love is the idol. We are forever leaving the gift to chase the idol, and calling the chase high standards.

I have watched this destroy more small churches than any decline in the culture ever did. A family arrives with a dream. The worship should be like the church they came from. The preaching should go deeper. The people should be friendlier, the youth program stronger, the coffee better. And for a while they are patient, and then the gap between the dream and the dusty reality opens up, and they grow critical, and the criticism curdles, and one day they are gone, off to find the church that matches the dream, which does not exist, and which they will leave too, in three years, for the same reason. They were never looking for a church. They were looking for a showroom. And the church is not a showroom. It never has been. The early church that Peter wrote to had a man in Corinth sleeping with his stepmother and a congregation getting drunk at the Lord's table, and Paul did not write them off as a failed plant. He cut on them. Painfully. By letter. Because they were living stones and the cutting was not done.

Go back and read what Peter actually does with the image, because it is more careful than we usually notice. He does not just say you are living stones and leave it there. He immediately quotes the Old Testament about the stone the builders rejected, that became the head of the corner (1 Peter 2:7, drawing on Psalm 118). Christ himself is the rejected stone. The one the professional builders looked at, the men whose whole trade was judging which stones were fit and which were not, and they took one look at him and threw him on the discard pile as useless. And that is the stone God made the cornerstone of the entire building. Now sit with what Peter is doing. He is telling a church of nobodies, slaves and ex-prostitutes and fishermen, that they are being built onto a cornerstone that the experts rejected, which means the whole house is being assembled out of material the world's builders would have thrown away. The discarded stone is the load-bearing one. The rejects are the wall. If you ever feel like the wrong material for the church, like you are too cracked or too late or too obviously unfinished to belong in the house of God, you have understood the gospel exactly backward. The rejected stone is the foundation of the whole thing. You are in good company on the discard pile. That is where the cornerstone came from.

I think of a deacon we ordained some years back. I will not give you enough detail to identify him, but the shape of it is true. When he first came to us he was, frankly, a hard case. Sharp tongue. A temper that had cost him jobs. A marriage hanging by a thread. If you had asked me in his first year whether this man would ever be fit to lead anything, I would have said no, gently, but no. He was not showroom material. He was rough stone, badly cracked, the kind a sensible builder discards. And I watched God cut on that man for fifteen years. I watched the temper get planed down, slowly, with a lot of setbacks, a lot of weeks where it came roaring back and you would have sworn no progress had been made at all. I watched the marriage get rebuilt, board by board, with help, with failure, with more help. And the man who stood up to be ordained was not a finished statue even then, he would tell you so himself, but he was load-bearing. He could hold weight. Young men in trouble go to him now, because he has been where they are and the scars are real and he does not pretend. If I had run that church like a showroom, I would have shown him the door in year two as a liability to the brand. Because I was, by the grace of God and not my own wisdom, running a workshop, I got to watch a rejected stone become a cornerstone for somebody else. That is the entire business we are in. We do not curate finished pieces. We house the cutting of stones the world threw away.

Here is the part of this that I think we get most wrong, and it is the part that turns the doctrine from a burden into a relief. We apply living stones generously to other people and almost never to ourselves. I am happy to extend grace to the loud man in the foyer. What I cannot stand is grace toward my own unfinished places. I want to be a finished statue. I want to have arrived. I am ashamed of the same sin surfacing in my prayers in my forties that surfaced in my twenties, ashamed that after all these years of ministry I still lose my temper at home, still battle the same old envy, still catch the same old pride looking back at me in the mirror of a hard week. And the shame is real and some of it is even appropriate, conviction is a gift. But underneath a lot of it is the same idolatry Bonhoeffer named, just turned inward. I have a dream of the finished version of myself, and I despise the real, half-cut version God is actually working on, and in despising the work I am despising the sculptor's timing, which is a polite way of saying I am despising the sculptor.

The chisel hurts. I do not want to pretend otherwise. The whole image of being cut is an image of pain, and the New Testament does not flinch from it. We are pruned (John 15:2). We are refined as silver is refined, in the fire (Malachi 3:3, 1 Peter 1:7). We are disciplined as sons, and the writer of Hebrews says plainly that no chastening seems joyful at the time, but grievous (Hebrews 12:11). Anyone who tells you that sanctification feels good while it is happening has either never been sanctified or has forgotten. It does not feel good to have your envy named and cut away. It does not feel good to have your pride exposed in a conflict you handled badly, to sit with the fact that you were the problem, that the sharp thing you said came out of you and you cannot put it back. That is the chisel. And the living stone, unlike the dead one, can feel every stroke of it. The cost of being alive under the sculptor's hand is that you feel the cutting. The dead statue feels nothing, because the dead statue is done, and being done is the same as being dead.

Now I have to answer the obvious objection, because if I do not, this doctrine becomes a blanket thrown over every sin in the building, and I have seen that done and it is ugly. If everyone is unfinished, does that mean nothing is ever out of bounds? If we are all living stones, can the man who is abusing his wife simply say he is a work in progress and expect the church to nod and bear with him? No. A thousand times no, and the New Testament is the one that says no, not me. Paul, who knew better than anyone that the Corinthians were unfinished, still told them to put the unrepentant man out of the fellowship (1 Corinthians 5). Bearing with the unfinished is not the same as ignoring the unrepentant, and the difference is the word repentance. The living stone under the chisel is a man who, however slowly and with however many setbacks, is letting himself be cut, is turning, is grieved by his own sin even when he keeps committing it. The stone that has to come out of the wall is the one that has set itself against the chisel entirely, that defends its sin, that demands the church bless what God is trying to cut away. Workshop grace is not the absence of standards. It is patience with people who are honestly, painfully, submitting to the standards and falling short, which is all of us. It runs out only where submission runs out, where a person stops being cut on and starts insisting the sculptor is the one who is wrong. The relapsed addict who comes back broken is a living stone. The man who quietly decides his sin is fine and dares the church to say otherwise has, for the moment, climbed off the bench, and love for him looks different, and harder, and is its own subject.

So what does this actually change, on a Tuesday, in a real church? It changes how you see the person who disappoints you, and it changes how you bear with yourself, and those two turn out to be the same change. When the man in the foyer talks too long, you can say, under your breath, he is not finished, and neither am I, and the sculptor is patient with us both. When your own old sin shows up again, you can say the same thing, without despair, because the reappearance of the sin is not proof that the work has failed. It is proof that the work is still going on, that you are still on the bench and still under the hand, which is the only place any of us has ever been made into anything. The opposite of the unfinished stone is not the finished stone. In this life the opposite of the unfinished stone is the abandoned one, the block left in the quarry, never chosen, never cut, never set in any wall at all. To be cut is to be loved. The chisel is the proof of belonging.

And this reframes the whole question of grace, which we say we believe and then quietly contradict in how we run our churches. The gospel says you belong before you become. You are set in the wall, named, claimed, counted as part of the house, while you are still being cut, before you are anywhere near done. We get this exactly backward. We act as though people have to become before they can belong, that they must clean themselves up to a certain standard before they are fully one of us, and so we hold the half-finished at arm's length, on probation, until they prove they are presentable. But God set Peter in the wall the night before Peter denied him three times with cursing. He had already called him the rock. The stone was named and placed and counted, and then it cracked, badly, in public, and the sculptor did not throw it out of the wall. He came and found it on a beach and cut on it some more, three questions for three denials, lovest thou me, and set it back, and built a church on it. That is belonging before becoming. That is the only kind there is.

There is one more thing in Peter's image that we skip, and it is the part that turns this from a private comfort into a description of the church, which is what it actually is. He does not say you are a living stone, singular, as if each of us were a free-standing piece. He says you are living stones, built up into a house. A stone alone is not yet anything. A stone becomes part of a wall only by being set against other stones, fitted to them, its rough edges ground down precisely where it meets its neighbor. The cutting, in other words, happens largely at the joints. God shapes you against the people he has set next to you. The brother who irritates you is not an obstacle to your sanctification. He is the chisel. Your patience is being cut into you by your need to be patient with him. Your humility is being cut into you by the man who is better at the thing you are proud of. Your forgiveness is being cut into you by the very people who keep needing to be forgiven. Take those people away, give me the solitary holiness I sometimes daydream about, alone with God and no annoying neighbors, and the cutting stops, because there is nothing left to cut against. The friction I keep wishing the church did not have is the exact tool God is using to make me fit to be part of a house.

I learned this, or began to, in a conflict I handled badly. There was a man in our church I could not get along with. I will not give you the particulars. We rubbed each other the wrong way from the start, and over a couple of years it hardened into something cold, the kind of low-grade enmity that two Christian men can carry for a long time under a thin coat of politeness. I told myself he was the problem, and some of it was him. But God used him to show me things about myself I had been hiding under fifteen years of being the pastor, the one who is supposed to be mature, the one whose job is patience. My pride had a hiding place and that man kept walking into it. We are, the last few years, something like friends, which neither of us would have predicted, and I am a slightly better man for the grinding, and so, he tells me, is he. Two rough stones, set next to each other by God, ground down at the joint until they fit. I did not enjoy a minute of the grinding. I would not trade what it cut out of me.

I want to say one more thing to the person who is tired of being cut, because I have been that person and I suspect you have too. There are seasons when you would honestly rather be a finished statue, even a dead one, than endure one more stroke of the chisel. You are weary of being worked on. You wish God would either finish you or leave you alone. I understand it. But hear what the alternative actually is. The finished statue is admired and untouched and alone in its perfection, and it goes nowhere and becomes nothing and feels nothing ever again. The living stone is set into a house, joined to other stones, load-bearing, part of something rising, and yes, still being cut, because the house is not done and neither are you. The cutting is not God's impatience with you. It is his commitment to you. He does not abandon the block half-shaped. He finishes what he starts, and the finishing is the whole of grace, but he finishes it on his timeline, in his shop, surrounded by other unfinished stones who are part of how he shapes you, and the dust and the friction and the noise of the place are not a sign that you have come to the wrong church. They are the sign that you have come to a working one.

A church of finished statues would be a graveyard. The living are still being cut.
chapters.verdict: A church of finished statues would be a graveyard. The living are still being cut.
reflect: Do you treat the unfinished people around you as material God is shaping or as problems to be managed?
Where do you demand to be a finished statue when God is still cutting you?
What would change if you saw the church as a workshop instead of a showroom?

chapters.title: The People in the Pews
chapters.summary: The future of the church does not rest on celebrity pastors or famous movements but on ordinary, faithful, mostly unseen believers who keep turning up across decades. God has always built his church chiefly through people whose names we will never know.
chapters.body:
I want to end this part of the book with the people we are most likely to overlook, because I have come to believe they are the ones God is actually using to build the thing, and we keep looking past them at the stage.

The way we talk about the church, you would think it ran on celebrities. We name the eras by the famous men. The age of this preacher, the movement of that conference, the network founded by the one whose books are in every airport. We track the church the way we track an industry, by its stars and its brands and its platforms, by who is rising and who has fallen, and the falls especially, because we cannot look away from the falls. And I am not innocent here. I have spent more hours than I will confess studying the famous churches and the famous men, learning their methods, wanting, if I am honest, a little of what they had. The platform pulls on a pastor like gravity. You tell yourself you want it for the kingdom. Mostly you want it.

But that is not how the church is built, and I think we know it, somewhere underneath the noise. The church is built by people whose names will never be on a book. Let me tell you about the people I actually mean, because they are real, even if these particular composites are stitched together from many faces over many years.

There is a woman in nearly every faithful church I have ever known. She is somewhere in her seventies now. She has taught the same Sunday school class, six-year-olds, for something close to forty years. Do the arithmetic on that. Forty years of cutting out construction-paper sheep. Forty years of Noah and the ark and the boy with the loaves and fishes, told to children who will not remember her name and whose parents largely take her for granted. She has buried a husband. She has watched the church shrink around her. She has never been to a conference. No one has ever asked her to speak. And she has shaped, by my rough count, something over a thousand children, planting the first seeds of the gospel into minds too young to know they were being planted in. Some of those children are pastors now. Some are missionaries. One of them, I happen to know, came back to faith twenty years later in a hospital bed and the thing that came up out of the dark to meet him was a song she taught him when he was six, a song he did not know he still had. She will die without ever knowing that. The plaque, if there is one, will be small.

There is a man who has shown up to set out the chairs at six in the morning for thirty years. Just the chairs. The coffee. The thermostat. He opens the door in the dark on Sunday and again on Wednesday and again for every funeral and every wedding and every committee meeting nobody else wants to attend. He is not eloquent. He has never led anything. He would be deeply uncomfortable being thanked from the front, and on the rare occasion someone tries, he waves it off and changes the subject. And the church has not had a single gathering in three decades that he did not quietly make possible, and when he finally cannot do it anymore, it will take four younger people to replace what he did alone, and they will discover, doing it, how much they never saw.

There is a couple who have had the new families over for dinner, every month, for as long as anyone can remember. They are not wealthy. The house is small and the food is plain. But they have a gift the celebrity church cannot manufacture at any budget, which is the gift of making a stranger feel, within twenty minutes, like he has always belonged. Half the people who stayed at our church over the years stayed because of a Sunday dinner at that table, though they could not tell you that, and the couple certainly could not, because they were not keeping count. They were just setting an extra place. That is how the church grows. Not mainly through the funnel. Through the extra place at the table, set by people whose names will never trend.

There is the man who prays. I do not mean the man who prays out loud well in the meeting, though that is a gift too. I mean the man, or more often in my experience the woman, who is up before the house wakes, with a worn list, going through the names. The sick. The wayward son. The pastor, by name, every morning, for years. You do not know who these people are in your church, mostly, because the whole nature of the thing is hidden, Jesus said go into your closet and shut the door (Matthew 6:6). But I have come to believe that whatever good has come through my preaching has been carried, the way a current carries a boat, on the prayers of two or three old saints I could name who were holding me up before God on mornings when I did not even know I needed it. When they die, and they are dying, one by one, I feel it in the pulpit. Something gets harder. The current slackens. We bury our intercessors with a paragraph in the bulletin and we have no idea what we are putting in the ground.

And there is the visitor of the sick, who does not preach and does not teach and could not lead a meeting to save her life, but who is at the hospital, in the chair beside the bed, on the afternoon when the family has gone home and the patient is most afraid. I have stood at a lot of bedsides. I have learned that the dying do not, in the end, remember the sermons. They remember who came. They remember the hand that was there at three in the afternoon on a Tuesday when the room was empty and the machine was beeping and the fear was rising. There is a kind of ministry that happens only in chairs beside beds, and it is done almost entirely by people whose names will never be spoken from a stage, and it is, I have come to think, nearer the center of what the church is for than anything that happens under the lights on Sunday.

These are the people Jesus was describing when he kept insisting the kingdom was small. A grain of mustard seed, the least of all seeds (Matthew 13:31-32). A little leaven hidden in three measures of meal, working invisibly through the whole lump (Matthew 13:33). A treasure buried in a field where no one can see it. He was not being humble for effect. He was telling us the actual mechanism of the thing.

Stay on the leaven a moment, because we read past it too fast. Leaven is not a flattering image. Everywhere else in the Bible leaven is the picture of corruption, the thing you sweep out of the house at Passover, the thing Paul warns spreads through the whole lump. And here Jesus picks up that disreputable little image and says, that, that is the kingdom of heaven. Hidden in the dough. Invisible. A woman working it in with her hands in her own kitchen, and you cannot see it doing anything at all, and then the whole batch rises. He did not say the kingdom is like an army, or a temple, or a great visible monument that announces itself. He said it is like the thing you cannot see, worked silently into ordinary stuff by ordinary hands, that changes everything from the inside while nobody is watching. The woman in the kitchen with her hands in the dough is the Sunday school teacher and the man who sets out the chairs and the saint up before dawn with her list. They are the leaven. You cannot photograph what they do. You can only, years later, notice that the whole lump has risen, and wonder how. The kingdom advances mostly underground, mostly hidden, mostly through the small and the unseen, and the visible, impressive, countable parts are the smallest part of what is really happening. We have built a whole church culture around exactly the parts Jesus said were the least reliable indicators, the size, the visibility, the platform, the crowd, and we have learned to overlook exactly the parts he said carried the weight, the hidden seed, the buried leaven, the cup of cold water given in a name no one famous will ever read.

Zechariah names our sin precisely, and I have had to sit under this verse more than once. The people rebuilding the second temple were discouraged, the foundation looked small and poor, and the word of the LORD came: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" (Zechariah 4:10). Despised. That is the right word, and it is a sharp one. We do not merely overlook the day of small things. We despise it. We hold it in contempt. A church of ninety feels like a failure next to a church of nine thousand. A faithful Tuesday with one struggling man in your office feels like nothing next to a stadium. The slow work of teaching one six-year-old, of setting out one row of chairs, of laying one course of brick a little crooked in the rain, feels beneath the scale of what we imagine the kingdom is supposed to be. And God says, who taught you to despise that? Because I do not despise it. The day of small things is the day I do most of my work. You despise what I treasure, and you treasure what I called the least.

I cannot read that verse without it turning on me, so let me be honest about how. I have stood in my own study on a discouraging week and despised the day of small things with my whole heart. Nine people at a prayer meeting I had hoped fifty would come to, and I had to fight the temptation to resent the nine, to feel the smallness of the room as a verdict on my ministry, when those nine were the most faithful souls in the county and had given up their evening to pray and I should have fallen on my knees with gratitude for them instead of doing math on the empty chairs. I have measured my own faithfulness by the size of the crowd it drew, which is exactly the sin this chapter is against, and I have preached this very point to congregations on Sunday and gone home Monday and despised the day of small things in my own kitchen. The pastor is not above the disease. Often he has the worst case of it, because the platform pulls hardest on the men whose job keeps them closest to it.

Now let me answer the objection, because a sharp reader will already be forming it. Are you saying numbers do not matter, that growth is bad, that we should be content with decline and call our smallness holy? No. I am saying no such thing, and the lazy version of this chapter would say that, and I want to cut it off. Numbers represent souls, and souls matter infinitely, and a shrinking church should grieve and pray and examine itself and never baptize its decline as humility. There is a false piety that wears smallness as a badge, that sneers at every growing church as shallow and calls its own dwindling a mark of faithfulness, and that piety is just pride with the math reversed, the same idol of the visible worshipped from the losing side. The day of small things is not a thing to be content with. It is a thing not to be despised. Those are different. A farmer does not despise the small green shoot, and he also does not pretend the shoot is the harvest. He honors it as the real beginning of a real harvest and he keeps working and he leaves the increase to God. To honor the small is not to settle for it. It is to refuse to measure it by the wrong ruler while it grows.

Eugene Peterson spent his life trying to call pastors back from the platform to the parish, and the whole weight of his work was a rebuke to the celebrity model that has eaten so much of our imagination. He called the pastor's true work mostly unglamorous and mostly unseen, the long, slow, local labor of knowing actual people by name and walking with them through actual years, and he warned that the moment a pastor starts performing for an audience larger than the congregation in front of him, something essential dies. He used to say, in effect, that the besetting temptation of the American pastor was to be a religious entrepreneur running a shop rather than a shepherd who lives among the sheep and knows the smell of them and stays. The shop can grow fast and large. The shepherding is hidden and slow and it does not scale, because love does not scale, because you cannot love a person at volume, you can only love them one at a time, by name, over years. And that unscalable, hidden, named, faithful love, Peterson insisted, is the actual work, and everything famous is mostly a distraction from it.

You learn this at funerals, if you are paying attention, and a pastor goes to a lot of funerals. I buried one of these saints not long ago. I will keep her unnamed, but she was the kind of woman this whole chapter is about, decades in the same pew, decades of casseroles carried to grieving houses, decades of quiet work nobody recorded. The funeral was small. The world did not pause. There was no notice anywhere outside the few rows of folding chairs. And one after another, ordinary people stood up and told the same kind of story, in different words. She came when my baby died. She drove me to chemotherapy for a year. She taught me to pray when I was nine and I never forgot it. She wrote me a card every birthday for thirty years and I have kept every one. And I stood at the front, looking out at a room that the obituary economy of the world would have called a nobody's funeral, and I thought, this is what the kingdom is. This is the harvest of a life of small things, finally made visible for one afternoon, and it is enormous, and almost no one will ever know, and she would have been embarrassed by the fuss. The visible church, the famous church, the church of platforms and brands, will not produce a single moment like that, because that moment is not for sale and cannot be engineered and does not scale. It only grows, slowly, hidden, in the dough, over a lifetime of hands working it in.

I think of the long arc of church history and how little of it was driven by anyone we can name. We tell the story through Augustine and Luther and Edwards, and those men matter, I have leaned on them through this whole book. But for every Augustine there were ten thousand North African believers whose names are gone, who taught their children the faith and fed the poor and refused the incense to Caesar and were forgotten by every record but the one that matters. The faith crossed the Roman world not mainly on the backs of famous bishops but in the ordinary witness of slaves and merchants and soldiers and housewives who told a neighbor, set an extra place, took in an abandoned baby, nursed a stranger through a plague that everyone else fled. The church survived the fall of empires and the long dark centuries and the cold seasons of decline not because of a few visible giants but because, in every single generation, in every town, there was a Sunday school teacher and a man who set out the chairs and a couple who set an extra place, and they kept at it, and they handed the faith forward one course of brick at a time to people who would do the same, and the line never broke. It has never once broken, in two thousand years, and it did not stay unbroken because of the famous. It stayed unbroken because of the faithful, and they are not the same people, and they have almost never been the same people.

Consider one stretch of it. In the year 165, and again around 250, terrible plagues swept the Roman Empire, the kind that emptied cities, that piled bodies in the streets faster than anyone could bury them. And the pagan response, recorded by their own writers and by frightened Christians alike, was to flee. The healthy abandoned the sick, even their own families, and ran for the hills, because to stay was to die. And the Christians stayed. They stayed and nursed the dying, their own and the pagans both, because they believed something about death that made staying possible, and a great many of them caught the sickness and died doing it. There is no monument to those nurses. We do not have one name in a hundred. But the pagans noticed. The emperor Julian, decades later, trying to revive the old religion, complained bitterly that the Christians cared for the sick, even the pagan sick, while his own priests did not, and that this was a large part of why the new faith kept growing and the old gods kept losing. The empire was converted, in no small part, by anonymous believers who carried water to dying strangers in plague years. Not by bishops. By nobodies, the leaven, the people whose names the record does not keep, doing the small hidden thing that turned out to be the largest thing of all.
