I want you to feel how relentless this pattern is, because it is the whole hope of the book gathered into one fact. Every single generation that was sure the church was finished had, hidden inside it, the people who kept it alive, and they were never the people the histories noticed. The historian counts the cathedrals and the councils and the kings. God counts the woman with her hands in the dough.

So here is what I want to leave you with, and it is the most hopeful thing I know, though it does not look hopeful at first. The future of the church does not depend on whether we produce the next great preacher or land on the next great method or recover the next lost cultural battle. It depends on whether, in ten thousand unremarkable churches in ten thousand unremarkable towns, there are still people willing to teach the six-year-olds, and set out the chairs, and set the extra place, and pray when nine show up, and lay their crooked course of brick in the rain, year after year, without applause, without a platform, without anyone ever writing their names down. And the staggering thing, the thing that should bring you to your knees, is that there always have been. In every generation that was sure the church was finished, there were such people, hidden, faithful, despised by a world that worships the visible, and through them, quietly, underground, like leaven in the meal, God kept building the thing he promised at Caesarea Philippi he would build.

He is building it through them still. He is probably building it through someone in your church whose name you have never thought twice about, and through you, on the days you are too tired to feel like anything but small. Do not despise that. God does not. The day of small things is the day he does his best work, and he has been doing it, faithfully, unglamorously, one unnamed saint at a time, since the morning the fire fell, and he has not stopped, and he will not stop, until the house is done.

So let me say this to you directly, whoever you are, because I suspect you are more likely to be one of the unnamed than one of the famous, and so am I, in the end, whatever the platform does or does not do. Teach the class. Set out the chairs. Set the extra place. Pray for your pastor by name in the dark before the house wakes. Sit in the chair beside the bed. Carry the casserole to the grieving house. Keep at it for forty years and tell no one and let no one thank you and do not measure it and do not despise it for being small. You will likely never see the harvest. The child you taught may come to faith in a hospital bed twenty years after you are gone, and you will not be there to know it, and it will not matter that you are not there to know it, because it was never about your knowing. It was about the building rising, course by course, through hands too humble to be remembered. That is the work. It has always been the work. And on the day the house is finished and the books of the famous are forgotten, the woman with her hands in the dough will be standing in a city she helped to build, hearing, for the first time, from the only mouth whose verdict matters, the words she never once heard on earth: well done.

The church will be saved, if it is saved, by people whose names you will never hear.
chapters.verdict: The church will be saved, if it is saved, by people whose names you will never hear.
reflect: Whose quiet, unseen faithfulness has God used to build you?
Do you measure the church's health by what is visible and celebrated or by what is hidden and faithful?
Where are you despising the day of small things in your own ministry?

chapters.title: A Kingdom Not of This World
chapters.summary: The church is constantly tempted to seek its security and significance through political power, but its founder explicitly refused that path, and the church is most itself when it witnesses from below rather than ruling from above. Distinguishing the kingdom from the nation is one of the hardest disciplines of faith after Christendom.
chapters.body:
There is a temptation that comes for the church in every age, and it is most dangerous in exactly the moment the church feels weak, which means it is dangerous right now. It is the temptation to reach for the sword.

I do not mean a literal sword, though the church has reached for those too, more than once, to its lasting shame. I mean the whole apparatus of worldly power. Political control. The levers of the state. The ability to make people behave through law rather than persuade them to believe through love. When the church feels its cultural ground slipping away, when the pews thin and the culture turns hostile and the old assumptions evaporate, the temptation rises with a special force, because power looks like the obvious solution to weakness. If we are losing because we are weak, then surely the answer is to become strong, to organize, to win elections, to get our people into the rooms where the decisions are made, to take back the institutions, to fight fire with fire. And it sounds like courage. It sounds like finally taking the faith seriously enough to defend it. But I have come to believe it is one of the great spiritual dangers of our moment, and that giving in to it would cost the church far more than the cultural ground it is so afraid of losing.

Let me tell on myself, because I am not writing this from a safe distance. A few years back, in an election year, I stood in the lobby of my own church after a service and watched two men I love, two men who had taken communion from the same tray ten minutes earlier, get red in the face arguing about a candidate. They were not arguing about a person. By the end they were arguing about whether the other one could really be a Christian at all. I stood there with a cup of bad coffee in my hand and I did not know what to say, and I will be honest, my first instinct was not pastoral. My first instinct was to figure out which of them was right. That is the tell. That is the thing I want you to watch for in yourself, because I caught it in myself that morning. The body of Christ was tearing in front of me and some part of me wanted to pick a side and join the tear. We had let the kingdom of God get small enough to fit inside a yard sign.

Go back to the wilderness, before any of the ministry, to the three temptations. The devil takes Jesus up to a high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them, and says, all this I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me (Matthew 4:8-9). Stop and notice what is actually being offered. Not sin in the crude sense. Not some obviously evil thing. He is offering Jesus the kingdoms. The power to run the world, to set it right, to enforce the good. And the thing is, Jesus did come to claim the kingdoms of the world. That part is true. The offer was not a lie about the destination. It was a lie about the road. The devil was offering a shortcut to the right destination by the wrong means, power without the cross, the crown without the suffering, the kingdoms handed over by a transaction instead of won by a death. And Jesus refused it absolutely. Get thee hence, Satan. He would have the kingdoms, all of them, every one, but he would have them his Father's way, from below, through a cross, not from above, through a deal.

I want you to feel how attractive the offer was, because if you do not feel it, you will not understand why the church keeps taking it. The devil was not asking Jesus to renounce the goal. He was offering to help. Think about all the good a person could do with the kingdoms of the world in his pocket. End the wars. Feed everyone. Stop the cruelty by decree. Make the whole earth behave. You could call it the most generous offer in history if you only looked at the result and never asked about the road. And that is precisely how the offer comes to us. Never as, will you abandon the good. Always as, will you take the shortcut to the good. Will you reach the right end by the wrong means. The temptation to the church is almost never a temptation to do evil. It is a temptation to do good by power instead of by the cross.

That is what makes it so hard to see and so hard to refuse. Nobody walks into the trap thinking, I would like to betray my Lord today by becoming an enforcer. They walk in thinking, I love these people, and the law could protect them, and I have a vote in my hand, so why would I not use every tool available to spare them harm. The reasoning is not wicked. The reasoning sounds like love. And it is in exactly that disguise that the shortcut does its work, because you cannot see the cliff for the good intentions piled up at the edge of it. I have sat with a father, a good man, a praying man, who told me with tears in his eyes that he was done being nice, that the time for persuasion was over, that the only language the other side understood was force, and that God was calling him to fight. And every word of it came out of love for his children. I could not fault his love. I could only watch where the love was being aimed, because love aimed at the sword does not stay love for long. It curdles into the very thing it set out to oppose. The man who picks up the sword to protect the good ends up, within a generation, swinging it at whoever the good now requires him to swing it at, and he calls the swinging faithfulness.

Here is a question I have learned to ask myself, and I would ask it of you. When you imagine the gospel finally winning, what does the winning look like in your mind? Be honest about the picture. Is it people changed from the inside, one heart at a time, the slow strange way the kingdom has always advanced? Or is it your opponents finally silenced, your laws finally passed, your enemies finally made to sit down and behave? Because those are two completely different victories, and only one of them is the kingdom of God. The other one is the kingdoms of the world with a cross painted on the side. I have caught myself wanting the second one and calling it the first, and that is the whole danger of this chapter living inside my own chest.

This is the pattern, and the church keeps forgetting it. When Jesus stood before Pilate, the one man in the room who actually held worldly power over his life, he said the sentence that should govern the church's relationship to every empire forever. "My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight" (John 18:36). If it were that kind of kingdom, my people would be fighting right now to keep me off this cross. But it is not that kind of kingdom. It does not advance the way the kingdoms of this world advance. It does not run on coercion. It runs on a cross, on a king who lays down his life rather than calling down the legions of angels that were, the text is clear, fully available to him (Matthew 26:53). He could have had the power. He refused the power. And he built his church on that refusal.

The early church understood this in their bones, because they had no choice. They had no political power for three hundred years. They could not vote. They could not lobby. They could not get their people appointed to anything. They were a despised minority with no access to the levers of the state, and the state periodically turned those levers against them, to kill them. And what did they do with their powerlessness? They turned the empire upside down. Not by seizing it. By out-loving it. By out-dying it. By caring for the sick when the plagues came and the pagans fled their own dying relatives in terror. When the great epidemics swept the Roman cities in the second and third centuries, the people who could afford to leave fled to the countryside and left the sick to die alone in the streets. The Christians stayed. They nursed people who were not their own. Many of them caught the disease and died doing it, and the strange thing the historians noticed afterward is that a higher number of the nursed survived than would have survived alone, and so the church grew partly because it was willing to die. They took in the infants that Roman families exposed on the hillsides to die, mostly girls, mostly unwanted, and raised them as their own. There was no law forcing any of this. There was no power behind it. There was only love that did not count the cost.

By living a quality of life together, a love within the community and toward outsiders, that was so strange and so compelling that the historian can actually trace the growth of the church partly through it. They influenced the empire profoundly, more than any voting bloc ever has. But they influenced it from below, from underneath, from the position of weakness, exactly the way their Lord had influenced the world from a cross. They had no sword, and they conquered Rome, and the moment they got the sword, under Constantine, the conquering started to go the other way, and Rome began to conquer the church.

Sit with that reversal, because it is the hinge of the whole matter. For three hundred years the church had no power and it converted the most powerful empire on earth. Then it got the power, and within a few generations it was blessing wars and torturing heretics and crowning kings. The same church. The only thing that changed was the sword. Whatever you think the sword does for the gospel, the record runs the other way. The church was at its most fruitful when it had the least to fight with, and at its most dangerous, to itself and to everyone around it, when it had the most.

I want to put a hard case to you, because the easy version of this argument is too easy. Somebody will say, but Pastor, surely some uses of power are good. Surely it was good when Christians used their influence to end the slave trade, or to outlaw the exposure of infants, or to build the hospitals. And yes. It was good. I am not telling you the state is the devil's tool and Christians must never touch it. I am telling you something narrower and harder. There is a difference between Christians, out of love, working to restrain a particular evil through whatever lawful means lie at hand, and the church staking its identity, its security, and its hope on holding the levers. William Wilberforce spent forty years working to abolish the slave trade, and that was the church loving its neighbor through the means available, from a posture of weakness, against the powerful, taking a beating for it for decades. That is not the same as the established church blessing the empire's wars because the empire signs its paychecks. The first is love using a tool. The second is the tool using love. The line between them is not whether you ever touch power. The line is whether power has become the thing you trust. You can tell the difference by what happens to your faith when the power goes away. Wilberforce's faith did not depend on winning. The established church's faith collapsed the moment the establishment did.

That is the warning that hangs over this whole chapter and this whole moment. Because the thing the church got under Constantine, the power, the establishment, the seat at the center, is precisely the thing we examined a few chapters back, the empire's version of the church, and it is precisely the thing that is now, mercifully, passing away. And the great danger is that as it passes, we will spend ourselves trying to grab it back. We will decide that the answer to the church's weakness is the church's power. We will pour our hope and our energy and our anxiety into political victory, into getting the right people into office, into using the state to enforce what we can no longer persuade the culture to believe. And in doing it, we will trade our birthright for a bowl of stew. We will trade the strange, slow, cross-shaped power that actually converts the world for the fast, hard, sword-shaped power that can only compel its compliance.

Now I can already hear the objection, because I have heard it from good people across more than one kitchen table, and it deserves a real answer, not a brush-off. Someone says to me, Pastor, that is fine for the early church, they could not vote, but we can. Are you telling me to sit on my hands while the country goes where it is going? Am I supposed to watch laws get passed that hurt my grandchildren and do nothing because it is not cross-shaped enough for you?

I want to be careful and fair here, because this is precisely where people stop listening, on one side or the other. I am not saying Christians should withdraw from public life, or refuse to vote, or fall silent on questions of justice, or pretend that laws do not matter. They do matter. The early church did not have access to the vote, and we do, and to refuse a genuine good that is in our hands would be its own failure of love for our neighbor. A Christian can and should work for just laws the same way a Christian works for a fed neighbor, as an act of love. That is not the temptation I am warning about. The temptation is something deeper and more corrosive than involvement. It is the relocation of hope. It is when the church's actual hope for the future, the thing it is really counting on, quietly migrates from the gospel to the political project. When we start to believe, somewhere underneath our doctrine, that the church will be saved if the right side wins, and lost if the wrong side wins. That is the idolatry. Not voting. The substitution of the kingdom of God with a kingdom of this world that we have painted with Christian colors and convinced ourselves is the same thing.

Here is how you can tell the difference in your own heart, because it is not always obvious, and I have had to run this test on myself. When your side loses an election, do you grieve like a citizen who lost a vote, or do you despair like a believer who lost his God? When your side wins, do you give thanks like a person who got a good and temporary mercy, or do you rejoice like a man whose salvation just arrived? The intensity is the tell. The despair is the tell. If a Tuesday in November can shake the foundation of your hope, then your hope was built on the Tuesday and not on the cross, and you have, without ever deciding to, swapped the kingdom for the nation. I have felt that despair. I have woken up the morning after an election with a weight in my chest that no follower of a risen Christ has any business carrying, and I have had to repent of it, because it was not grief. It was idolatry with grief's face on.

There is a second tell, and this one cuts closer, because it shows up in church and not just in the voting booth. Watch who you are willing to break fellowship over. If you can sit at the communion rail beside a brother who is wrong about the doctrine of the Trinity, who is muddled on the deity of Christ, who barely understands the cross, but you cannot bear to take the cup beside a brother who votes the other way, then you have told on yourself. You have revealed where your true creed lives. The early church drew its hard line at the confession that Jesus is Lord, and it drew that line through the middle of the empire, with Romans and Jews and slaves and free and Greek and barbarian all crowding into the same room, people who agreed about almost nothing except the one thing that mattered, and that one thing was enough to make them family. We have a harder time now sharing a pew with someone who shares our Lord but not our party. That is not a political problem. That is a worship problem. Something has climbed up onto the throne that does not belong there, and the proof is that it can do what heresy could not, which is split the body of Christ.

Augustine drew the line that has helped me hold this, in The City of God. He said there are two cities running all the way through history, intermingled, tangled up together so that you cannot fully separate them this side of the end. The city of God and the city of man. And the city of man is organized around the love of self and the will to power, and the city of God is organized around the love of God even to the contempt of self. And the deadly error, the one Augustine warned against most, was confusing the two. Mistaking any earthly city, any empire, any nation, however Christian its founders or its flags, for the city of God itself. Rome was not the city of God, even Christian Rome, even after Constantine, and Augustine watched Christians make that mistake and then watched their faith collapse when Rome fell, because they had bound the eternal city to a temporal one and could not tell them apart anymore. When Rome was sacked in the year 410, the panic among believers was not just a panic about safety. It was a crisis of faith, because so many of them had quietly decided that Christian Rome was the kingdom of God on earth, and when the kingdom of God on earth could be sacked by barbarians, what was left to believe? Augustine wrote his great book over more than a decade to pull the two cities apart again, to tell a frightened church that the city it really belonged to had not fallen and could not fall. The church that ties its hope to a nation will rise and fall with that nation, and every nation falls.

So what does it look like to refuse the sword and still love the world? It looks like the early church. It looks like influence from below. We feed people, not to win them as voters but because they are hungry and Christ is in them. We tell the truth in the public square, not to seize the square but because the truth is good for our neighbors and silence would be a failure of love. We build institutions of mercy, schools and hospitals and shelters, the way the church always has, the way the church built most of the West's institutions of mercy in the first place, from below, by love, before it ever had the power to mandate anything. The first hospitals in the West were not built by emperors. They were built by Christians who believed a stranger's body was worth their money and their time. The first schools that taught the poor were not state programs. They were the church doing from below what no law required it to do. That is the influence I want for us. Not the influence of the man who controls the building, but the influence of the woman who runs the soup kitchen out of the basement of it and never gets her name in the paper.

And we hold political outcomes with an open hand, working for justice as best we can while refusing to stake our hope on the result, because our hope was never of this world to begin with, and the kingdom we belong to does not arrive in an election, from above, but comes down from God out of heaven, on a day he has fixed, in a way no sword could ever achieve and no sword could ever stop. I think about those two men in my church lobby more than they know. I have watched, in better seasons, the same kind of men kneel together at the same rail and weep together at the same funeral, and in those moments the yard signs simply do not exist, because something larger has reclaimed the room. That is the church. It is not the wing of a party. It is the body of a crucified king who refused the kingdoms when they were handed to him on a mountain, and who will receive them all in the end, from his Father, by the only road that ever leads there.

A church that grasps for the sword has forgotten the cross that built it.
chapters.verdict: A church that grasps for the sword has forgotten the cross that built it.
reflect: Where have you confused the advance of the gospel with the victory of a political side?
What would it look like to influence the world the way the early church did, from below rather than from above?
Has your hope for the church's future quietly become a hope for the right people to gain power?

chapters.title: The Hope That Pulls
chapters.summary: Christian hope is not optimism about trends but confidence in a promised future that reaches back into the present to shape it. The future God has guaranteed becomes the engine of present faithfulness rather than a distant consolation.
chapters.body:
There is a difference between optimism and hope, and almost everything in the Christian life depends on which one you are actually running on.

Optimism is a reading of the trends. It looks at the data, weighs the probabilities, and concludes that things will most likely improve. It is a posture toward the future based entirely on what can be seen and projected, which means it is always, by its nature, at the mercy of the evidence. When the numbers are good, the optimist is up. When the numbers are bad, the optimist is down. It is a mood that tracks the conditions, the way your spirits track the weather. And optimism about the church in the West is extremely hard to sustain right now, if you are honest, because the trends, read straight, are not encouraging. Declining attendance. Declining belief. A whole younger generation drifting away, fewer of them ever drifting back. If your confidence in the church's future is fundamentally optimism, then the data is eventually going to crush it, because the data, for now, in our corner, is mostly bad, and no amount of positive thinking changes the spreadsheet.

I have watched optimism die in real time, and it is not a pretty thing to watch. A man takes a struggling church because he is sure he can turn it around. He has the energy and the gifts and the will, and for a while the numbers tick up, and the optimism feeds on the tick, and then the tick stops, and then it reverses, and the very optimism that built him up on the way up tears him down on the way down, because it was always tied to the graph, and the graph turned. I have been that man in certain seasons. I have ridden a good month like it meant something eternal and then sat in a dark office over a bad quarter like the gospel itself had failed. That is what optimism does. It hands your soul to a spreadsheet and tells you to wait and see how you feel.

And it is not only pastors who live this way. I think of a young couple in the church who tried for years to have a child. Every month was a referendum. Hope up, hope down, the whole emotional weather of their marriage rising and falling with a test in a bathroom. Except it was not hope at all, it was optimism wearing hope's clothes, and it nearly destroyed them, because it had attached the deepest longing of their hearts to a number that kept coming back the wrong way. What finally steadied them was not better odds. The odds never improved. What steadied them was a slow shift from reading the trend to trusting the One who held the whole of their lives, child or no child, and that is the difference I am circling in this chapter. Optimism asks, what do the signs say. Hope asks, what has God said, and stands on that when the signs say nothing good at all.

Hope is something else entirely, and we have to stop using the two words as if they meant the same thing, because confusing them is killing people's faith. Hope is not a reading of the trends. Hope is confidence in a promise. It does not look at what can be seen and projected. It looks at what God has actually said he will do, and it holds that against every piece of contrary evidence, because its ground is not the data at all. Its ground is the character of the one who made the promise. "Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" (Hebrews 11:1). The evidence of things not seen. Read that slowly. Hope sees something the trends cannot show, and stakes everything on it, precisely because the thing it sees is not on the trend line.

I want to be careful that you do not hear me running down optimism as if it were a sin. It is not a sin. It is a temperament, a gift some people are born with and others are not, and there is nothing wrong with a cheerful disposition that expects the best. The trouble is not optimism. The trouble is mistaking optimism for faith, and then, when the optimism fails, as it always eventually does, concluding that faith has failed with it. I have watched that mistake gut people. A naturally sunny believer hits the first real darkness of his life, the diagnosis or the divorce or the prodigal child, and his cheerful expectation that things would work out simply collapses, and because he had never learned the difference, he assumes God collapsed too. He did not lose his faith. He lost his optimism and could not tell them apart. That is why this distinction is not a word game. It is the difference between a faith that survives the worst day of your life and a faith that was only ever a good mood with religious vocabulary.

Jürgen Moltmann wrote the book that named this for the modern church, and it matters who he was when he wrote it. His Theology of Hope came out in 1964, and the argument was that Christian faith is, from the first page to the last, oriented toward the future that God has promised. That the resurrection of Christ is not merely a past event to believe in but a future breaking backward into the present, a down payment and a guarantee of the new creation, pulling all of history toward itself like a magnet. And here is the part that gives the book its weight. Moltmann had been a prisoner of war. He was a young German soldier, captured near the end of the Second World War, held in Allied camps for years, and it was there, in that captivity, with no earthly future left to hope in, with his country in ruins and his own future erased, that he first encountered the God of hope. He has said the hope he found there did not come from his circumstances, because his circumstances offered nothing. It came from somewhere outside the circumstances entirely. Picture it. A defeated soldier behind wire, his nation a smoking ruin, no reason on earth to expect anything good, and into that emptiness a hope arrives that the emptiness did not produce and could not explain. That is the whole point. If his hope had been optimism, the camp would have killed it in a week, because the camp gave optimism nothing to feed on. It was hope, and hope does not feed on the camp. It feeds on the promise. And he came home from those camps and built a whole theology on the conviction that the church lives forward, drawn by a promised future, rather than backward by a remembered past or sideways by a measured present.

Notice too where the resurrection sits in all of this, because it is the ground under everything. Christian hope is not a wish or a temperament or a sunny way of reading life. It is staked to a single event in history that either happened or did not. Paul knew this, and he was brutally clear about it. "If Christ be not risen," he wrote, "then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). He did not hedge. He did not say, well, even if the tomb were full, the teaching would still be lovely and the community still meaningful. He said the whole thing stands or falls on whether a dead man walked out of a grave on a particular morning outside a particular city. And that is what gives hope its spine. Optimism is a feeling about the future. Hope is a verdict about the past, about an empty tomb, that determines the future. The resurrection already happened. It is the first piece of the new creation to arrive, the down payment handed over early, and because that piece is real and in the bank, the rest is guaranteed. Hope does not look ahead at a maybe. It looks back at a fact and reasons forward from it.

This is the move I most want to land in this chapter, so let me try to make it concrete. The Christian future is not merely a destination we are walking toward, sitting passively at the end of the road waiting for us to show up. The Christian future is a power that reaches back into the present to change it now. The future God has guaranteed is not inert. It is active. It pulls. It draws the present forward into conformity with itself. Paul prays for the Ephesians that they would know "what is the hope of his calling" (Ephesians 1:18), and he prays it because the hope of the calling is meant to do something in the present, this week, this Tuesday. It is meant to reorganize how a person lives right now in the light of a city they will not personally reach for years, maybe not in this life at all.

I want to draw the contrast between hope and optimism out a little further, because once you see it you cannot unsee it, and it explains a great deal about why some believers crumble under hard news and others do not. Optimism needs the trend to cooperate. The moment the trend turns, optimism has nothing to say. It is a fair-weather companion. It will sit with you in the bright morning and abandon you the instant the clouds come in. Hope is the opposite. Hope was made for the clouds. Hope does its best work in the dark, because the dark is precisely where the trend goes silent and only the promise is left speaking. This is why you so often find the deepest hope, not in the comfortable churches with the rising graphs, but in the persecuted ones, the poor ones, the ones the world has long since written off. They have nothing left to be optimistic about. They have only the promise. And the promise turns out to be enough, more than enough, and they sing in a way the comfortable church has forgotten how to sing. I have met believers from places where the church grows under pressure I will never face, and what struck me was not their grimness but their gladness, a gladness that did not depend on the news, and I came away suspecting they understood something about hope that my soft, well-fed, anxious American faith barely grasps.

Think about how a genuinely guaranteed future changes present behavior, because we already know this from ordinary life. The runner who knows for a fact that the race ends at a finish line a mile up the road spends himself completely differently than the runner who fears the road might go on forever. He can empty the tank, because he knows where it ends. The soldier who knows the war is already won, that the decisive battle is behind him and the outcome is no longer in doubt, fights differently than the soldier who fears it could all still be lost. Or take something closer to the kitchen table. A woman saves and scrimps and goes without for years, denying herself a hundred small comforts, and she does it cheerfully, because she has a deed in a drawer and she knows the house at the end of it is real. Take the deed away and the same scrimping becomes misery, because now it is just going without, with nothing certain on the other side. The certainty does not just wait at the end. It reaches back and changes how she lives every day in between. The whole logic of the New Testament's ethics runs on exactly this engine. Because the future is secure, live now in its light. "Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself" (1 John 3:2-3). Watch the logic. The hope purifies. The man does not clean himself up in order to earn the future. The guaranteed future reaches back and changes the man who holds it. The destination remakes the traveler before he ever arrives.

This is why hope, real hope, is never passive, and why it has nothing whatsoever to do with sitting around waiting for heaven while the world burns. That is the great slander against Christian hope, that it makes people useless, so heavenly minded they are no earthly good. I have found the opposite to be true every single time. The most hopeful Christians I have ever known were also, without exception, the most active. The most willing to give themselves to causes the world had written off as lost. The most able to labor for years at things they knew full well they would never see completed. I think of an old saint in my own congregation who planted trees in her seventies, ordinary slow-growing shade trees, knowing perfectly well she would never sit under them. When somebody asked her why, she looked at them like they had asked why water is wet. Somebody will, she said. That is hope. That is a woman living from a future she will not personally see, and the reason is this. They were not working in order to secure an uncertain future by the sweat of their own effort. They were working in joyful response to a future that God had already secured. And that changes the entire quality of the work, root and branch. The pragmatist works in fear, frantically trying to engineer a future he is terrified will not arrive unless he engineers it. The hopeful Christian works in freedom, building toward a future he knows is coming regardless of his success or failure, and therefore building without the desperate, grinding exhaustion of the man who believes it all finally rests on his own shoulders.

Let me answer an objection here, because it is a fair one and I have felt it myself in the small hours. Somebody says, this all sounds lovely, but it sounds like a way of excusing failure. If the future is guaranteed no matter what I do, why try at all? Why not let the building rise on its own? But that gets the relationship exactly backward, and the runner shows you why. The runner does not run less hard because the finish line is fixed. He runs harder, because the fixed finish line is the only thing that makes the running mean anything. A race with no finish is not a race, it is just exhaustion. It is the certainty of the end that releases everything he has. Hope does not excuse the labor. Hope is what makes the labor bearable, and joyful, and free, because it takes the outcome off your shoulders and leaves you only the faithfulness, which was the only thing that was ever yours to carry in the first place.

I came to faith out of atheism, so I know the country on the other side of this border better than I sometimes let on, and I will tell you what hope looked like from there. From there it looked like a coping mechanism. A pretty story frightened people told themselves so they could sleep. I was not impressed by it and I did not envy it, because I could see, or thought I could see, that it was wishful thinking dressed up in stained glass. And I have to say this honestly. If Christian hope were optimism, I would have been right. If it were just a sunny disposition about how things tend to work out, it would deserve the contempt I had for it. What I had not reckoned with, what eventually undid me, was that the Christians I could not dismiss were not optimists at all. They were not telling themselves things would probably be fine. Several of them were watching things be very much not fine and standing anyway, on something, and the something was not a mood. It was a claim about a man and a tomb. You cannot argue a person out of a mood by reasoning about a tomb. But you can be slowly, unwillingly drawn toward a tomb that will not stay shut in your mind, and that is more or less what happened to me. The hope was not soft. The hope had a hard fact under it, and the hard fact would not leave me alone.

I have buried people whose hope humbled me, and changed me, and I have come to think that the deathbed is where the difference between optimism and hope finally becomes visible, because the deathbed is where optimism runs out of road. I sat with a man once, near the end, who had every earthly reason to despair. There was no good reading of his trends. There was no positive spin left to put on his situation, and he knew it, and the people who loved him knew it. The hospice nurse had stopped pretending. The family had stopped pretending. And he was not despairing. When I finally worked up the nerve to ask him how, he did not give me a strategy or a brave face or a line about staying positive. He said, more or less, that he had read the last chapter and he knew how the story ended, and that the present was hard, harder than he could say, but that the present was not the end. He was lying in that bed living from the future. The city was pulling him forward through a present that had nothing left to offer his optimism and everything still to offer his hope. I went into that room to comfort him and I came out comforted, which is how it usually goes when you are around someone who actually believes what we all say we believe. I have done a lot of funerals. I can tell you that the ones who go out in hope and the ones who go out in optimism do not look the same at the end, because when the road runs out, optimism has nothing left and hope is just getting started.

Let me press the objection one step further, because there is a colder version of it. Somebody says, easy for the dying man to read the last chapter, he had nothing left to lose. But I have to live in the middle of the book, with a mortgage and a marriage and a church that is shrinking, and the last chapter feels a thousand pages away. I understand that. The middle of the book is where most of us live, and the middle is genuinely hard, and I will not pretend the promise makes the middle stop hurting. It does not. Moltmann came home from the camp to a ruined country and a slow rebuilding, not to instant glory, and his hope did not spare him a single hard year. What the hope did was change what those hard years meant. The same drudgery, the same disappointment, the same long obedience, but now it is drudgery inside a story that ends in a city, and not drudgery inside a story that ends in nothing. The work does not get easier. The work gets meaning. And meaning, it turns out, is most of what we are actually running out of when we say we are exhausted. We can carry almost any weight if we believe it is carrying us somewhere. It is the suspicion that the weight goes nowhere that finally breaks a person, and that suspicion is exactly the thing the empty tomb was given to kill.

That is the posture I want for the church in this generation, and I want it for you, personally, in whatever you are facing. Not the optimism that rises and falls with the attendance numbers and the cultural mood. Not the despair that reads the trends and concludes the building must be collapsing. But the hope that holds the promise steady against the evidence, that lives from a future God has guaranteed with the resurrection of his Son, that labors in freedom precisely because the outcome is already secured and the work cannot finally fail. The trends may run against us for a long time yet. They may run against us for the rest of our lives. I am not going to lie to you and tell you the graph is about to turn, because I do not know that, and neither does anyone selling you a conference ticket. The hope does not depend on the trends. It depends entirely on the one who said he would build his church, and who has never once failed to finish what he began.

Read the last chapter. The city comes down. The dwelling of God is with men. Every tear is wiped away (Revelation 21:3-4). That is not optimism. There is no trend on earth that predicts it, no spreadsheet that forecasts it, no data that supports it. It is hope. The substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. And it is meant to reach back, right now, into this gray and difficult and discouraging present, and pull you forward into a faithfulness you could never sustain on the evidence alone.

Hope is not a guess about the future. It is the future arriving early to change the present.
chapters.verdict: Hope is not a guess about the future. It is the future arriving early to change the present.
reflect: Is your hope based on what you can see happening, or on what God has promised regardless of what you see?
How would living from a guaranteed future change what you do this week?
Where have you settled for optimism when God offers you hope?

chapters.title: What We Are Building Toward
chapters.summary: The end of the story is not escape from the world but the marriage of heaven and earth in the New Jerusalem, a future so concrete that it reshapes what the church should value now. We build toward a city, and the city tells us what matters.
chapters.body:
We have spent generations preaching the wrong ending, and the wrong ending has quietly produced the wrong church.

The ending most Christians actually imagine, whatever our doctrine says on paper, is escape. The soul leaves the body, the world gets left behind, and we float up to a disembodied heaven of clouds and harps and endless church services, eternally elsewhere, eternally somewhere that is not here. It is the ending of a thousand hymns. It is the ending of ten thousand funeral sermons, including, I am ashamed to say, some of mine from early on. He has gone home. She has flown away to a better place. I stood at a graveside as a young pastor and told a grieving family that their mother had escaped this veil of tears and gone up to be a spirit forever, and I meant every word, and I had the Bible mostly wrong, and nobody corrected me because everybody in the tent believed the same wrong thing. The trouble is, it is not the ending the Bible actually describes. The Bible's ending runs in the opposite direction. Not us going up to heaven, but heaven coming down to earth. "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven" (Revelation 21:2). The movement is downward. Toward the world, not away from it. And the great voice from the throne does not announce that the redeemed have escaped at last to be with God in some far-off place. It announces the opposite. "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3). God moves in. God comes down and takes up residence. Heaven and earth, separated since the garden, are married at last, and the wedding happens here.

This is not a minor adjustment to a footnote. It changes what the church is building toward, and therefore it changes what the church should be building right now, today, this week, with these hands.

N.T. Wright has labored for decades to recover this against centuries of escapist preaching, and his argument in Surprised by Hope is simple and, once you see it, devastating. If the Christian hope is escape from the world, then the world does not ultimately matter, and the church's work in the world is just rearranging the deck chairs on a sinking ship while we wait for the rescue helicopter to come. Why polish the brass on a boat that is going down? But if the Christian hope is the renewal of the world, resurrection, new creation, heaven and earth joined, then everything done in faith in this world matters eternally, because this world is not going to be thrown away, it is going to be healed. The body is not a prison the soul escapes from. The body will be raised. The earth is not a doomed husk we evacuate. The earth will be renewed. The end is not evacuation. The end is restoration, and restoration of a kind that goes beyond the original, because the renewed creation will have been through death and out the other side and can never die again.

Let me say plainly why this is not a small theological quibble, because I used to think it was. I used to think the question of whether we go up to heaven or heaven comes down to earth was the kind of thing seminary professors fight about while ordinary people get on with loving Jesus, and it did not much matter which way you came down. I no longer think that. I have watched the escape ending hollow out churches from the inside. A church that believes the world is a sinking ship it is waiting to escape will, sooner or later, stop caring about the ship. Why would it not? You do not repair what you are abandoning. You do not love a place you are only passing through. And so the escape ending produces a peculiar kind of Christian, warm toward heaven and cold toward his own street, fervent about the rapture and indifferent about the family three doors down, and he does not even feel the contradiction, because his theology told him the street does not finally count.

There is even closer evidence, and it cuts me, so I will say it about myself. The escape ending lets a man treat his own body as disposable while it lasts. If the body is just a shell the soul sheds at the end, then why honor it now, why grieve when it suffers, why care for the dying flesh of the people around you with any tenderness beyond keeping them comfortable until they are gone. But the resurrection of the body changes how you sit beside a hospital bed. You are not waiting for someone to escape their failing flesh. You are tending, for the last time on this side, a body that God himself intends to raise, the same body, healed, made glorious, never to fail again. That changes how you hold a hand. It changes how you wash a body for burial. It changes the funeral, and the grave, and the slow visiting of the very old whom the world has filed away as already finished. None of them is finished. Every one of them is a seed in the ground.

Read the resurrection chapter in First Corinthians slowly sometime and notice how physical Paul keeps it. He will not let it float off into the spiritual. He keeps talking about a body. It is sown in corruption, he says, it is raised in incorruption, sown in dishonor, raised in glory, sown in weakness, raised in power, sown a natural body, raised a spiritual body (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). And the word he uses for spiritual there does not mean made of vapor. It means animated by the Spirit, no longer running down toward death, but it is still a body, raised, real, the same person, the way the risen Christ still bore the marks in his hands and ate fish on the shore. Our escapist hymns quietly drop all of that. They sing the soul up and out and leave the body in the dirt as so much discarded clothing. Paul will not. He plants it like a seed and waits for the field.

I have come to think the wrong ending also explains a strange flatness in a lot of our preaching about the future, including, again, my own for years. If the end is just escape to a featureless somewhere-else, there is almost nothing to say about it. Clouds. Harps. Rest. It is vague because it is supposed to be vague, a blank screen onto which the tired project their tiredness. But the Bible's ending is not vague. It is specific to the point of being almost embarrassing in its concreteness. Walls of a particular height. Gates of a particular number, twelve of them, named for the tribes. Foundations garnished with stones you could name in a jeweler's shop. A river running down the middle of the main street, clear as crystal, and the tree of life growing on both its banks, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, a different one every month, and its leaves for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:1-2). That is not a vague place. That is a place you could draw. You could plant a garden in it. You could get lost on a side street and find your way home for supper. The vagueness was never in the text. The vagueness was in us, and we put it there because we had decided the destination was an escape from places and not the redemption of one.

And notice carefully what the restored end actually contains, because the details are doing theological work. It is a city. Which means it is full of culture. Architecture. Streets and gates and walls. Gathered human life. The works of human hands, taken up and made glorious. "And the kings of the earth do bring their glory and honour into it" (Revelation 21:24). Something of human civilization, purified of its sin, is carried into the New Jerusalem and laid at the feet of God. The garden at the beginning was raw, untouched nature. The city at the end is nature plus everything good that humanity built out of nature across all the long centuries of history, healed of its corruption and offered up. The end is not less than the garden. It is the garden plus the harvest of all human history, redeemed. Sit with that image of the kings bringing their glory in. Whatever was genuinely good and true and beautiful in all the building of all the centuries, the music and the craft and the just laws and the healed bodies and the patient love, does not get burned up as worthless. It gets carried through the gates and laid down before the throne. The end is a homecoming for everything good that was ever made.

There is an objection here that I take seriously, because the cynic in me raises it. Does any of this not flirt with the old dream of building heaven on earth by our own hands, the very thing every chapter of this book has warned against? Are we not one short step from the proud confusion of the two cities, the church that thinks its programs are constructing the kingdom? It is a fair worry, and the answer is a single verb, and you have to keep your eye on it or the whole thing tips over. We do not build the city. We build toward it. The city comes down. John does not see the saints stacking the New Jerusalem up out of the rubble like ambitious masons. He sees it descending, finished, from God, out of heaven. Our hands do not lay its foundation. Our hands lay things here, in faith, that God in his mysterious economy gathers up into what he alone brings down. The difference is the difference between a child building a sandcastle and a child carrying a basket of his own small good things to a feast that someone else has prepared. The feast is not his doing. But the basket is not nothing, and it is welcome at the table.

If that is the ending, then the church's work right now is not waiting-room activity. It is foundation-laying for the city. When you build something good and true and beautiful, in faith, a marriage that lasts, a craft done with excellence, a just institution, a faithful congregation, a healed relationship, a work of mercy that no one will ever hear about, you are not killing time until the rescue. You are building something that, in ways you cannot trace or measure, will somehow be gathered up into the city. Paul says it as plainly as he ever says anything: your labor "is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Corinthians 15:58). Not in vain. Which has to mean it carries forward, somehow, into the end. The good you build in faith does not evaporate when the world is made new. It is taken up. The continuity between this world and the next is far greater than our escapist hymns ever let us imagine.

I cannot tell you the mechanism. I do not know how a kindness done in a nursing home in Fenton in the year of our Lord shows up in the New Jerusalem, any more than I can tell you exactly how a buried seed becomes a wheat field. Paul himself reaches for that very image when people press him on how the dead are raised, and he more or less says, you fool, look at a seed, it goes into the ground as one thing and comes up as another, and you cannot trace the road between, but the field is real. I take it the same way. I do not need the diagram. I need the promise. And the promise is that the labor is not in vain, which means there is a road, even a hidden one, between the good you do here in faith and the city that comes down there in glory.

I sat at a kitchen table not long ago with a man who builds cabinets for a living, and he asked me, half joking, whether his work would mean anything in heaven or whether he had wasted forty years on hinges and drawers while he should have been doing something spiritual. I told him I did not know exactly what becomes of a cabinet in the new creation, and I am not going to pretend I do. But I told him what I am sure of, which is that the care he put into a joint no one would ever see, the honesty of his measure, the refusal to hide a flaw with putty, the years of doing it well when no one was watching, that those are city things, and that the God who notices a cup of cold water given in his name does not overlook forty years of quiet integrity in a workshop. He got quiet. I think nobody had ever told him his work was holy. The escape ending had taught him, without ever saying it out loud, that the only thing that finally counts is the soul, and that his hands were just passing the time. The new-creation ending told him his hands had been building, all along, with material the city is made of.

This rescues ordinary faithfulness from the meaninglessness that the escapist ending quietly assigns it. I have stood beside people who spent their whole lives in obscure, unglamorous service. The woman who taught children's Sunday school for fifty years and never led anything bigger, who could probably still name every child who passed through her little classroom and pray for them in order. The man who quietly paid the bills nobody else would pay and never let his name be attached, who slipped a folded check under my office door more than once and made me promise not to say. The saints whose names will never appear in any history of any church. And the escapist ending makes all of their work look small, a way of pleasantly passing the time until heaven, religious busywork on a doomed planet. But the biblical ending makes that same work look enormous, because it turns out to be precisely the kind of work the city is made of. The New Jerusalem is not built of grand gestures and famous names. It is built of ten thousand thousand acts of faithful, ordinary, unrecorded love, each one taken up by God and made permanent in a world that has stopped dying. When I bury one of those quiet ones, and the room is half empty because the world never noticed them, I have come to believe I am burying a stonemason of the city, and the world's empty pew is no measure at all of the weight of what they built.

This is also, I have come to think, what saves the church from two opposite errors about its work in the world, errors that have each captured large parts of the church in our lifetime. The first error says the world does not matter, so the church should retreat into a spiritual ghetto and wait for the end, ignoring justice and beauty and culture and the suffering of actual bodies, because none of that is eternal anyway. The escapist ending produces this. It produces a church that can sing about heaven while the neighborhood around it rots and feel no contradiction. I have driven past those churches, doors locked all week, lawn gone to seed, a community dying within sight of the steeple, and the people inside on Sunday genuinely believe they are being faithful, because their ending told them the neighborhood was not their concern. The second error says only the world matters, so the church should become a program of social improvement and quietly let go of God, of prayer, of conversion, of the cross, of everything that cannot be measured in outcomes. The merely earthly hope produces this. It produces a church that becomes indistinguishable from a nonprofit and then wonders why no one bothers to come to the one with the steeple, when there is a better-funded nonprofit down the road that never asks you to sing. The biblical ending refuses both of them at once. It says the world matters precisely because God is going to redeem it, not replace it, so the church works hard for the good of the world as a foretaste of the coming city, while never for one second confusing the foretaste with the feast, never pretending we can build the New Jerusalem ourselves by our own programs. We build toward it. We do not build it. The city comes down from God out of heaven. We do not stack it up from earth. But what we build here in faith gets gathered into what he brings down there in glory, and so neither error can hold.

Augustine held these two realities together in his two cities, the city of man and the city of God, intermingled all through history, fully distinguishable only at the very end. He never once thought the church could build the city of God on earth by its own effort. That was the error he feared most, the proud confusion of the two cities, the empire that thinks it is the kingdom. He had watched men make Rome into God and then lose their faith when Rome bled, and he would not let the church repeat the mistake. But neither did he ever think the Christian's daily work in this world was meaningless, because the city of God was being built by God, through that very work, gathered out of the rubble of history toward its certain completion. We labor in the city of man. We are citizens of the city of God. And we build, in the one, toward a completion that only God will bring in the other.

So when people ask me what the church is actually for, and they do ask, sometimes skeptics across a table who expect a thin answer and are ready to knock it down, I have stopped giving them the small answers. Community. Comfort. Moral instruction. A nice place to belong and raise the kids. Those answers are all true as far as they go, but they are not the size of the thing, and a skeptic can smell a small answer from across the room. The church is the community that knows where history is going and lives now in the light of where it ends. The church is the people who have read the last chapter, heaven and earth married, the city descended, the dwelling of God with men, every tear wiped from every eye (Revelation 21:4), and who therefore build, in this present darkness, things fit for that city. Marriages fit for the city. Mercy fit for the city. Beauty and justice and faithful ordinary love, fit for the city. None of it wasted. All of it gathered. All of it built, in faith, toward a home we are going to live in.

I think this is why the escape ending always, in the end, produces a tired church, and the new-creation ending produces a working one, even in the same hard town with the same thin budget. If you are waiting for a helicopter, every passing year is just more waiting, and waiting wears a soul down to nothing. But if you are laying foundation for a city that is coming, every passing year is another course of brick that will stand, and that knowledge does something to a person that no pep talk ever could. I have watched it. I have watched a congregation that had been merely surviving, merely hanging on for the rapture, come slowly alive when they understood that the meal they cook for the grieving family, the porch they repair for the widow down the road, the marriage two of them are fighting to save, are not killing time. They are the very stuff of the city, gathered up, none of it lost. The work did not change. The town did not change. What changed was what the work was for, and that turned out to be most of everything.

And let me name the danger one more time so I am not misheard at the very end, because this is the chapter where a person could run off the road in the wrong direction. We are not the builders of the New Jerusalem. The minute we start to believe we are constructing the kingdom by our programs and our progress, we have become the proud city of man wearing the kingdom's clothes, and that confusion has wrecked more good movements than persecution ever did. The city comes down. We do not stack it up. But neither do we sit on our hands and wait, because the same God who brings the city down has handed us baskets to fill in the meantime, and told us, on his own word, that what we carry in faith is not in vain. So we hold the two truths in two hands and we refuse to drop either one. We do not build it. We build toward it. And the building toward, done in faith, is gathered into the bringing down, by a grace we will not fully understand until we are standing inside the gates looking back.

So ask it of yourself, plainly, before you close this chapter. What did you build this week that is fit for that city? Not what did you accomplish. Not what moved the numbers. What did you make, or mend, or forgive, or carry, in faith, that the kings of the earth could bring through those gates without shame? Most of us, if we are honest, will find the answer is smaller than we wish. But it is never nothing. The seed goes into the ground looking like nothing. And the field is real.

The end is not a rescue from the world but the healing of it, and that changes what we build.
chapters.verdict: The end is not a rescue from the world but the healing of it, and that changes what we build.

chapters.title: Suffering and the Shape of the Building
chapters.summary: The church has always risen most surely through suffering rather than around it, and the cross is not an interruption of the building but the pattern of it. A theology of the unfinished church must make sense of the pain, not preach around it.
chapters.body:
I have to stop and talk about suffering, because a book about hope that does not reckon honestly with suffering is a book that will fail you on the day you need it most, and I have read too many of those. I have, God help me, written a few sermons like that too, early on, before I knew better. Bright sermons. Sermons that solved the problem of pain in twenty-five minutes with three points and a closing illustration about a sunrise. And then I would stand at a graveside on a Thursday and watch one of those tidy sermons evaporate in the cold air over an open hole in the ground, and I would understand, again, that I had been preaching at the pain instead of into it.

Everything I have written so far could be misread as a kind of triumphalism, as if the building simply rises, smoothly, inevitably, and all we have to do is trust the architect and enjoy the ride up. But that is not how it goes, and you know it is not how it goes, because you have lived some version of the pain that makes a person pick up a book like this in the first place. The marriage that did not make it despite the prayers. The child who walked away from everything you tried to give him. The diagnosis. The church split that broke friendships you thought were permanent. The long depression that no amount of faith seemed to lift. If the building is rising, then it is rising through all of that, not around it, and any hope I offer you that cannot account for the suffering is not hope. It is just optimism wearing a cross necklace.

Let me tell on myself, because I do not want to write this chapter from a clean distance. I have sat in living rooms where there was nothing to say. I sat once with a young mother whose baby had died, a woman from our congregation who had prayed harder for that child than I have prayed for anything in my life, and she looked at me across her kitchen table, the casseroles already crowding the counter behind her, and she asked me why. Not the theological why, the philosophy-seminar why. The other one. The why that is really a wail with a question mark stapled to the end of it. And I will be honest with you. Every neat thing I knew about the problem of evil went silent in my mouth. I did not give her an answer. I do not think there is an answer you can hand across a kitchen table to a woman whose baby is in the ground. What I did, mostly, was stay, and weep a little with her, and come back the next week, and the week after that. And I have come to think that staying was closer to the truth of the gospel than any answer I could have produced, because the gospel's response to suffering is not finally an explanation. It is a presence.

So let me say the hard thing plainly, and then I will spend the rest of the chapter trying to make it bearable instead of cruel. The church has always risen most surely through suffering, not in spite of it but somehow by means of it. This is not a sentiment. It is a pattern you can trace across two thousand years, and it starts at the very center, with the cross itself. The whole building is founded on a Friday afternoon execution. The cornerstone is a man tortured to death by the state. There is no version of Christianity, none, that goes around the cross, because the cross is not an obstacle on the way to the kingdom. The cross is the way the kingdom comes. "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit" (John 12:24). Jesus said that about himself, about his own coming death, and then he said it about everyone who would follow him. The pattern of the seed is the pattern of the whole thing. Death first, then fruit. Burial first, then harvest. There is no path to the harvest that skips the burial, and the church has spent a lot of energy in comfortable centuries pretending otherwise, and it has produced a soft and brittle faith that snaps the first time real weight comes down on it.

I have watched that brittle faith snap, up close. A man in his fifties, a deacon, a pillar, the kind of man who could quote you chapter and verse and had taught the adult class for years. He lost his job and then, eighteen months later, his wife to a fast and ugly cancer, and somewhere in there his faith simply came apart in his hands, and he told me, with a kind of bewildered anger, that none of it had been what he was promised. And I realized, listening to him, that somewhere along the way he had absorbed a promise the Bible never made him. He thought the faith was a fence that kept the suffering out. He had built his whole life inside that fence, and when the suffering came through it anyway, as it always does, he concluded the fence had failed, and he walked out of the only thing that could have held him. Nobody ever told him, out loud, that the cross is the center and not the exception. He learned a Christianity with the cross moved off to the side, and a Christianity with the cross off to the side cannot survive a Thursday graveside, his own or anyone else's.

The early church knew this because they had no choice but to know it. Tertullian, writing around the year 200, while Christians were being killed for sport in the arenas of an empire that found their deaths entertaining, said that the blood of the martyrs is seed. Seed. Not waste, not tragedy, not the failure of the project, but seed sown into the ground from which more church grows. And history bore him out in the most literal way. The empire tried to stamp the church out by killing it, and the killing made it grow, because people watched Christians die well, die with a peace and even a joy that made no sense, and the watchers wanted to know what these people had that took the terror out of death. Think about what that actually looked like, in the stands. You came to the arena for blood sport, the way a man today might go to a fight, and you watched some young woman who would not curse Christ to save her own life walk out onto the sand singing, of all things, and you went home that night unable to shake it. The persecution that was meant to be the end of the church turned out to be one of the engines of its expansion. The building went up through the fire. It always has.

Now I want to be careful, because this teaching gets abused, badly, and I have seen the abuse do terrible damage. There is a version of this that becomes cruel, that tells the suffering person their pain is good for them and they should be grateful for it, that hands a grieving mother a tidy theological explanation for her dead child and calls it comfort. I am not doing that, and I will not do that, and the Bible does not do that. Job's friends did that. They sat with him in silence for seven days, which was the best thing they ever did, and then they opened their mouths and started explaining his suffering to him, and by the end of the book God himself is angry at them for it. "Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right," he tells them, of all the pious and orthodox things they had said over their suffering friend. Be careful explaining other people's pain to them. God was.

And Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, even though he knew, knew for certain, that he was about to raise him from the dead in five minutes (John 11:35). Sit with how strange that is. He knew the resurrection was coming, knew it was minutes away, and he still wept, which tells you that the coming joy does not cancel the present grief, does not make it fake or unspiritual or a failure of faith. The shortest verse in the Bible is God himself crying at a funeral he is about to undo. So when I say the building rises through suffering, I am not telling you to be glad about your suffering, or to slap a verse on it and move along. I am telling you that God is not absent from it, and not wasting it, and that the pain you are in is not proof that the building has stopped going up. It may be, in ways you cannot possibly see from inside it, exactly how it is going up in you.

Jürgen Moltmann understood this from the inside, not as a theory but as a man who had been broken and remade by it. He was a young German soldier in the Second World War, captured, held in prisoner of war camps for years with his country in ruins and his future erased, and he has written that it was there, with nothing left to hope in and the photographs of the death camps posted in the prison so the prisoners would see what their nation had done, that he first met the God who suffers. Not the distant, untouchable God of the philosophy textbooks, the one who sits above all pain in serene perfection, but the crucified God, the one on the cross, the one who had been where Moltmann was. He came home and spent a long life arguing that the cross is not an embarrassment Christianity has to explain away but the very center it has to preach, that the God revealed there is a God who takes suffering into his own being rather than holding it at arm's length. A God who is only powerful, only above it all, is no comfort in a prison camp. A God who has hung on a Roman cross and cried out in real abandonment, my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, is a God a broken man can actually pray to, because that God has already prayed those exact words first.

Because here is what I have watched, over fifteen years of standing close to people in their worst seasons. I have watched comfort produce shallow Christians and suffering produce deep ones, again and again, until I could no longer pretend it was a coincidence. The people in my congregation with the most substance, the ones whose faith has roots that go down into bedrock, the ones you want next to you when your own world is falling apart, are almost never the ones who had it easy. They are the ones who went through something that should have destroyed them and came out the other side holding onto God by their fingernails, and somehow, in the holding on, got welded to him in a way that ease could never have welded them. I think of an older woman in our church, widowed young, who raised three children alone in a hard town on almost nothing, and buried one of those children before she buried her husband. If you want to know what God is like, you do not go ask the comfortable. You go sit with her. She has a steadiness that frightens me a little, the steadiness of someone who has already lost most of what a person is afraid of losing and found that God was still there underneath it. Comfort could never have built that woman. Only the furnace built her.

Paul names the chain explicitly. "Tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope" (Romans 5:3-4). There is a sequence there, a forge. Pressure produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces a hope that cannot be embarrassed because it has already been tested in the fire and held. You do not get the hope at the end without the tribulation at the beginning. The forge is part of the design. And notice what Paul does not say. He does not say we glory in tribulation because tribulation is good. He does not pretend the pain is sweet. He says we glory in tribulation knowing what it works, knowing where the sequence ends. The glory is not in the pain. The glory is in the God who refuses to waste it.

I think of Joseph at the end of his long, brutal story, sold by his own brothers, enslaved, falsely accused, forgotten in a prison for years, every reasonable hope deferred until it must have seemed dead. Remember the shape of those years. He is thrown in a pit by the people who were supposed to love him most. He is sold to strangers. He does the right thing in Potiphar's house and gets prison for his trouble. He interprets a dream for a man who promises to remember him and then forgets him for two full years. There is no tidy upward arc to Joseph's life. There is a long descent that does not look like it is going anywhere good. And when he finally stands before the brothers who started it all, he does not say it did not hurt, or that it was fine, or that it all worked out so no harm done. He says something far stronger and far stranger. "Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses are true at the same time, and the gospel lives in the tension between them. They meant it for evil, real evil, and Joseph does not pretend otherwise. And God meant the very same events for good, and Joseph does not pretend otherwise about that either. God did not stop the evil. He did not airlift Joseph out of the pit or the prison. He went down into the pit with him and built something through the whole ruined mess that could not have been built any other way, and Joseph could only see it looking backward, from the far side, decades later. That is almost always how it works. You cannot see what God is building through your suffering while you are in it. You can sometimes see it after. And the rest you will only see in the city, when the scaffolding comes down and the whole strange, painful, mud-spattered construction finally makes sense.

This is why I have no patience anymore, none, for the version of Christianity that promises to spare you the cross. You know the one I mean. It comes on the television and it fills the big rooms and it sells the books, and it promises health and wealth and your best life now, and it treats suffering as a sign of insufficient faith or unconfessed sin. That gospel is not just wrong, it is cruel, because it abandons people in exactly the moment they need a true God most, and it adds the crushing weight of shame to the weight of grief they were already carrying. I have watched it happen. I have sat with people who came out of those rooms with a sick child, and they were not only grieving the child, they were tormented by the suspicion that they had somehow caused it, that if they had only believed harder, given more, confessed some hidden thing, the child would have lived. As if your cancer were a faith problem. As if your dead child were evidence you did not believe hard enough. That is not the religion of a crucified Lord. The religion of a crucified Lord makes a particular and difficult promise, and it is not the promise we wish it were. It does not promise to spare you the cross. It promises that the cross is not the end of the story, that there is a third day on the far side of every Friday, that the God who hung there with the nails through his hands is with you in your own dark Friday and will not abandon you in the tomb, and that the building he is raising through your pain is real, and good, and will stand.

There is an objection here, and it is a fair one, and I have felt it myself, so I am not going to dodge it. If God can bring good out of suffering, why does he not just bring the good without the suffering? Why the pit and the prison? Why not skip to the throne? I do not have a full answer to that, and I distrust anyone who says they do. But I notice that God himself, when he came, did not skip it. He had every power in heaven available to him. He could have saved the world from a throne, by decree, without a single drop of blood. He chose the manger and the carpenter's shop and the road and the cross.
