Whatever the reason that suffering is woven so deep into the way God redeems the world, it is a reason God submitted himself to first, before he ever asked it of you. He is not standing outside the furnace handing out advice. He went in.

There is a second objection, and it is harder, and it comes not from the philosophy seminar but from the kitchen table again. Fine, someone says, God went into the furnace, God suffered too, but I do not need a God who suffers alongside me. I need a God who stops the suffering. What good is company in a pit? I want out of the pit. And I feel the force of that, I do, and I have felt it on my own behalf in seasons I will not detail. But I have come to think it misjudges what we are actually given. We are not given a God who merely sits with us in the dark and shares the misery, as though the best heaven could do was suffer along helplessly. We are given a God who goes into the dark and comes out the far side of it, dragging the door off its hinges as he goes. The tomb is not where the story of Jesus ends. It is where the story of every tomb begins to end. The reason the early Christians could sing in the arena was not that they had made peace with death. It was that they believed death had already been beaten, in the body of a man, three days after a Friday, and that what was coming for them was not finally an ending but a following, out the same door he had already broken. Company in the pit would be a small thing. A God who has been through the pit and come out, and who is therefore able to bring you out too, is everything.

I have to add a word here about the people who do not come out, at least not in this life, because I do not want to write a chapter that quietly assumes every Friday ends in a visible Sunday before the funeral. Sometimes the marriage does not heal. Sometimes the prodigal does not come home. Sometimes the depression does not lift, and a faithful believer goes down into the dark and stays there for years, doing everything right, and the fog does not break. I have walked with people like that, and I have learned to stop promising them an outcome I cannot guarantee, because the comfort that depends on a happy ending you can see is the same shallow comfort the prosperity preachers sell, just dressed more soberly. The promise is not that you will see the harvest before you die. Joseph saw his. Many do not. The promise is that the seed in the ground is not lost, that the God who keeps your tears in a bottle is keeping count of every dark year you held on when holding on felt like nothing, and that the building rising through your endurance is real even if you never once feel it rise. Faithfulness in the unlit furnace, with no visible fruit, no felt presence, no answered why, is not a lesser faith. It may be the deepest faith there is, the faith of a man clinging to a God he can no longer feel, on the strength of a word he can no longer hear clearly, simply because he has decided that the God who hung on the cross will not lie to him in the end.

Let me come back to that young mother at the kitchen table, because I left her there and I do not want to leave her there. I told you I had no answer for her, and that is true. But I want to tell you what happened over the following two years, because it is the closest thing to an answer I have ever actually seen. She did not get over it. People do not get over a thing like that, and anyone who tells you they did is lying or did not love the child. But slowly, in a way I could not have engineered and would never dare to promise, something grew in her that had not been there before. She started to notice other grieving people the way only the grieving can notice them. When a couple in our church lost a pregnancy, she was at their door before I was, with no theology, no three points, just her presence and the terrible authority of someone who knew. She became, without ever intending to or wanting the job, the person in our congregation that the broken-hearted found their way to. The thing that should have destroyed her had, instead, hollowed out a space in her wide enough to hold other people's pain, and she filled that space with a tenderness I have rarely seen anywhere else. I am not saying God killed her baby to make her tender. I will never say that, and I do not believe it, and Job's friends can keep that theology. I am saying that God refused to let even that go to waste, that he went down into the worst thing that ever happened to her and built something out of the ruin that has since saved other people, and that she could only see it looking backward, the way Joseph did, from the far side of a grief she would still undo in a heartbeat if she could.

So if you are suffering as you read this, and somebody always is, I am not going to hand you a tidy explanation, because I do not have one and I distrust the people who claim they do. But I will tell you what I am sure of, what I have staked my life and my ministry on. The pain you are in is not the building coming down. It may be, in the hidden way these things work, the building going up. The seed has to fall into the ground and seem to die before it can bring forth the harvest. Your tears are not wasted, and they are not unseen, and there is a specific promise about them, that one day God himself, with his own hand, will wipe every one of them away (Revelation 21:4), which is not a thing you do to tears that never mattered. He gathers them. He keeps them in a bottle, the psalmist says (Psalm 56:8). Stop on that image, because it is one of the tenderest in all of Scripture. A bottle. He does not ignore your crying and he does not merely tolerate it. He collects it, the way you would keep something precious, the way a man keeps the letters of someone he loved. And then, on the last day, he wipes them away with his own hand, and not before, because they were real, and they counted, and they were part of how he built you into the wall.

The building goes up through the cross, not around it, because that is the only way it ever has.
chapters.verdict: The building goes up through the cross, not around it, because that is the only way it ever has.
reflect: Are you waiting for suffering to pass before the real work of God can resume, or asking what God is building through it?
Where have you preached or believed a version of faith that promised to spare you the cross?
What has been built in you through pain that comfort could never have built?

chapters.title: The Church Across the Earth
chapters.summary: The future God is building is global, and the church's center of gravity has already shifted away from the West that imagines itself central. The unfinished church is rising fastest in the very places the old Christendom thought of as its mission field.
chapters.body:
When Western Christians despair about the future of the church, they are almost always making a geographical error without realizing it. They mistake their corner of the church for the whole of it. They look out one window and conclude the whole sky is dark.

I do it too. I want to be honest about that before I say anything else, because it is easy to write this chapter as though I had risen above the mistake, and I have not. I stand in our sanctuary in Fenton on a winter Sunday, and I count the seats, the way every pastor counts whether he admits it or not, and I see the empty stretches where families used to sit, and a kind of low dread settles in my chest, and the thought forms almost before I can stop it: it is all running out. The faith is running out. And then I have to catch myself, because what I am actually looking at is one room, in one small town, in one fading corner of one aging civilization, on one cold morning, and I have just quietly extrapolated from that one room to the entire purpose of God across the whole earth. That is not a small mistake. That is the mistake of a man standing in his own backyard in the rain, concluding it is raining on the planet.

The story most of us absorbed without ever being taught it directly goes something like this. Christianity is a Western religion. It was born in the Mediterranean, raised by Europe, carried across the world by European missionaries, and is now declining in its heartland as secularism advances and the lights of faith go out one cathedral at a time. The faith is shrinking, we assume, because it is shrinking here, in Europe and in North America, which is where we happen to live and therefore where we happen to look. But here is not the world. Our window is not the sky. And the actual map of global Christianity, the real one, tells a story so completely different from our despair that it ought to reorder how we think about the church's future from the ground up.

The center of gravity of the Christian church has moved, and most Western Christians have not noticed, because it moved away from us. For most of the last two thousand years, the typical, average Christian on earth was a European. White, Western, living somewhere between Ireland and Russia. That is simply no longer true, and it is not even close anymore. Today the typical Christian is far more likely to be a Nigerian, a Brazilian, a Chinese believer in a house church the government cannot count, a Filipino, a Kenyan, a Korean. The faith that is declining in Europe is exploding across the global South and the East. There are, by most serious estimates, more practicing Christians in China today than there are members of the Communist Party, and they are worshipping in churches the state did not authorize and cannot fully see. Think about what that costs them, and then think about what it costs you to go on a Sunday morning. They gather in apartments and back rooms knowing a knock on the door could mean prison, and they keep gathering, and they keep multiplying, faster than a watching state can suppress them. The church in sub-Saharan Africa has grown from a small minority a little over a century ago to many hundreds of millions of believers now, one of the largest and fastest movements toward Christ in the entire history of the faith, happening in our lifetimes, mostly off the radar of the Western Christians busy writing the obituary.

Let me make that concrete, because the numbers are so large they stop meaning anything. On a given Sunday morning, while I am standing in my half-empty Michigan sanctuary feeling the cold draft of decline, there are churches in Lagos and Nairobi and Seoul so full that people are standing in the aisles and spilling out the doors, services running for hours, congregations planting other congregations faster than they can build buildings to hold them. There are believers in Iran, of all places, coming to Christ in numbers that the authorities find genuinely alarming, often with no missionary anywhere near them, reading a Bible they obtained at some risk and finding in it a Lord they were told their whole lives to hate. The same morning. The same hour, more or less, allowing for the turn of the globe. One faith. And I am over here taking its pulse with my fingers on the one wrist that happens to be slowing down.

The scholar Philip Jenkins documented this great shift in his work on what he called the next Christendom, and the central fact he laid out is simple and staggering. The future of Christianity is not Western and is increasingly not even mostly Western. The church's center of gravity has moved south and east while the West was preoccupied with measuring its own decline. We have been counting the empty pews in our own building and concluding the religion is dying, while across the world the same religion is in a noonday of growth the West has not seen in centuries. Jenkins points out something even more unsettling for our assumptions, which is that the Christianity growing in the global South often looks very little like the comfortable, accommodated, theologically softened Christianity of the dying West. It tends to be more fervent, more supernatural in its expectations, more willing to take the Bible at its word, more like the book of Acts than like a Western committee meeting. The faith is not just relocating. It is, in some ways, reverting to type, to a form the early church would recognize faster than we would.

I want to slow down on that, because it is the part that should make a comfortable Western pastor like me genuinely uneasy, and I think the unease is good for me. The Christians who are multiplying fastest are, by and large, not the ones who have made the faith easiest. They are not the ones who trimmed it down to fit the educated sensibilities of a secular age, who quietly set aside the resurrection as a metaphor and the miracles as ancient credulity and the cross as a tragic misunderstanding, who reduced the whole thing to a program of being decent to one another. That version of Christianity, the one that bent over backwards to be respectable to its cultured despisers, is precisely the version dying fastest in the West. It turns out that a faith with nothing left to offend the modern mind also has nothing left to convert it, and a church that asks nothing and claims nothing supernatural and costs nothing is a church people can take or leave, and they are leaving. Meanwhile the faith that is exploding is the costly, demanding, blood-and-resurrection kind, held by people who have far less reason than we do, by every worldly measure, to believe anything hopeful at all. That ought to chasten us. We assumed for a long time that the way to save the faith in a skeptical age was to make it smaller, safer, more reasonable. The global church is quietly demonstrating that we had it exactly backward.

Let me name the obvious risk, because I am not interested in trading Western triumphalism for a romanticized Southern version of it. The church growing across Africa and Asia and Latin America is not a flawless church. No church is, and I have spent this whole book insisting that the church is unfinished everywhere. There are real dangers in rapid growth, the prosperity preaching that has followed the faith into some of those regions like a parasite, the shortage of trained teachers, the blending of the gospel with older spiritualities, the temptation toward the very fusion of faith and power that wrecked the Western church under Christendom. I do not want to hand a struggling believer in Michigan a fantasy of a perfect church somewhere else to feel bad in comparison to. That would just be nostalgia pointed sideways instead of backward. The global church will have its own crises, is having them, and may one day write books mourning its own decline the way we write ours. The point is not that the South is pure and the West is corrupt. The point is that the building is rising, with all its scaffolding and mud, in places we were not watching, and that is enough to break the spell that says the project is failing.

I think about the first time this really landed on me, not as information but as something that rearranged me. I was at a gathering of pastors, the kind of thing I do a fair amount of through the network I help run, and there was a man there from East Africa, soft-spoken, who had walked a long way to be there and would walk a long way back. We got to talking, and I, in the reflexive way of an American pastor, asked him how his church was doing, half-expecting the kind of weary answer I would have given about my own. And he looked at me with a sort of gentle confusion and said that they could not build fast enough, that they were meeting under trees and in homes because there was nowhere to put everyone, that the problem was not how to keep people but how to find enough teachers for the people who kept coming. And then he asked me, with real concern, not condescension, what was happening to the church in America, because he had heard it was struggling, and he wanted to know how he and his people could pray for us. I have not forgotten the direction that conversation ran. He was praying for us. The man meeting under a tree, with no money and no building and no security, was carrying my comfortable, declining, climate-controlled American church to God in his prayers, because he had heard we were in trouble. That is the actual map of the church. I had it upside down, and a man under a tree turned it right side up.

And this is exactly what we should have expected, if we had been reading the right ending all along. The promise was never confined to one continent or one people. "I will build my church" was spoken over a global project from the very first day. The risen Christ told the disciples, before he ascended, that they would be his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth" (Acts 1:8). Not unto Europe. Not unto the respectable parts of the Roman world. The uttermost part of the earth. And the vision John is given at the end of everything is explicitly, insistently, every-national. He sees "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" (Revelation 7:9). And the New Jerusalem itself has the glory and honor of the nations, plural, carried into it (Revelation 21:26), the whole earth's peoples gathered in. A church that was only ever Western would have been a failure of the vision, a promise half-kept. A church that is becoming genuinely global, in our own day, before our eyes, is the vision coming true on schedule.

I find this both humbling and thrilling, and I want to be honest about the humbling part first, because the Western church needs the humbling more than it needs the thrill.

For centuries we assumed we were the center, and we built that assumption into everything. We were the senders. Others were the sent-to. We were the teachers, the ones with the seminaries and the theology and the resources. Others were the taught, the mission field, the recipients of our generosity and, too often, of our condescension. We exported the faith with one hand, which was genuinely good and right, and with the other hand, too often, we exported our culture, our politics, our colonial assumptions, our sense of our own superiority, until the gospel and the Western package were tangled together so tightly that even we could not always tell them apart. We sent the carpenter from Nazareth wearing a Western suit and carrying a Western flag, and the people we sent him to had to do the hard work of figuring out which parts were Jesus and which parts were us. And now the situation has reversed in ways the Western church is barely able to process emotionally. Churches in Nigeria and Brazil and Korea are sending missionaries to Europe and to North America. To the post-Christian West that has become, in Newbigin's exact phrase, a mission field again. I have met some of these missionaries. There are Nigerian pastors planting churches in England, in cities where the medieval cathedrals stand half-empty as tourist attractions, and they are puzzled by us, gently puzzled, the way you would be puzzled by a wealthy relative who has somehow forgotten everything that made the family rich in the first place. The taught have become the teachers. The sent-to have become the senders. The center has moved, and we are no longer it. And learning to receive the faith, humbly, from people we once flattered ourselves we were teaching is going to require a depth of humility the Western church has very rarely had to practice. We are about to be evangelized by our own former mission fields, and how we receive that will tell us a great deal about whether we have learned anything at all.

Let me sit with the objection that rises here, because someone is thinking it. If the global church is growing so fast, then why should I care about the decline of my church, in my town, in my country? Is this not just a comfortable way of looking past my own grief to feel better about a graph? No. And I want to be careful, because that is exactly the wrong use of everything I am saying. The growth of the church in Nairobi does not refill the seats in Fenton, and it does not bring back the young people who have left, and it does not make the cold draft in our sanctuary any warmer. The point is not that you should stop caring about your corner. The point is that you should stop confusing your corner with the building. Both things are true at once. Your local grief is real, and the global hope is real, and a faith big enough to live in holds both without using one to deny the other. I am not asking you to feel better. I am asking you to see straight.

I think there is also a particular sin hiding in the Western despair, and I want to name it because naming it has helped me. Underneath a lot of our grief about decline is a quiet assumption that we were the main thing. That God's project was essentially a Western project with some outposts elsewhere, and that if it fails here it fails. That is not humility grieving. That is wounded pride grieving, the pride of a people who have been at the center so long they cannot imagine the center being anywhere else, who half-believe that the survival of the Christian faith depends on the survival of their particular version of it. And there is something almost comic, when you step back, about a Christian in a wealthy and comfortable corner of the world, with central heating and full bookshelves and complete freedom to worship, looking at a faith that is multiplying among the poor and the persecuted across the rest of the planet and pronouncing it dead because his own congregation shrank. It is the firstborn son in the parable, standing in the field, refusing to come in to the feast, sullen that the celebration is happening for someone other than him. The Father has to go out and plead with that son. Come in. Your brother who was dead is alive. The music you are hearing through the wall is not a funeral. It is a homecoming, and it is happening whether you come in to it or not.

But there is real glory in this for those who can see past their own wounded sense of centrality. Because what the global picture reveals is that the church was never a Western institution with a Western future and a Western expiration date. It was always God's global project, from the foot of that rock at Caesarea Philippi onward. And the contraction we feel so acutely in our own particular corner is happening at the very same moment the building is rising faster than at almost any time in history in corners we were simply not looking at. The scaffolding came down on one wing of the great construction site, our wing, and we stood in the sudden quiet and concluded that the whole building must be getting abandoned, when in fact the crews had simply moved to where the work was now most alive, and the hammering we could no longer hear in our own wing was deafening on the other side of the world.

This ought to do something quite specific to our despair, and I want to name it precisely so it is not mistaken for denial. The decline we see at home is real. I have said it before and I will keep saying it, because I am not interested in comforting you with a lie. There is grief in our decline and there are lessons in it, hard ones, about Christendom and nominalism and the cost of comfort, and we should learn them. But the decline is local. It is real, and it is local. It is not the verdict on the church. It is the verdict on the church in one place, in one season, under one specific set of conditions that we have already examined, the long end of Christendom, the slow exhaustion of a borrowed and nominal faith. To read the global future of the church off the European attendance numbers is exactly like reading the global weather off your own backyard. It is raining here. It is genuinely raining, and you are genuinely getting wet, and I am not going to tell you that you are dry. But it is not raining everywhere. In much of the world the church is standing in a noonday sun of growth that our corner has not felt for a very long time.

Newbigin saw all of this before most of us, and he saw it from a particular and instructive vantage point, which is worth pausing on. He gave the strong years of his life as a missionary in India, in a place where Christians were a small and often despised minority and the faith had to make its way against the whole weight of an ancient and confident culture. And then he came home to England, in his old age, expecting to find the sending church that had sent him, the Christian heartland, and instead he found a country that had quietly stopped believing while keeping the buildings. He found, in his own homeland, a mission field. He had spent decades learning how to commend the gospel to people who had never assumed it, and he came home to discover that this was now the exact skill his own country needed and had entirely lost, because England had assumed the faith for so long it had forgotten how to actually offer it to anyone who did not already hold it. There is a strange mercy in that reversal. The very thing the Western church exported and then forgot, the missionary posture, the patient commending of Christ to a culture that does not assume him, is now being carried back to us by the children of the people we taught. The student has come back to teach the teacher the lesson the teacher forgot.

There is a passage in Isaiah I keep coming back to, where God speaks to his servant and says that it is "a light thing" that the servant should merely raise up the tribes of Jacob and restore the preserved of Israel. Too small a task. Hear the holy impatience in that. God looks at what we would call a tremendous undertaking, the restoration of a whole nation, and he calls it a light thing, too small, not worthy of the scope of what he intends. So God says he will make him "a light to the Gentiles," that his salvation may reach "unto the end of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6). It was always too small a thing for the church to be one people's private possession, one culture's chaplain, one continent's heritage. The scope was always the end of the earth, every nation, every tongue. And the church we are actually watching emerge in this generation, global, multiplying, sending in every direction at once, no longer organized around a single Western capital, is far closer to that promised scope than the comfortable Christendom we are busy mourning ever was. We are not watching the church die. We are watching it finally become as large as the promise.

There is a practical edge to all of this that I do not want to leave out, because it is easy to make the global church into a comforting abstraction and then change nothing about how I actually live. If the center has moved, then the Western church has a choice to make about its posture, and the choice is between condescension and partnership. For a long time the relationship ran in one direction. We sent money and missionaries and we received gratitude, and that arrangement, however well meant, kept us in the position of the patron and them in the position of the recipient, and a patron does not have to learn anything from the people he is helping. The harder and better thing now is to receive. To read the theologians of the global South and not just assign them to a course on world Christianity. To learn how the persecuted church prays, because they pray differently than the comfortable church, with an urgency we have mostly lost. To let a Nigerian pastor or a Chinese house-church believer correct something in our own discipleship, which means first admitting they might have something to correct. I have started, in our small way, building real relationships with churches outside the West, not as our mission projects but as our teachers, and I will tell you it has been good for the pride of a Midwestern Baptist pastor in ways that were not comfortable and were exactly what I needed. The day the Western church learns to sit at the feet of the churches it once flattered itself it was teaching is the day it starts to recover something it lost a long time ago.

So when a discouraged believer in a half-empty sanctuary in a small Michigan town asks me whether the church really has a future, and they do ask, sometimes after a service, hanging back until the others have gone, asking it quietly as though it were almost too dangerous to say out loud, I want to gently widen the question before I try to answer it. The church you can see from that particular pew may well be in a hard season, and I am not going to dismiss your grief over the empty seats around you. I feel it with you. I count the same seats. But the church God can see from his throne is a multitude that no man can number, gathered out of every nation and kindred and people and tongue, and it is rising. The building never stopped. We were just standing in one quiet wing of it, in the cool of the evening of one civilization, mistaking the quiet of our own corner for the silence of the whole.

The church is not dying. It is moving, and we mistook our corner of it for the whole.
chapters.verdict: The church is not dying. It is moving, and we mistook our corner of it for the whole.
reflect: When you imagine the global church, do you picture the West or the world?
How does the explosive growth of the church elsewhere reframe the decline you see at home?
What would humility look like for the Western church in a world where it is no longer the center?

chapters.title: The Costly Minority
chapters.summary: As the church loses its cultural majority it must rediscover the disciplines that sustained it as a minority before Christendom, becoming again a community whose visible difference is its witness. This is not a strategy for survival but a recovery of the church's actual nature.
chapters.body:
If Christendom is ending, and it is, then the question that actually matters is not how we keep it on life support. The question is what kind of church we become on the other side of it. And for that we have to learn, or relearn, how to be a minority, because that is what we are becoming, and that is in fact what the church was built to be.

We are not the first generation of Christians to face this. We only feel like it because we have such short memories, and because Christendom lasted so long that we forgot there was ever a before. But the church spent its first three centuries as a minority, and not a comfortable, tolerated minority either. A suspect one. A persecuted one, in waves. A community that had to explain itself to neighbors who assumed the worst, who whispered that these Christians were cannibals because of something they said about eating a body and drinking blood, who called them atheists because they would not burn a pinch of incense to the gods of the city, who blamed them when the harvest failed or the plague came or the river flooded. They won converts one at a time and lost some of them to martyrdom, they had no cultural wind at their back and no establishment to lean on and no assumption working in their favor. And out of that exact situation it grew, and grew, and eventually turned the empire upside down. So the question before us is not new, and the answer is not novel, and that is the most hopeful thing I can tell you in this chapter. We have done this before. The manual exists. We just have to take it down off the shelf and read it as if it were written for us, because it was.

Tertullian, again, the same man who told us the blood of the martyrs is seed, gives us a window into what it actually looked like to be that minority. He wrote a defense of the Christians to the Roman authorities around the year 197, and in it he simply describes how his people lived, and the description is a kind of accidental portrait of a costly minority that knew exactly who it was. They met. They pooled their money, not under compulsion but freely, into a common fund, and used it not for feasts and drinking but to support the poor, to bury the destitute, to care for orphaned children and aged servants and people shipwrecked or sent to the mines for the faith. And he records the famous thing the pagans said of them, almost in wonder, almost in suspicion. See how these Christians love one another. It was meant partly as a sneer, and Tertullian throws it back as a badge. That was the witness. Not the size of the buildings, because there were none. Not the influence in the Senate, because there was none. A community whose love for one another was so visible that the outside world had a saying about it. We have buildings and influence and budgets the early church could not have dreamed of, and I am not at all sure the world has a saying about how we love each other. That comparison should keep a pastor awake, and some nights it keeps me awake.

What did the early church have, as a minority, that we as a fading majority let atrophy? Several things, and I want to name them concretely, because this is the part of the book that has to become practical or it is just consolation.

First, they had a clear and difficult initiation. You did not drift into the early church the way people drifted into the Christendom church. You could not. There was nothing to drift into and no social reward for joining and considerable social cost. To become a Christian, you went through a long process of catechesis, often lasting years, in which you were taught the faith and your life was examined and reshaped before you were ever baptized. In some places the catechumens, the ones still under instruction, were dismissed from the service before the Lord's Supper, sent out the door, because they had not yet crossed the threshold that gave them a place at the table. Baptism, when it finally came, was a serious threshold, a death and resurrection, a public and sometimes dangerous declaration that you now belonged to Christ and not to Caesar. Picture it. You went down into the water having spent two or three years being formed, having your old life pulled apart and a new one built, knowing that coming up out of that water might cost you your standing, your family, your trade, in some seasons your life. There was no nominal Christianity in the early church for a simple reason. Nominal Christianity could get you killed, and nobody dies for a faith they hold nominally. The membrane around the community was thick. You knew when you were in, and so did everyone else, and it cost you something to be there.

We let that membrane get thin to the point of vanishing, because under Christendom we did not need it. When the whole culture was nominally Christian, the church could be casual about its boundaries. Walk in, sit down, you are basically one of us. And that worked, more or less, as long as the culture was carrying the faith along on its current. But the current has reversed. The culture is no longer carrying anyone toward Christ. It is carrying them away. And a church with a thin membrane in a culture flowing the wrong direction will simply be emptied out, which is precisely what is happening. Let me put this in terms a pastor lives with. I have received people into membership in about fifteen minutes, a handshake and a form and a welcome from the front, people I barely knew, who barely knew what they were joining, and I have watched a good number of them drift right back out the same wide door within a year or two, because nothing held them. There was no threshold to cross and therefore nothing to stand inside of. The recovery the moment demands is a recovery of serious formation. Of catechesis that actually teaches the faith to people who do not absorb it by cultural osmosis anymore. Of a membership that means something, that you cross into deliberately, that asks something of you. I have started, in my own ministry, late and clumsily, to make the door narrower, to ask more before someone joins, to teach for months and not minutes, and I will tell you honestly that some people do not like it, and some of them go elsewhere, to a church with a wider door. But the ones who come through a narrow door tend to stay, because they actually arrived somewhere. The point is not to keep people out. The point is to actually make Christians, instead of assuming the culture will make them for us, because the culture has resigned from that job and is not coming back.

Second, they had a visible difference of life. The early Christians were known. Their neighbors could point to them and say, those people live differently. They did not expose their unwanted infants on the hillside the way everyone else did. In the Roman world a father could simply decline a newborn, especially a girl, and the child would be left outside the city walls to die or to be taken by whoever wanted a slave, and this was so ordinary that no one thought twice about it. The Christians went out and gathered those babies up and raised them as their own. They cared for the poor, including the poor who were not their own. They stayed in the plague cities and nursed the dying when the pagans, sensibly, fled. Think about the courage in that, the plain physical courage. A sickness is sweeping the city, nobody understands it, the wealthy and the wise are loading their carts and getting out, and these strange people are walking the other direction, into the houses of the dying, to hold the hand of a stranger and give him water, and catching the thing themselves, and dying of it, and being counted, by their neighbors, as the only ones who stayed. They were faithful in marriage in a culture that was not. They forgave. They did not retaliate. And this visible difference was not a marketing strategy. It was simply what following Jesus produced in them, and it was the single most powerful evangelistic force the early church had, more powerful than any argument, because it was an argument you could not refute, made of lives you could watch. Jesus said it plainly. "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (John 13:35). Not by your arguments. Not by your political victories. By your love. The watching world is converted, when it is converted, mostly by Christians it can watch.

Under Christendom we lost this too, because when everyone is a Christian, there is no visible difference to see. The Christians lived like everyone else because everyone else also called themselves Christians, and the salt lost its savor, exactly as Jesus warned it could (Matthew 5:13). Here is the uncomfortable test, and I put it to myself first. If belonging to my church were suddenly to cost a person their reputation, their easy social standing, maybe a job, would there be anything in the way we actually live, day to day, that would make the cost look worth paying? Would a watching neighbor see, in us, the kind of love that gathered the abandoned babies and stayed in the plague cities? Or would they see people who look exactly like everyone else on the street, with the same anxieties, the same grudges, the same frantic grasping, the same marriages quietly failing, who happen to drive somewhere on Sunday? I am not always sure of my answer, and that is the indictment, and I am inside it. The recovery the moment demands is a recovery of visible difference. Not weirdness for its own sake, not a retreat into a holy huddle, but a community whose life is so marked by love and integrity and forgiveness and care for the weak that the watching world is genuinely puzzled by it and eventually drawn to ask what accounts for it. We will not out-argue the culture back to faith. We have been trying that for a generation, manning the comment sections and winning the debates and losing the people, and it has not worked. We might, by grace, out-love it, the way the early church did, from below.

Let me answer an objection before I go to the third thing, because someone has been waiting to raise it since I started talking about narrow doors. Is this not just exclusion dressed up as faithfulness? Are you not building a club, a clique, a holy in-group that looks down on the people outside? I take that seriously, because the church has in fact done exactly that, has used the language of holiness to build walls of contempt, has made the threshold a way of feeling superior to the people on the other side of it. That is a real sin and I am not defending it. But notice what the early church actually did with its thick membrane. It did not turn inward and despise the world. It turned outward and gathered the world's abandoned babies. The same community that asked years of formation before baptism was the community most reckless in its love for outsiders, that ran toward the plague the rest of the city ran from. The membrane was not a wall against people. It was a wall against nominalism, against the easy in-and-out that produces Christians who were never actually formed into anything. You can have a serious threshold and an open heart at the same time. In fact you almost have to, because only a community that has actually been formed by the gospel has anything worth offering to the people outside it. A church with no membrane has nothing distinct to invite anyone into. It is just the surrounding culture with a steeple.

Third, they had each other, deeply, in a way our individualism has nearly destroyed. The early church was not a building you visited on Sunday. It was a community you belonged to with your whole life, that knew your business and bore your burdens and shared its goods so that, as Acts says, there was not a needy person among them (Acts 4:34). They could survive as a minority because they were not alone. The community itself was thick enough to sustain a faith the culture would no longer sustain for you. When the world says you are a fool for believing this, and your own family thinks you have lost your mind, you cannot hold the faith alone on the strength of your own conviction at two in the morning. You hold it because on Sunday you are among forty people who also believe it, who know your name, who fed you when you were sick, who will come if you call. The community is the thing that makes the belief survivable when the culture turns. And this is exactly what we will need, and exactly what our consumer Christianity is worst at providing. A faith you practice alone, on your own terms, attending a service the way you attend a movie, watching the stage, leaving when it ends, known by no one and accountable to no one, that kind of faith was always thin, but Christendom propped it up. I see it every week, the people who slip in after it starts and slip out before it ends, who would be mortified if anyone learned their actual situation, who want the music and the sermon and none of the knowing. I do not judge them, because I understand the instinct, the deep American instinct to keep yourself to yourself. But after Christendom that faith will simply collapse, because there will be nothing holding it up but the individual's own willpower, and willpower runs out. The Christians who survive what is coming, and more than survive, who thrive in it, will be the ones who are deeply, inconveniently, committed to an actual community of actual people who know them and will not let them quietly drift away.

Bonhoeffer learned all three of these the hard way, in the hardest school there has ever been, and I cannot write this chapter without him standing in the room. He watched the established church of a supposedly Christian nation, the church of Luther, with its centuries of prestige and its place at the center of German life, fold itself almost entirely into the Nazi state in the 1930s. That was Christendom's final logic playing all the way out, the church so fused with the culture that when the culture went mad the church went mad with it, blessing the very thing it should have died resisting. And Bonhoeffer's answer was not to find a better strategy for keeping the church respectable. His answer was to start an illegal seminary, at Finkenwalde, where he formed a small community of young pastors in exactly the three disciplines I have been describing, serious formation, visible difference, shared life, deliberately recovering the marks of a costly minority because he could see that the comfortable majority church had just demonstrated it could not stand. Out of that underground community came his little book on life together and his book on discipleship, where he wrote the line that has indicted comfortable Christians ever since, that when Christ calls a man he bids him come and die. The Gestapo eventually shut the seminary down and scattered the men. They hanged Bonhoeffer in April of 1945, days before the camp was liberated, days before the war he had resisted from inside was over. He paid the full price of the costly minority. And what he left the church was not a survival plan. It was a witness that the church is most truly itself precisely when it has been stripped of every cultural support and has nothing left to stand on but Christ, which turns out to be the only thing it ever actually stood on anyway.

I want to say clearly that I am not describing a strategy for survival, a clever plan to outlast the secular age. I am describing a recovery of the church's actual nature, the thing it was before the empire adopted it and dressed it up in borrowed robes. The disciplines of the costly minority, serious formation, visible difference, deep community, are not survival tactics. They are simply what the church is, stripped of the cultural supports that let us forget it for a while. Christendom let the church be lazy about all three, because the culture did the work for us. It catechized our children through the schools and the holidays and the assumed background of belief. It produced a baseline of Christian-ish behavior just by social pressure, the way a small town keeps people in line by the simple fact that everyone knows everyone. It provided a community of sorts just by everyone being nominally in. And now all three of those props are being kicked out from under us at once, and it feels like collapse, and from a Christendom point of view it is collapse. But from the point of view of the early church it is just the props coming off a building that was always meant to stand on its own foundation.

There is a freedom in this, hidden inside the loss, that I do not want you to miss. The church does not need the culture's approval to do the one thing it was actually made to do. It never did. It made disciples, formed saints, loved the poor, and witnessed to the resurrection for three hundred years with the full hostility of the most powerful empire on earth arrayed against it, and it did all of that better, arguably, than it did during the long comfortable centuries when the empire was on its side. The approval was never the source of our strength. We just came to lean on it so heavily that we mistook the crutch for the leg. And here is what I have come to believe about crutches. A man who has leaned on one long enough is genuinely afraid the first time someone takes it away, and that fear is real, I am not mocking it. Take the crutch away and there is a moment of terror, a lurch, a certainty that you are about to fall. And then, if we have any faith at all, the discovery that the leg was there the whole time, that the Spirit who fell in the upper room never depended on Constantine's blessing, that the church can walk, and run, and even leap, on the strength it was given at the start, which no emperor gave and no culture can take away.

I have watched the difference between propped-up faith and chosen faith play out across my own congregation, and it has made me a believer in the narrow door even when it costs me numbers. There was a couple, years back, who came to us out of a hard place, no church background to speak of, the wife pregnant and frightened and the husband barely willing to be there at all. By the old Christendom reflex I would have welcomed them in fast, signed them up, counted them, and moved on. Instead, almost by accident, the season of their lives forced a slower thing. People in the church carried them. A few families took them in, fed them, sat with them through the birth and the sleepless months and the marriage that nearly came apart twice. The husband asked his hard questions over a lot of kitchen tables, the way I once asked mine, and nobody rushed him, and nobody pretended the questions were stupid. It took years. And the faith that came out the far side of those years was not a thin thing they could set down when the culture frowned. It was load-bearing. That couple is now among the people who carry others, and I am fairly sure none of it would have happened if I had processed them through a wide door in fifteen minutes. The slow, costly, deeply involved way is not less efficient. It is the only way that actually makes Christians, and I had to relearn it from people in my own pews who were doing it instinctively while I was still counting heads.

Let me put the whole thing where I live, because I do not want to leave it floating in the centuries. I came to faith from atheism, with no Christendom carrying me along, no family current, no cultural assumption pushing me toward the door. For me, belief never once earned a social credit. If anything it cost me, among the people I had run with, who could not understand what had happened to a man they thought was too smart for all that. And what I want you to hear is that the faith I came into that way, against the grain, at some cost, with no props, is the only kind I have ever known how to hold, and I have watched it hold under weights that I have seen the propped-up kind buckle under. I am not afraid of the costly minority, not finally, though I feel the cost coming and I do not pretend it will be comfortable. A church that has to choose Christ deliberately, against the cultural grain, at some real price, is a church far closer to the New Testament than the one I was handed, the one where everyone was a Christian and therefore no one was. If the price of becoming the church again is losing the comfortable majority, then I will grieve the comfort, and I will pay the price, because the thing on the other side of the cost is the actual church, the one Christ said he would build, and it was always meant to cost something, because it was bought at the highest cost there is.

The church does not need the culture's approval to do the one thing it was made to do.
chapters.verdict: The church does not need the culture's approval to do the one thing it was made to do.
reflect: What would your faith cost you if belonging to the church no longer earned you any social credit?
What practices would the church need to recover to form people who can stand alone against the culture?
Is your Christianity strong enough to survive without the supports that Christendom used to provide?

chapters.title: The Long Faithfulness
chapters.summary: Most of the church's real work is hidden, slow, and unspectacular, and the great temptation of the present moment is to despise the ordinary faithfulness that the building actually rises on. Endurance, not excitement, is the virtue the unfinished church most requires.
chapters.body:
I want to talk now about Tuesdays, because the building does not rise on Sundays. It rises on Tuesdays, and Wednesdays, and the long gray middle of the week when no one is watching and nothing seems to be happening, and that is the part of the church's life that almost no book and almost no conference ever talks about, because it does not sell.

Let me show you a Tuesday. It is the kind I have lived a thousand times and will live a thousand more if God gives me the years. The alarm goes at five. The house is dark and cold. I do not feel anything, which is the part nobody warns you about. I make the coffee, and I sit in the same chair I have sat in for years, and I open the Bible to the place I left it, and I pray for my five sons by name, one at a time, the way I have prayed for them since the oldest was small. There is no fire in the room. There is no felt presence. Some mornings it is honestly just a man and a cold cup and a list of names and the ceiling. And then I get up, and I go answer the email, and I sit with a man whose marriage is coming apart and I have nothing new to tell him, only the old things, said again. And I drive home in the dark, and nothing measurable has happened, and that is most of the ministry, and it is most of the Christian life, and I think we have been quietly lied to about that, and the lie is killing people.

We are formed by a culture of the spectacular, and the church has caught the disease badly. We are drawn to the dramatic conversion, the explosive revival, the church that grew from nothing to thousands, the moment when God shows up unmistakably and the room shakes. And those moments are real, and they are gifts, and I have tasted a few of them and would not trade them. But they are not the substance of the church's life. They are the rare and bright exceptions. The substance is ordinary. The substance is a man getting up at five in the morning to pray for his children before work, again, the way he has every morning for thirty years, with no fireworks, no felt presence, just the dogged decision to show up before God one more time. The substance is a woman teaching the same Sunday school lesson she has taught a hundred times to children who will not remember her name. The substance is a couple staying married through a decade that gave them every excuse to quit. The substance is a pastor preaching, faithfully, to the same congregation, week after week, year after year, watching them grow by inches, burying the old ones and baptizing the new ones and grinding through the conflicts and the budget meetings and the slow, slow work of forming a people. The building rises on a thousand ordinary Tuesdays, and most of those Tuesdays will feel like nothing whatsoever is happening.

I think of a woman in our church, and there is one in nearly every church, so you know her too. She taught the four-year-olds for fifty years. Fifty. She started when Eisenhower was president and she stopped only when her hands could no longer manage the scissors and the paste. Do the arithmetic on that and it will stagger you. Hundreds of children. Thousands of Sundays. The same flannelgraph Noah, the same little chairs, the same song about the wise man and the foolish man, sung with the same hand motions, year after year after year. No one ever wrote about her. No conference ever called. When she died, the children she had taught were grown and scattered, and most of them, if you stopped them on the street, could not have told you her name. And yet I would put her hidden labor up against any platform in the country on the day the books are opened, because that is where the building actually went up. Not on the stages. In the little chairs.

And this is what I keep coming back to about a life like hers. She would not have called it heroic, and that is exactly what made it heroic. She did not stay fifty years because she had a vision of fifty years. Nobody could carry that. She stayed because she came back next Sunday, and then the one after that, and the staying accumulated underneath her without her ever deciding to be a person who had taught for half a century. Faithfulness almost never feels like faithfulness while you are doing it. It feels like Tuesday. It feels like getting the materials out one more time when you would rather not, like cutting the construction paper when your arthritis is bad, like loving children who will forget you. The grand word for it, perseverance, gets written into the books afterward, by other people, looking back. From the inside it is just the next ordinary thing done one more time, and that is why so few finish, because we are waiting to feel the grandeur, and the grandeur never comes, and we mistake its absence for a sign that we are on the wrong road.

The Bible is far more comfortable with this than we are. We skip past it looking for the action, but the action is mostly the exception. Consider how much of redemptive history is just waiting. Abraham waited twenty-five years between the promise of a son and the birth of Isaac. Twenty-five years of ordinary days, getting older, no son, the promise hanging there unfulfilled, and the text barely comments on it, just lets the decades pass. Moses spent forty years on the back side of a desert herding someone else's sheep before the bush ever burned. Forty years. Think about that. Forty years of finding lost lambs and watching the same sun cross the same sky, and not one verse of it recorded, because nothing happened that the world counts as happening, and yet that is where Moses was made. Joseph sat in a prison cell for years on a false charge. David was anointed king as a boy and then spent years running for his life in caves before he ever sat on a throne. And even the Lord himself spent thirty years in obscurity, working in a carpenter's shop in a town so unremarkable that people asked whether anything good could come out of it, before three years of public ministry. Thirty years of ordinary Tuesdays. The Son of God made tables. He sanded joints and matched grain and built things that some Galilean family used for a generation and then burned for firewood, and not one of those tables survives, and not one of those days is recorded, and they were not wasted, because the hidden years are not the waiting room before the real life. They are the real life. We would have told him he was wasting his gifts and needed to scale up.

And that is exactly the temptation I want to name, because I think it is the great one of this particular moment, with all our anxiety about decline and all our hunger for the method that will turn it around. The temptation is to despise the ordinary. To grow contemptuous of the slow, hidden, unspectacular faithfulness that the building actually rises on, because it does not move the numbers fast enough to soothe our fear. We want the revival. We want the surge. We want to see something happen, now, visibly, that we can point to and measure and put in the report and post about. And in our hunger for the spectacular we walk right past the actual work of God, which is happening quietly, all around us, in people who will never be on a stage, at a pace that no dashboard can detect.

Now somebody is going to push back here, and it is a fair push, so let me take it head on. Are you saying we should not want growth? Are you baptizing decline and calling our shrinking churches faithful just because they are small? No. I am not. I have no interest in dressing up failure as faithfulness, and there is a version of this chapter that does exactly that, that comforts dying churches by telling them their death is a kind of holiness, and I despise that version because it is a lie that lets people quit while feeling righteous about it. The fields are white to harvest and the laborers are few and a church that does not care whether anyone is saved has lost the plot entirely. So hear me carefully. I am not against the harvest. I am against the impatience that uproots the seed to check on it. I am not against fruit. I am against measuring the tree every morning and despairing when the leaves have not changed overnight. The point is not that results do not matter. The point is that results are God's to give and ours to wait for, and the waiting is the test, and most of us fail it not by aiming too low but by quitting too soon.

There is a second objection underneath that one, and it is harder, and I have felt it in my own chest in the small hours, so I am not going to pretend it away. It goes like this. How do I tell the difference between faithful endurance and stubborn refusal to admit the thing is over? Between the farmer waiting on a hidden harvest and the fool watering a field that has plainly gone to salt? It is a real question, and there is no formula that answers it cleanly, which is why we need the whole counsel of God and a few honest friends and not a slogan. But I will tell you what I have come to. Faithfulness is measured by obedience, not by outcome. The question is never first whether it is working. The question is first whether God has actually called you to this work, in this place, with these people, and whether you are doing it the way he asked, with love, with integrity, with prayer. If the answer is yes, then the absence of visible result is not your verdict to render. It is his account to keep. There is a kind of quitting that is wisdom, hearing God release you to a new field, and there is a kind of quitting that is simply fatigue dressed up as discernment, and the test, most of the time, is brutally simple. Are you leaving because God has clearly sent you elsewhere, or are you leaving because you are tired and you cannot see results and you want out? I have lied to myself about that distinction more than once, and it took friends who loved me enough to call it what it was.

Eugene Peterson spent his life resisting this, and his whole pastoral vision was a long argument for the ordinary against the spectacular. He took that phrase from Nietzsche, a long obedience in the same direction, and built a ministry on it, and refused, again and again, the pressure to turn the pastorate into a performance or the church into a corporation chasing growth. He wrote about the pastor's vocation as something closer to a farmer's than a CEO's, deeply local, deeply slow, attentive to particular people and particular places over long stretches of time, suspicious of anything that promised quick results, because he had learned that the soul does not grow quickly and you cannot rush a harvest. He stayed in one congregation for decades when he could have gone anywhere, and he came to see that the staying was the point, that the slow accumulation of ordinary days in one place with one people was not a failure to scale up but the actual shape of pastoral faithfulness. The farmer does not stand over the field shouting. He does not yank the corn upward to speed it along. He plows, he plants, he waters, he waits, and he sleeps while it grows in a dark he is not permitted to watch. We have not honored that vision. We have honored the men who built big things fast, and some of them built whitewashed tombs, and some of them burned out, and some of them fell, and the quiet farmer-pastors who stayed and stayed and stayed have mostly gone unnoticed, which is exactly how they would have wanted it, and exactly the problem.

There is a moment in the life of Jesus that I do not think we read often enough, because it is so quiet we slide right over it on the way to the miracles. Before he chose the twelve, before any of the public work that fills the gospels, Luke tells us that thirty years passed in which the only thing recorded is that he "increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man" (Luke 2:52). One verse for thirty years. And then between that verse and the next thing we know about him stand three decades of a workshop in Nazareth, a town small enough and poor enough that Nathanael could ask, with real contempt, whether anything good could come out of it. The eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made, spent the overwhelming majority of his earthly life doing nothing the world would record. Sweeping shavings off a floor. Settling the legs of a table so it would not rock. Eating supper with his mother. Going to synagogue on the same sabbath he had gone to the week before. If thirty silent years in a carpenter's shop were not beneath the dignity of the Son of God, then your ordinary Tuesday is not beneath yours, and the restless contempt you feel for your own hidden, unremarkable obedience is a contempt you would have aimed straight at him.

There is a verse that has become a kind of anchor for me in the gray seasons, when I cannot see any visible result and the temptation to chase something more exciting is strong. Paul tells the Galatians, "let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not" (Galatians 6:9). Look at the structure of that promise, because everything is in the structure. The reaping is real. It is coming. In due season we shall reap, that part is a guarantee, not a maybe. But the reaping is on God's timeline, in due season, not ours, and the entire condition placed on us is the negative one. If we faint not. The promise is not that we will see the harvest soon, or that we will feel the harvest coming, or that the work will be exciting. The promise is that the harvest is real and it is coming, and the only thing that can rob us of it is fainting, quitting, giving up on the ordinary work because it felt like nothing was happening. The great enemy of the long faithfulness is not failure. It is weariness. It is the slow erosion of resolve that comes from doing the right thing for years with no visible reward, until one day you simply cannot bring yourself to do it anymore. Notice that word, faint. It is not the language of the battlefield, of being struck down by an enemy. It is the language of the long march, of the runner whose legs simply give out in mile twenty because there was no enemy at all, only distance. That is how most Christians fall. Not in a great moral collapse that makes the news. They just slow down, and then they stop, and one Tuesday they do not get up at five anymore, and no one notices, least of all them. And against that erosion, the only weapon is the conviction that the reaping is real even when it is invisible, that the seed is growing underground while the farmer sleeps, that the building is rising even on the Tuesdays when nothing seems to move.

I have wanted to quit more times than I would admit from a pulpit, and let me tell on myself, because this book is no good if I keep playing the man who has it figured out. There have been seasons when the ordinary work felt utterly pointless, when I preached to people who did not seem to change, prayed prayers that seemed to hit the ceiling, poured years into a congregation and could not see that any of it had made a particle of difference, and the thought came, more than once, that I should go do something that produced a visible result, something where my effort connected to an outcome I could actually see. I have sat in the office after a Sunday that took everything out of me and counted the cars in the lot and felt the number land in my stomach like a verdict on my life. I have looked at men I came up with who chose other work, who can point at a building they built or a number they hit or a deal they closed, and I have felt the cheap and bitter envy of a man who plants seed he is not allowed to dig up. And what kept me, when anything kept me, was not a feeling. It was the conviction underneath the feeling, that the building rises on Tuesdays, that the reaping is real and coming in due season, that the seed grows in a hiddenness I am not permitted to see into, and that my one job is not to produce the harvest but to keep from fainting. To show up again. To plant again. To preach again to the people who do not seem to change, and trust that the changing is happening underground, slowly, in a soil I cannot inspect.

And here is what I have found, on the rare occasions I have been allowed to see it. Sometimes, years later, you find out the building was rising the whole time. The young man who never seemed to listen, who sat in the back with his arms crossed and his phone out, comes back at forty and tells you that one sermon, a sermon you do not even remember preaching, a Sunday you would have counted as a failure, saved his life in a hotel room you never knew he was sitting in. The woman you visited faithfully for years, who never said much, who you half wondered if you were wasting your afternoons on, dies, and her daughter pulls you aside at the funeral and tells you, with her voice breaking, that those visits were the thing that kept her mother's faith alive in the dark at the end, that her mother counted the days until you came. The seed you planted and forgot about, that you were sure had died in the ground, comes up in a season you are not even there to see. It does not happen often, and it is not supposed to, because if it happened often we would start working for the sight of it instead of out of faithfulness to God, and the whole thing would curdle into performance. But it happens just often enough to confirm what we are asked to believe without seeing, that the long faithfulness is not wasted, that the ordinary Tuesdays are the building going up, course by hidden course, and that the God who sees in secret is keeping a far more accurate account than any of our dashboards ever could.

I think this is also why the New Testament keeps reaching for the slowest images it can find when it wants to describe how God grows a person or a church. Not an explosion. Not a flash flood. A farmer, a vineyard, a field of wheat, a seed, a tree planted by water that brings forth its fruit in its season and whose leaf does not wither. Even the kingdom itself, when Jesus reaches for a picture of it, comes out as a mustard seed and a little leaven worked quietly through three measures of meal, the smallest and most hidden things, doing their work where no eye can follow. There is a reason for that, and I do not think it is an accident of an agricultural age that we have outgrown. It is that the things God most wants to grow in us, and in his church, are precisely the things that cannot be rushed. You can manufacture a crowd in a weekend. You cannot manufacture a saint. You can engineer a spike in attendance. You cannot engineer the slow, deep, costly formation of a person who has learned, over forty years of ordinary obedience, to love his enemies and forgive his brother and hold his tongue and trust God in the dark. That kind of fruit comes only in due season, on a timeline you do not control, in a hiddenness you are not allowed to inspect, and the whole agricultural vocabulary of Scripture exists to teach us patience with a God who works that way on purpose.

So do not despise your ordinary Tuesdays. Do not measure the building by what you can see rising this week. Do not let the hunger for the spectacular talk you out of the slow, hidden, faithful work that is the actual substance of the church's life and the actual shape of the cross. Plant your seed. Show up again. Preach again, pray again, forgive again, love the same difficult people one more time. Refuse to faint. The reaping is real, and it is coming, in due season, and the only thing that can cost it to you is quitting before the harvest you were never promised to see in advance.

The building rises on a thousand ordinary Tuesdays, and most of them will feel like nothing is happening.
chapters.verdict: The building rises on a thousand ordinary Tuesdays, and most of them will feel like nothing is happening.
reflect: Are you more drawn to the spectacular than to the faithful, and what has that cost you?
What ordinary, unglamorous work has God called you to that you keep waiting to graduate out of?
Could you serve faithfully for decades without ever seeing a visible result, and if not, why not?

chapters.title: Who Will Build It Next
chapters.summary: The unfinished church depends on the handing-on of faith to the next generation, and the present crisis is in large part a crisis of transmission, of one generation failing to give the faith to the next in a form they can carry. The building rises only as it is handed on.
chapters.body:
Every generation of the church is, at most, one generation from extinction, and that is not a slogan, it is a plain mathematical fact, and it is the thing I lie awake thinking about more than declining attendance or cultural hostility or any of the rest of it.

The building rises only as it is handed on. There is no other mechanism. The faith is not in the genes. It is not in the water. It is not transmitted automatically by being born into a Christian home or a Christian country, which is precisely the lie Christendom told us for so long that we believed it without examining it. The faith is handed, deliberately, from one generation to the next, person to person, and if any single generation fails to hand it on, the chain breaks, and the building stops, not because God's promise failed but because the human work of transmission failed, and God has, in his strange humility, made the rising of the church dependent on that human work. He builds it. And he builds it through people handing the faith to people, which means that the question of who will build it next is not a side issue. It is the issue.

Let me put a number on the fear, because numbers have a way of making a vague dread into a thing you can actually look at. A man comes to faith at thirty. He has, if God is kind, fifty more years. In those fifty years he will sit in church somewhere around two thousand five hundred times. He will hear thousands of prayers, hundreds of sermons, sing the same hymns until he could sing them in his sleep. And at the end of all of that, here is the only question that determines whether his fifty years added a single course to the building or merely warmed a pew. Did anyone receive the faith from him? Did he hand it on, intact, to someone who could carry it after he was gone? Because if not, then the whole thing stops at his grave, no matter how many sermons he absorbed, no matter how full his Sundays were. He was a link, and the chain ran into him, and it did not run out the other side, and a link that only receives is not a link at all. It is a dead end with a Bible.

I have come to believe that the crisis the Western church is in is, in large part, a crisis of transmission. We did not fail, mostly, to believe. Plenty of the parents whose children have left the faith believed it themselves, sincerely, deeply. What we failed to do, in vast numbers, was hand it on in a form the next generation could actually carry. We handed them a Christianity that was tangled up with a culture that was passing away, so that when the culture went, the faith went with it, because we had glued the two together and never taught our children to tell them apart. We handed them a faith of rules without reasons, of behavior without belief, of go to church because that is what we do, without ever giving them the substance underneath that could survive the question why. I have sat across kitchen tables from broken parents, more times than I can count, who cannot understand what happened. We raised them in it, they say. We never missed a Sunday. We did everything right. And I have learned to ask, gently, what their dinner conversations sounded like, what their children saw when the church doors closed and the family was alone, whether the faith was ever talked about as a true thing about the world or only enforced as a rule of the house. And too often the honest answer is that the children got the rules and the schedule and the disapproval, and never once saw the parent on his knees, never once heard the parent wrestle out loud with a hard question, never once watched the faith cost the parent anything real. They got the husk. We were shocked when they set it down, as if a faith we had never really given them in the first place should have held.

There is a passage in the book of Judges that has frightened me since the first time I read it closely, and I think every parent and every pastor should be made to sit with it. After Joshua, after the whole generation that had seen God split the sea and bring the walls of Jericho down, the text says this. "And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the Lord, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel" (Judges 2:10). Read that slowly, because it is the most efficient description of catastrophe in the entire Bible. One generation saw. The next generation, the very children of the ones who saw, knew not the Lord. It did not take five hundred years. It did not take a hostile empire or a great persecution or a clever heresy. It took one failed handoff. The mighty men who had walked through the parted water did not get the works of God from their own ears into their own children's hearts, and the chain snapped in a single generation, in the very house of the people who had seen the most. That is how fast it goes. That is how thin the thread is. And it tells me that the question of transmission is not a slow background worry. It is a one-generation emergency, always, in every age, including the comfortable ones, especially the comfortable ones, because comfort is exactly the soil in which a generation stops bothering to tell its children what God has done.

The Bible takes the handing-on with a seriousness we have lost. Listen to the command God gives Israel, the great central command of how the faith is to survive across generations. "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Notice it starts in the parent's own heart, first, these words shall be in thine heart, because you cannot hand on what you do not actually possess, and a generation of parents handing on a faith they themselves held only nominally is exactly how we got here. And then notice the saturation of it. Sitting, walking, lying down, rising up. That is not a religious schedule. That is the whole of an ordinary day, dawn to dark, every waking hour. It is the faith talked about in the truck on the way to school and at the dinner table and in the dark at bedtime when the child asks the question children ask, why did Grandma have to die. Not a program. Not an hour on Sunday outsourced to professionals. The whole texture of ordinary life, soaked in the faith, talked about constantly, modeled relentlessly, so that the child absorbs it not as a subject they are taught but as the air they breathe and the world they live in. We have largely abandoned that model. We outsourced the faith of our children to the youth group, to the Christian school, to the professionals, the way we outsource everything, and the professionals, however gifted, cannot do what the saturated home was designed to do, and was commanded to do, and the results are in. I say this as a man who runs a church with a youth program and believes in it. But I have watched too many parents drop their kids at the door on Wednesday night as though they had now discharged the duty, as though faith were a thing you could subcontract, and it cannot be, it never could, the command was given to the parent and there is no clause that lets him hire it out.

Paul gives us the picture of how it is supposed to run, in a single dense verse to Timothy, and I want you to count the generations in it. "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2). Count them. Paul, to Timothy, to faithful men, who teach others also. Four generations of transmission in one sentence. Paul received it, handed it to Timothy, Timothy is to hand it to faithful men, those faithful men are to hand it to others, and so on, down the centuries, all the way to whoever handed it to you, all the way to whoever you are handing it to now.
