And notice when Paul wrote it. He was in a Roman prison at the end of his life, with his execution close enough that he could feel it, the second letter to Timothy, his last words on record. He is not building an empire. He is not chasing a crowd. He is a dying man making sure the baton gets into the next hand before his own hand goes cold. That is the whole mechanism of the church's survival across two thousand years, that single relay, run faithfully, link after link, and never once allowed to break, no matter what empire rose or fell or what culture turned hostile. The building rises as the faith is handed on. It stops where the handing stops.

And here is what I want to press on you, gently but with everything I have, because I think it is the most practical thing in this whole book. You are a link in that relay, right now, whether you have accepted it or not. You received the faith from someone. Maybe a parent, maybe a grandmother, maybe a friend, maybe a stranger who handed you a book or sat with you in a hard hour. Somebody, somewhere up the chain, did the work of handing it to you, and most likely they are not famous and you may be the only person who still remembers their name, and the building rose, in you, because they did not let the relay drop on their leg of it. And now the baton is in your hand. And the only question that finally matters about your leg of the race is whether you hand it on, by name, to someone, before you set it down for the last time.

Let me make the relay visible to you, because I think we lose the wonder of it by living too close to it. Sit in any church on a given Sunday and look at the gray heads in the pews. There is a man who learned the faith from a grandmother who learned it from a circuit-riding preacher who can no longer be named. There is a woman whose mother knelt by her bed every night of her childhood, whose mother had it from a Sunday school teacher in a coal town, whose teacher had it from a missionary, and back and back the line runs, every link a real person with a real name once, most of them now forgotten by everyone alive. Run the chain back far enough and it does not stop at a denomination or a country or a century. It runs back through the Reformers who recovered it, through the monks who copied it out by candlelight when the lights of the old world went dark, through the martyrs of the early centuries who would not deny it to the lions, all the way back to a fisherman standing in front of a rock face full of dead gods, hearing a carpenter say that he would build his church. Two thousand years. Thousands of handoffs. Run faithfully, link after link, never once dropped long enough to break, until the baton arrived, improbably, in your own hand. When you feel the weight of that, the question stops being academic.

Now think about how thin it has gotten in one or two generations of Christendom's slow rot. There are families in my own town where the grandmother prayed, the mother attended out of habit, and the grandchildren have never once been told that God is real. Three generations from a living faith to a closed door, not because anyone rebelled, not because anyone argued their way out, but because each link held a little less tightly than the one before, and the heat slowly leaked out of the thing, until the grandchildren inherited a vague respect for a religion nobody in the house actually believed. That is not the devil's masterpiece. It is just neglect. It is the relay dropped not in defiance but in distraction, by people who assumed it would carry itself, who thought the faith was in the family the way the family name was, and never noticed it slipping until it was already on the ground.

I want to make this concrete, because it is too easy to keep it abstract and feel like we have done something. To whom are you actively handing on the faith, by name, right now? Not the church in general. Not the next generation as a vague category we are all worried about. A name. A specific person, younger than you in the faith, into whom you are deliberately pouring what you have received. For most of us the honest answer is no one, and I want to sit in that with you rather than rush past it, because it is the crisis, not in the abstract but in our own hands. We have received much and we are handing on nothing, treating the next generation as a problem for the church to solve, a demographic to worry about, a youth ministry line item, rather than as the very thing we ourselves are personally responsible to build. And the objection comes fast. I am not a teacher. I am not gifted. I do not know enough, I would not know what to say. But the relay does not run on giftedness. It ran through fishermen and tax collectors. It runs on people who take a younger person by the name and walk with them and hand them, deliberately, over years, the faith they themselves received. You do not have to be eloquent. You have to be willing to be known, and to let someone watch you follow Jesus up close, in the ordinary, where it is not impressive, where you fail and repent and get up again, because that watching is the lesson, and you are more qualified to give it than you think and far less likely to give it than you should be.

I think often about the older men and women who built me, because I did not build myself, and I came to faith from atheism with nobody in my background to hand me anything. I was a broken link from the start, the chain did not run through my family to me. I was raised without a father, which means the first and most natural relay, the one God designed to run from a dad to his children, was simply not there for me, snapped before I ever knew it existed. And so the faith reached me sideways, through people who were not obligated to bother with an arrogant young ex-atheist with too many questions and too sharp a tongue. There were men who took me on, who answered the questions, who put up with the arrogance and waited for it to wear down, who did not flinch when I tried to argue them into a corner, who handed me what they had received from people I never met, who handed it to them from people none of us will know this side of the city. I am a link in a chain that stretches back two thousand years to a rock at Caesarea Philippi, and the only reason I am holding the baton at all is that a long line of mostly forgotten people refused to drop it on their leg, and somewhere in that line a man I had no claim on decided that a fatherless skeptic was worth his Tuesday afternoons. And the only thing that finally matters about my life and ministry, when it comes down to it, is whether I do the same, whether the chain runs through me to others, or whether it stops here, with a man who received much and handed on little.

And I want to be honest about how unspectacular the actual handing-on looks, because if you are waiting for a dramatic moment in which you solemnly pass the faith to someone, you will wait forever and hand on nothing. It almost never looks like that. It looks like a standing breakfast on Thursday mornings with a younger man, where mostly you talk about his job and his marriage and the score of the game, and only once in a while does anything you would call discipleship happen, and you drive home half the time wondering if you are wasting both your mornings. It looks like answering the same question about suffering for the fourth time without sighing. It looks like letting a young couple watch how you handle a phone call that brings bad news, because they happened to be in the room, and that unguarded minute taught them more about trusting God than any lesson you ever planned. The relay is not a ceremony. It is proximity over time. It is letting yourself be known closely enough, and long enough, by someone coming up behind you, that they catch the faith off your actual life, the way you catch a cold, by being near someone who has it. Which is humbling, because it means I cannot hand on what I do not have, and there is no faking it at that range. A man can preach a faith he does not live to a crowd of strangers for years. He cannot hand it to a young man who eats breakfast with him every week. The relay exposes you. That is the cost of it, and the reason so few are willing to run it.

So I am pouring my life, as best I can, into people whose names I could give you, and into five sons who did not ask to be the next link but are, and into a congregation full of young families I will not be here to see grow old. I think about my boys especially, because the relay that broke before it reached me does not have to break again, and that is a mercy I do not get over. They are watching me. Not my sermons, mostly. Me. They are watching whether the man who preaches the long faithfulness on Sunday is the same man at the breakfast table on Thursday, whether the faith is real enough to govern my temper and my phone and the way I treat their mother. That is the relay, run at home, in the only form a child can actually receive it, which is a life. And I will tell you what frightens me, as a man who grew up without a father and therefore had no map for how a Christian father does this. There were no Thursday mornings in my childhood. There was no man in the house teaching anything as we sat or walked or lay down or rose up. The chair was empty. So I am handing on a faith I never received from a father, in a role I had to learn with no example, which means I get it wrong constantly, lose my temper at the very sons I am supposed to be discipling, apologize more than I would like to admit, and start again the next morning. But the broken link can be repaired in the next generation. The chain that did not run to me can run through me. That is not a small hope. For a fatherless boy who came to God out of atheism, it is very nearly the whole of what I am for. Because the building rises only as it is handed on, and I would rather hand on the faith to a handful of people who actually carry it than gather a thousand who never receive it deeply enough to give it to anyone else. The numbers were never the point. The relay was the point. And a generation obsessed with the size of the crowd while failing to hand the baton to the next runner is a generation that will be the last to hold it, no matter how large the crowd was when they let it fall.

So do not leave this chapter as a worry about the youth in the abstract. Leave it with a name. Before you turn the page, think of one person, younger than you in years or in the faith, into whose life you could begin, this week, to pour what you yourself received. Not a program. A person. Call them. Ask them to breakfast. Open your life and let yourself be known up close. It will be ordinary, and unspectacular, and you will wonder more than once whether anything is happening, and you will be running the only race that has ever carried the faith from one century to the next. The building rose to you because someone, somewhere up the chain, refused to drop the baton on their leg of it. Whether it rises past you is now, quite literally, in your hands, and there is no one else the work has been given to.

A church that cannot hand on its faith is a building with no one left to raise the next course.

chapters.title: The Day the Scaffolding Comes Down
chapters.summary: One day the church will be finished, the scaffolding removed, the building revealed as the bride and the city it was always becoming. This final completion is the weight the whole vision rests on, and it gives the present labor its meaning and its end.
chapters.body:
There will be a day when the scaffolding comes down.

I have built this whole book on the image of an unfinished building, a church under construction, a project still rising, and I have leaned on it hard because I believe it is true to how Scripture actually pictures us. But I would be telling you only half the truth, and the less important half, if I left you on the construction site. Because the part that makes the unfinishedness bearable, the part that keeps the scaffolding from being a sentence of permanent incompleteness, is this. It does not go on forever. The construction is not eternal. There is a day, fixed in the purpose of God before the foundation of the world, when the last stone is set, the scaffolding is struck down and hauled away, the dust is washed off, and the building stands revealed at last as exactly what it was always becoming through all the long centuries of mud and noise. The church is unfinished now. It will not be unfinished then.

John saw that day, and he wrote it down for us, and I cannot read it without my throat tightening. After the long apocalypse, after the wars and the plagues and the fall of every false city that ever set itself up against God, he sees the church revealed in her finished glory at last. "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband" (Revelation 21:2). The bride. The city. Two images for one single reality, the church completed, the building finished, the long construction over at last. Sit with that pairing for a moment, because it is not random. A building is a thing you make. A bride is a person you love. And the church is both at once, which is why no merely architectural picture is ever enough, because you do not weep over a finished structure the way you weep at a wedding, and the day the scaffolding comes down is a wedding day, the long engagement of the whole of history finally ended, the bride brought home at last. And then the great voice from the throne declares what the whole finished building was always for, the entire point of every course of brick from the first one Peter spoke of to the last one God himself will set. "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God" (Revelation 21:3). That is it. That is the whole purpose of the building, going all the way back. A dwelling place for God among his people. That is what we have been building toward, in every hidden Tuesday and every ordinary act of love and every link in the long relay of faith. That is what all the scaffolding was always, finally, for.

And then comes the sentence that breaks me every single time I read it, the one I want carved somewhere I will see it every day. "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away" (Revelation 21:4). Look at the tenderness of it, because the picture is not grand here, it is small and close and almost unbearable. God does not send an angel to do this. He does not issue a decree about the abolition of grief from a distant throne. He comes near enough to touch a face. He wipes the tears away himself, with his own hand, one face at a time, the way you would wipe the tears from a child who has cried himself out and finally come home. The former things. All of it. Every bit of what this book has been about. The conflict in the church and the failures of its leaders. The scandals and the splits and the slow leak of the young out the back door. The decline and the despair and the empty pews. The funerals. The doubts. The cancer and the dead child and the marriage that did not make it. The long gray Tuesdays of faithfulness with nothing visible to show for them. The former things. Passed away. The scaffolding struck and hauled off, and the building standing in a glory that makes the whole long, mud-spattered, blood-stained, tear-soaked construction finally, completely make sense.

I have stood at a great many gravesides, and I want to tell you that this is the only thing I have ever had to say at one that was worth the saying. I have buried people I loved. I have buried children, which is a thing no one should have to do and a great many people have to do anyway, and I have stood at the edge of a small hole in the cold ground with parents who had run completely out of words, and I have learned that in that hour every clever thing a pastor knows turns to ash in his mouth, and only one thing stands. Not that it was God's plan, which the grieving rightly cannot bear to hear. Not that they are in a better place, which is too thin to hold the weight. Only this. That there is coming a day when the One who made them will wipe the tears from your face with his own hand, and the death that took them will itself be put to death, and the former things, this hole, this cold, this unspeakable Tuesday, will have passed away, and you will hold them again in a world that has been through the grave and come out where the grave has no more power. That is not a sentiment. It is either true or the whole thing is a cruel joke, and I have staked my life and my five sons and every funeral I have ever preached on its being true.

Now I have to say something to the reader who has gotten this far and is quietly wondering whether all of this is a beautiful way of not facing facts. Maybe you are a person of doubts, the way I once was, and a chapter about a city descending out of heaven sounds to you like exactly the kind of comfort frightened people invent because they cannot bear the dark. I respect that, more than you know, because I came to faith out of atheism and I did not get there by being talked into pretty things. So let me say it plainly. If this is not true, then it is the cruelest lie ever told, and we of all people are most to be pitied, and Paul says exactly that, in so many words, about the resurrection, and I love him for not flinching from it (1 Corinthians 15:19). I am not offering you a feeling. The whole weight of this rests on one event, in one place, on one morning, when a stone was rolled away from a tomb that everyone, including the disciples, fully expected to find occupied. The reason I can write about a finished city I will never see from here is that something has already come back from the far side of death and walked into a garden in a body that could eat fish and be touched, and that fact, if it is a fact, changes what we are allowed to hope for. The hope of the finished church is not a mood. It is a conclusion, drawn from an empty tomb, and it stands or falls on whether that tomb was actually empty, and I have bet my one life that it was.

I will not see that day from here, and I have made my peace with that, mostly, though not every day. Neither will you. This is the hard, clarifying truth I most want to leave you holding, because it is the one that orders everything else and sets you free. The building will not be finished in our lifetimes. We will lay our few courses of brick, and then we will die, the way every single generation of the church has laid its courses and died, two thousand years of crews come and gone, and the work will pass to others, and then to others after them, and on and on until the day God himself completes it with his own hand. We are not the generation that finishes the church. There is no such generation among the living, there never has been, and the proud delusion that we might be the ones, that the kingdom hangs on our success, has done enormous damage to enormous numbers of exhausted Christians. We are one crew among the centuries of crews. And our task is not to see the building done. Our task is to lay our few courses faithfully, well, in the dark and the mud, and then to hand the work on to the next crew and lie down.

I learned this, in the end, at the only place it can really be learned, which is a graveside. Some years into my ministry we buried an old man from our church, a man who had been a deacon for longer than I had been alive, who had set up the chairs and locked the doors and counted the offering and visited the sick for fifty years and never once stood on the platform or held a title anyone outside the building would recognize. There were not many people at his funeral. He had outlived most of his friends, which is its own quiet sorrow that nobody warns you about. And standing at the edge of that grave on a cold morning, watching them lower a man whose entire life had been poured, faithfully and almost invisibly, into a small church in a small town, I had the thought that has shaped me ever since. He died with the building unfinished. Of course he did. The pews he had set up ten thousand times were still being filled by people he would never meet, and the church he had given his life to was still, that very morning, only halfway up, scaffolding everywhere, the work nowhere near done. And he had laid down his tools and lain down in the ground without ever seeing the cathedral his hidden courses were holding up. For one cold minute that struck me as unbearably sad. And then it turned, the way the gospel turns things, and I saw it the other way. He had not failed to finish. He had been faithful to the end of his leg of the race, and the finishing was never his to do, and it never had been, and the One whose job it actually was had not died and had not quit and was, that very morning, still building. The old man had run his stretch and handed the work on, and the work went on without him, toward a day he would see after all, from the inside, raised.

That sounds like loss, and there is loss in it, I will not pretend there is not. There is something in us that wants to see it finished, that wants our work to be the work that completed the thing. But I have come to find it the deepest freedom the gospel offers to anyone who labors. Because if it were my job to finish the church, I would have no choice but to despair, since I cannot finish it, no one can, the thing is too large and I am far too small and my few years are far too short. But it is not my job to finish it. It never was. It is my job to lay my courses well and hand them on. The finishing belongs entirely to the one who said at the beginning that he would build it, and his arm is not shortened, and his timeline is not mine, and the building will stand in glory long after my name is forgotten by everyone but him. "He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). He will perform it. He. Not I. He will strike the scaffolding, on the day he alone has appointed, and the building will be his, finished, perfect, the dwelling of God with men.

I think often about the medieval cathedral builders, the ones who began cathedrals they knew with absolute certainty they would never live to see completed. Take the great cathedral at Cologne, in Germany. They laid its foundation stone in the year 1248, and they did not finish it until the year 1880. Six hundred and thirty years. For most of those centuries it stood half-built, a stump of a choir with a medieval crane rusting on top of an unfinished tower, a wooden arm sticking into the sky over the Rhine for generation after generation, a kind of standing joke about a thing that would never be done. And then, six centuries on, men who could not have imagined the world the first masons lived in finally set the last stone and the towers went up and the building was what it had always been meant to be. Think of the man who cut the foundation stone in 1248. He worked in faith. He cut his stone and set it true, knowing he would see the finished cathedral only from the grave, if at all, knowing his own children and his children's children and twenty generations after them would live and die with the thing still wrapped in scaffolding, trusting that those who came after him would carry the work on, and that one day, long after his bones were dust beneath the floor he helped lay, the thing would stand finished and full of light and worshippers, and his hidden courses down in the crypt would be holding up a glory he never saw. That is the church. That is exactly what we are. We are foundation-layers in a cathedral whose spire we will not see, laboring in faith toward a completion God has guaranteed and will bring about in his own time, not ours, and never asking to be the ones who set the final stone.

Jürgen Moltmann understood what this kind of hope does to a person who actually holds it, and he understood it because he found it in a place where every other kind of hope had been stripped away from him. He was a young German soldier, captured at the end of the war, held in prison camps for years, and it was there, with his country in ruins and his future erased and every earthly thing he might have hoped in turned to ash, that the Christian hope got hold of him. And out of that he came to argue, across a long life of writing, that hope is not the icing on Christian faith but the very air it breathes, that the church does not merely have a doctrine about the future but lives, now, out of a future that God has already secured and that comes toward us rather than receding from us. A church that hopes like that is not a church waiting nervously to see how things turn out. It is a church laboring in the certainty of how things turn out, which is an entirely different posture, the posture of people who already know the last page and are therefore free to work the middle ones without panic. The future is not a question mark we are anxiously hurrying toward. It is a promise hurrying toward us, and the difference between those two pictures is the difference between a church that frets and a church that builds.

Augustine knew the same thing, and he knew it watching an empire die. He wrote the City of God while Rome fell and the lights of his civilization went out one by one, and he refused to grieve it as the end of anything that finally mattered, because the city he belonged to was being built across the whole length of history by a builder who does not abandon what he begins, and its completion was certain because its architect does not fail. He died in the year 430 with the Vandals at the gates of his own city of Hippo, the world he had known collapsing around his deathbed, and he died unafraid, because he had fixed his eyes on a city no army could sack and no century could end. That is the hope I am after for you. Not optimism, which is just a guess about visible trends and dies the moment the trends turn. Hope, which is a settled confidence in a builder, and survives the fall of Rome, and survives the death of Christendom, and will survive whatever your own gray decade is doing to your faith right now.

And here is the final weight, the one thing above all others I want you to carry out of this book and keep. We will not see the building finished from here. But we will be in it when it is. That is the part the cathedral image misses, and that the gospel supplies, and it changes everything. The medieval mason who died with his cathedral half-built never saw it finished and never knelt in it complete. His story ended in the crypt, under the floor, in the dark. But ours does not. Because the church is not only the building we are building. The church is also the living stones, and the living stones are raised. We do not merely contribute our small labor to the temple and then perish into the dust, our part done, ourselves discarded. We are raised. We are gathered. We are present, in our own raised and glorified bodies, on the day the scaffolding comes down. The very same resurrection that completes the building includes the builders. Do you understand what that means? The man who cut the stone in 1248 will be there in 1880's completed glory and far beyond it, not as a memory carved into a plaque but in the flesh, raised, standing in the finished thing his hands began. You will not see the finished church from this life, that is true, and you must make your peace with it. But you will see it. You will stand in it. You will be a stone in the wall and a guest at the wedding and a citizen of the city on the day the dust is finally washed away and God moves in and every tear is wiped, by his own hand, from every eye, including yours.

One of the reflect questions at the head of this chapter asks whether, when the scaffolding comes down, you will be found laboring or merely lamenting, and I want to put real weight on it before I close, because it is the question this whole book has been walking toward. There are two ways to spend the years you are given on the unfinished site. You can spend them lamenting. You can stand in the mud with your arms crossed, grieving the garden you cannot return to, or fretting over the city you cannot build by Friday, or shaking your head at the wiring hanging out of the walls and the dust on everything and the crew that does not work the way you would work it, and you can be, in your own heart, mostly a critic of a building you were called to help raise. Or you can spend them laboring. You can pick up the one trowel God put in your hand and lay the one course he gave you to lay, badly some days, crooked some days, in the rain most days, and leave the architecture and the timeline and the finishing to the architect. The day the scaffolding comes down will find every one of us doing one of those two things. I have done my share of the lamenting, more than my share, and I can tell you it builds nothing and it costs you the only life you get. Be found laboring. When that day comes, and it is coming, you will not wish you had criticized the building more carefully. You will be glad of every crooked course your hands set true.

So lay your courses. Lay them in the dark, in the mud, in the long ordinary faithfulness that shows no visible progress and feels, most weeks, like nothing at all. Lay them at five in the morning over a cold cup of coffee with a list of names. Lay them in the little chairs with the four-year-olds, in the visits to the widow who never says much, in the marriage you keep choosing one more difficult year at a time, in the baton you press, by name, into a younger hand. Lay them in the seasons when the building seems to be coming down rather than going up, when the pews empty and the culture turns and your own heart grows cold. Lay them without the despair of the man who thinks he has to finish, and without the nostalgia of the man who keeps turning back toward a garden he can never reach, and without the frantic, exhausting pragmatism of the man who is convinced the future is his to engineer and his alone. Lay them in hope. The hope that holds the promise steady against all the evidence. The hope that lives from a future God has already guaranteed with an empty tomb. The hope of a building still rising, course by hidden course, under the hands of a builder who has never once, in all the long history of the world, failed to finish what he began.

He said he would build his church. He is building it right now, this morning, through people like you, who feel like rubble far more days than they feel like stone. He has not changed his mind. He has not laid down his tools. And one day, a day he has fixed and we cannot hasten and we cannot delay, he will strike the scaffolding, and the dust will settle, and the city will stand, and God will be with his people, and every tear will be wiped away, and the long unfinished work of two thousand years will be revealed as what it always quietly was beneath all the mud and noise and grief: a dwelling place for God, built by his own hand, and finished, at last.

We will not see the building finished. But it will be finished, and we will be in it.

What course of brick has God given you to lay, knowing you will not see the building done?
When the scaffolding comes down, will you be found laboring or merely lamenting?
